### Library entrance closure: Monday to Thursday

The library will remain open on its usual schedule while the pavement outside the east entrance is replaced from Monday through Thursday. The east entrance, which faces the bus shelter, will be closed to everyone during the work. Please use the west entrance, which faces the playground.

It has no steps, but one section has a temporary firm mat over uneven ground. The mat is on the route to the west entrance; the east entrance remains closed, including to wheelchair users. The bus shelter will remain available, but the direct path from it to the east entrance will be behind a temporary barrier.

During library opening hours, staff can meet visitors at the bus shelter and accompany them to the west entrance. If you would like this assistance, call the library desk before setting out. You can also request assistance on arrival by calling the number displayed at the shelter, but a staff member may not be available immediately. The library cannot provide transport around the building.

The returns slot beside the east entrance will also be inaccessible. Books due Monday through Thursday may be returned on Friday without a late charge, including books borrowed from another branch.

Heavy rain may delay the work. If the closure is extended, an updated notice will be posted at both entrances and at the bus shelter. The Friday return arrangement will remain in place unless the updated notice announces a further extension.

**Temporary closure of the east entrance, Monday to Thursday**

The east entrance to the neighborhood library will be closed from Monday through Thursday while the pavement immediately outside it is replaced. The east entrance is the one facing the bus shelter. The entrance facing the playground is the west entrance, which stays open. The library itself will keep its usual opening hours throughout.

During the work, the direct path between the bus shelter and the east entrance will be behind a temporary barrier. This is why the entrance has to close. The bus shelter itself stays in use, and you can still wait there as usual.

**Which route to use**

If you are coming from the playground side, use the west entrance as normal.

If you are coming from the bus shelter, follow the signed path along the south side of the building to the west entrance. This adds approximately 120 metres to your journey. The path has no steps, but one section crosses uneven ground under a temporary firm mat. Please note that the mat is on the route to the west entrance. The east entrance is closed to everyone during the work, including wheelchair users, and there is no step-free or other access through it.

**If you would like help with the route**

During library opening hours, staff can meet you at the bus shelter and accompany you along the path to the west entrance. If you would like this, call the library desk before you set out. You can also ask for it once you arrive, using the number displayed at the shelter, but a staff member may not be free to come straight away. Staff can walk with you only. We cannot provide transport around the building.

**Returning books**

The returns slot beside the east entrance will also be out of use during the closure. Any book due on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday of that week can be returned on Friday without a late charge. This applies to books borrowed from another branch as well as from this one.

**If the work takes longer**

Heavy rain may extend the work beyond Thursday. If that happens, an updated notice will be posted at both entrances and at the bus shelter. The Friday returns arrangement described above will stand unless that updated notice announces a further extension.

The east entrance to the neighborhood library, the one facing the bus shelter, will be closed to everyone from Monday through Thursday while the pavement outside it is replaced. The library will stay open on its usual schedule. The east entrance is not an alternative for wheelchair users, since it is closed to everyone during the work, and the mat is on the route to the west entrance.

You can also ask on arrival by using the number displayed at the shelter, but a staff member may not be available immediately. We cannot provide transport around the building.

The returns slot beside the east entrance will also be inaccessible. Books due Monday through Thursday, including books borrowed from another branch, may be returned on Friday without a late charge.

Heavy rain may make the work take longer. If it does, an updated notice will be posted at both entrances and at the shelter. The Friday return arrangement will stay in place unless the updated notice announces a further extension.

A drawing is a record of what we notice. One drawing can show where a patch of sunlight falls. It cannot show whether the patch changes position. In this booklet, we will watch the sunlight on our classroom floor and make drawings we can compare.

We will observe over three school days. Work with the same partner each day. Look at the beginning of the morning lesson and immediately after lunch. That gives you six observation spaces. Your drawings will record the position of the light you can see. They will not answer every question about why it is there.

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan. Write the time beside it. If part of the edge is fuzzy, mark that part with a dotted line. You have a pencil and a ruler. A ruler can help you draw a straight line. It cannot make a fuzzy edge sharp. If two groups draw the edge differently, compare what each group noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Sometimes there may be no patch to see. Write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave its floor plan unmarked. Yesterday’s patch belongs in yesterday’s drawing. Recording that no patch is visible counts as an observation. It does not give you a measurement of the patch’s position. The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds or record how thick they are.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern your observations support and one question that remains. If too few patches were visible to establish a pattern, say so. Explain which observations are missing.

There is no particular pattern you must discover. Your booklet needs to show what you could see and what you could not. A careful record of a patch nobody could see can be more useful than a confident drawing of where someone thinks it was.

Here is the rewritten introduction.

---

A drawing of light is a record of where the light was. It is not a record of why. This booklet asks you to notice one patch of sunlight on the classroom floor and to draw it honestly, six times, over three school days.

You will work with the same partner each day. You will look twice a day: once at the start of the morning lesson, and once as soon as you come back from lunch. One drawing cannot tell you whether the patch moves. It can only tell you where the patch was when you looked. Six drawings give the patch a chance to show you something. They still will not explain it.

Each time, draw the outline of the light on the printed floor plan and write the time beside it. Some edges will be sharp. Some will be fuzzy. Where the edge is fuzzy, use a dotted line for that part. Do not decide that the edge must really be sharp underneath. A pencil and a ruler are provided. The ruler is for straight lines. It cannot make a soft edge hard. If another group has drawn the edge differently, talk first about what each of you saw. Only then decide whether either drawing needs to change. Sometimes neither does.

Some days there will be no patch at all. Write "no patch visible" in the space for that observation and leave the map blank. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. A blank map with a note is a true observation. It is not a measurement of the patch's position, and your booklet should not pretend it is. The curtains will stay where they always are. The class will not control the clouds, and we will not record how thick they were.

At the end, lay all six observation spaces side by side with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern you can support with your drawings. Write one question that your drawings leave open. If too few patches showed up to support any pattern, say so, and name which observations are missing. You are not required to find a particular pattern. Nobody will be marked down for a cloudy week. A careful account of what you could not see is worth more than a confident drawing of a patch that nobody saw.

A drawing is a record of what you saw. For the next three school days, we will draw where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor. You will work with the same partner each day. You will make one drawing at the beginning of the morning lesson and another straight after lunch. One drawing cannot show whether the patch moves. Six drawings can. Remember what the drawings do and do not tell you. They show where the light was when you looked. They do not explain why it was there.

Each time, mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan and write the time beside it. Some edges will be fuzzy. Draw that part with a dotted line rather than deciding it must really be sharp. A pencil and ruler are provided. The ruler will make your lines straight, but it will not make a fuzzy edge any less fuzzy. If you notice that another group has drawn the edge differently from you, compare what each of you noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Some days there may be no patch at all. When that happens, write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave the map itself blank. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. A blank map with a note is still an observation. It is not a measurement of where the patch was. The curtains will stay where they usually are, but we will not control the clouds or record how thick they are.

At the end, look at all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern your drawings can support, and one question that is still open. If too few patches were visible to show a pattern, say so, and explain which observations are missing. You are not required to discover a particular pattern. A careful account of what could not be seen can be more useful than a confident account of a patch nobody saw.

# Introduction

A map is a choice about what to notice. This booklet asks you to watch a patch of sunlight on the classroom floor and record where it falls. You will do this over three school days, working with the same partner each day, and you will make observations at the start of the morning lesson and again just after lunch. Each day, you will make two observations, so six in total.

Repeating the activity matters. A single drawing cannot show whether the position of the light changes. What each drawing shows is where the light could be seen at that moment. It does not explain why the light is there, and it does not answer every question you might have about it.

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan and write the time beside it. If the edge is fuzzy, draw that part with a dotted line. You do not need to decide that the edge is sharp. A pencil and ruler are provided, but a ruler will not make a fuzzy edge clearer. If your group's edge differs from another group's, that is useful information. Compare what each group noticed before deciding whether either drawing should change.

Some days the light may not be visible. When that happens, write "no patch visible" in the space for that observation and leave the map unmarked. Do not draw where the patch was the day before. A day with no visible patch still counts as an observation. It does not, however, tell you the patch's position. The curtains will stay in their usual position, and the class will not control the clouds or record how thick they are, so some conditions will vary in ways we cannot measure.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern the observations support, and one question that remains open. If too few patches were visible to show a pattern, say so, and name the observations that are missing. You are not expected to find a particular pattern. An honest account of what could not be seen is often more useful than a confident account of a patch nobody observed.

# Watching the Light

A drawing is a choice about what to notice. In this booklet we will notice one thing: where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor.

## What we will do

The activity takes place over three school days. You will work with the same partner each day. You will make an observation at the beginning of the morning lesson and another immediately after lunch. That gives six observations in all.

We do this more than once because one drawing cannot show whether a position changes. It shows only where the light was, once. Several drawings can show more.

Our drawings will show where the light can be seen. They will not tell us why it is there. That is a different question, and the drawings do not answer it.

## How to mark the floor plan

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan. Write the time beside it.

Sometimes the edge of the light is fuzzy. Where it is, draw that part with a dotted line. Do not decide that the edge must be sharp just because a sharp line is easier to draw. A pencil and ruler are provided, but the ruler does not make a fuzzy edge less fuzzy. It is good for straight lines. It cannot tell you where the light ends.

You may find that another group has marked the edge differently. Do not change your drawing straight away, and do not tell them to change theirs. First compare what each of you noticed. Then decide whether either drawing needs to change.

## When there is no light

# Watching the Light

A drawing is a choice about what to notice. Ours will notice one thing: where the patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor. It will not tell us why the light is there. It is a good drawing for showing where the light can be seen, and a poor one for explaining everything else.

The activity runs over three school days. You will work with the same partner each day. You will observe twice a day, at the beginning of the morning lesson and straight after lunch. That gives six observations. We repeat the observation because one drawing cannot show whether the position changes. Several drawings can start to.

**Making a mark.** On the printed floor plan, draw the outline of the light and write the time beside it. If part of the edge is fuzzy, draw that part with a dotted line. Do not decide that it must be sharp. You have a pencil and a ruler, but the ruler cannot make a fuzzy edge less fuzzy. If another group has marked the edge differently, compare what you each noticed before deciding that either drawing needs to change.

**When there is no light.** Some days you may not see a patch. Write "no patch visible" in the space for that observation, and leave the map unmarked. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. A blank observation still counts as an observation. It does not count as a measurement of the patch's position. The curtains will stay where they usually are. The class will not control the clouds or record how thick they are.

**At the end.** With your partner, look across all six observation spaces. Write:

- one sentence about a pattern you can support, and
- one question that remains.

If too few patches were visible to show a pattern, say so, and name the observations that are missing. You do not have to discover any particular pattern. A careful account of what could not be observed can be more useful than a confident account of a patch nobody saw.

Welcome to the garden! Your assigned bed has the same number as your membership card. Some painted numbers have faded, so check the plan on the noticeboard if you are unsure. Please ask a steward before planting in a bed whose number you cannot read. The narrow strip beside the compost bins is planted collectively; it is not an unclaimed bed.

Tools with blue handles are shared. Please return them to the shed before you leave, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without blue handles may belong to another gardener, so do not assume they are shared. You will find the shed code on your membership card. Please close the door when you leave to keep rain off the lower shelves.

The watering rota covers the collective strip and the young fruit trees, but not individual beds—even those belonging to gardeners on the rota. If you will be away, you can arrange separately for another gardener to water your bed. Only add the arrangement to the noticeboard once they have agreed, so a request does not look like a job someone has accepted.

Weeds without seed heads can go into the green compost bay. Put weeds with seed heads into the covered brown bin. If you are unsure whether a plant has set seed, put it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This is simply a sorting precaution, not a judgment about anyone’s gardening.

Stewards are usually here on Saturday mornings. Check the noticeboard for the next session and any cancellation. We are glad you are here, and we would always rather answer a small question before planting than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else’s bed.

Welcome to the garden! We're glad you're here. This note covers the basics, and the stewards are always happy to help with anything it doesn't answer.

**Your bed**
Your assigned bed is marked with the number on your membership card. Some of the painted numbers have faded, so if you're unsure, check the plan on the noticeboard. That's the reliable guide. When you leave, close the door behind you, because rain reaches the lower shelves when it's left open.

Weeds without seed heads can go in the green compost bay. Weeds with seed heads go in the covered brown bin. If you can't tell whether a plant has set seed, put it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. That's just a sorting precaution, not a judgment on anyone's gardening.

**Getting help**
Stewards are usually around on Saturday mornings, and the noticeboard lists the next session and any cancellations. Please don't hesitate to ask. We'd much rather answer a small question before you plant than help move a thriving crop out of someone else's bed.

Welcome to the garden. We're glad you're here, and we'd rather answer a small question before you plant than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else's bed.

**Your bed and the shared strip**

Your assigned bed is marked with the number on your membership card. A few of the painted numbers have faded, so if you're unsure, the plan on the noticeboard is the reliable guide. If you still can't read a bed's number, please ask a steward before planting in it. The narrow strip beside the compost bins isn't an unclaimed bed: it is planted collectively and belongs to everyone.

**Tools and the shed**

Tools with a blue handle belong to the shared collection. Please return them to the shed before you leave, even if you plan to visit again later that evening. Tools without a blue handle may belong to another gardener, so don't assume they're shared. The shed code is on your membership card. Please close the door when you go, because rain reaches the lower shelves when it stands open.

**Watering**

The watering rota covers the collective strip and the young fruit trees. It doesn't cover individual beds, including those belonging to people who have signed up for the rota. If you'll be away, you can make a separate arrangement with another gardener. Please add it to the noticeboard only once they've agreed, so a request never looks like a job someone has accepted.

**Weeds and compost**

Weeds without seed heads can go in the green compost bay. Weeds with seed heads belong in the covered brown bin. If you can't tell whether a plant has set seed, put it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. It's simply a sorting precaution, not a judgment about anybody's gardening.

**Stewards**

Stewards are usually present on Saturday mornings. The noticeboard lists the next session and any cancellations, so check there first, and come and ask us anything.

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, a new option in the desktop application’s **Reading settings**. Turn it on to pause the application’s spoken image description when you move keyboard focus to another control. By default, descriptions continue speaking when focus moves, just as they did before.

When Pause on Focus is enabled, returning focus to the image does not automatically resume the description. Use the existing **Read Description** command to hear it again from the beginning. “Pause” means that speech stops while the saved description is kept; it does not mean you can resume from the word where it stopped. The setting does not change the descriptions themselves.

Pause on Focus works with both automatic descriptions and descriptions you request manually. It does not turn automatic descriptions on. If you previously turned automatic image descriptions off, they will remain off after the update, and you can still use Pause on Focus for manually requested descriptions.

The option controls only image descriptions spoken by the application. A separate screen reader controls its own speech, even when describing the same image, so moving focus may not stop all speech if both are active. Pause on Focus also has no effect on audio inside a video, which remains controlled by the video player. The option is available only on desktop; the mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

If a description continues after keyboard focus has visibly moved, please report it and include the action that moved focus. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, include that too—but you do not need to identify the source before reporting an issue. Knowing what action moved focus is more useful than receiving the contents of the image.

**New in this release: Pause on Focus**

This release adds a new option, Pause on Focus, to the Reading settings. It controls what happens to a spoken image description when you move keyboard focus to another control.

**What changes, and what stays the same**

Until now, a description that had started speaking kept going after focus moved on. That is still the default, so nothing changes unless you turn the new option on.

With Pause on Focus enabled, moving keyboard focus to a different control pauses the current description. Moving focus back to the image does not resume it. To hear the description again, use the existing Read Description command, which starts from the beginning.

The option is called "pause" because speech stops without discarding the saved description. It does not mean playback can pick up at the word where it stopped. The content of descriptions is not affected by this setting.

**What the option does not control**

Pause on Focus only applies to descriptions spoken by the application itself. Two other sources of speech are outside its reach:

- **A separate screen reader.** Speech from a screen reader is controlled by that reader, even when it is describing the same image. Turning on Pause on Focus will not necessarily silence all speech when focus moves.
- **Audio inside a video.** This remains controlled by the video player.

These distinctions matter most when more than one source of speech is active at the same time.

**How it works with your existing settings**

- If you have already turned off automatic image descriptions, they stay off after updating. Pause on Focus does not turn them back on.
- The option also pauses descriptions you request manually, so it is still useful with automatic descriptions disabled.
- Pause on Focus is available in the desktop application only. The mobile version keeps its current behavior.

**Reporting problems**

If a description keeps speaking after focus has visibly moved, please let us know. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or from a separate screen reader, include that, but you do not need to identify the source before reporting. The most helpful detail is the action that moved focus. Sending the contents of the image is not necessary.

# Pause on Focus: Stop Image Descriptions When You Move On

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, a new option in the Reading settings. It applies to spoken image descriptions during keyboard navigation.

## What changed

By default, a description that has started speaking keeps going when keyboard focus moves to another control. That behavior is unchanged. If you'd rather the description stop when you move on, turn on Pause on Focus.

## How Pause on Focus works

- **Moving focus to another control pauses the current image description.**
- **Returning focus to the image does not resume it.** To hear the description again, use the existing **Read Description** command. It starts again from the beginning.
- **"Pause" means the speech stops, not that it resumes later.** The saved description is kept, but playback cannot pick up at the word where it stopped.
- **Descriptions themselves are not changed.** This setting only affects playback.

## What this option does not control

Pause on Focus applies only to descriptions spoken by this application. Other speech may continue when focus moves:

- **Speech from a separate screen reader** is controlled by that reader, even when it describes the same image. Turning on this option may not stop all speech when focus moves.
- **Audio inside a video** is controlled by the video player and is not affected.

If you use two speech sources at once, keep these distinctions in mind.

## Automatic descriptions and availability

- If you already turned off automatic image descriptions, they remain off after updating. Pause on Focus does not turn them on.
- Pause on Focus can pause a description you requested manually, so it can still be useful with automatic descriptions turned off.
- This option is available in the **desktop application only**. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

## Reporting a problem

If a description keeps speaking after focus has visibly moved, please let us know. If you can tell whether the speech came from this application or a separate screen reader, include that. You don't need to determine the source to report the issue. The most helpful report includes the action that moved focus. You don't need to include the contents of the image.

## New option: Pause on Focus

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, a new option in **Reading settings** for people who navigate with a keyboard and hear spoken image descriptions.

### What it does

Until now, an image description that had started speaking kept going even after you moved keyboard focus to another control. That is still the default, so nothing changes unless you turn the option on.

With **Pause on Focus** turned on:

- **Moving focus away** from the image stops the description that is currently being spoken.
- **Moving focus back** to the image does not restart it automatically.
- **To hear it again**, use the existing **Read Description** command. The description plays again from the beginning.

We call it "pause" because the saved description is kept, not deleted. Playback does not pick up from the word where it stopped. The setting also doesn't change the content of any description.

### How it works with your existing settings

- **Automatic image descriptions:** If you previously turned these off, they stay off after you update. Pause on Focus does not turn them back on.
- **Descriptions you request manually:** Pause on Focus stops these too. It can be useful even if automatic descriptions are turned off.

### What it doesn't cover

Pause on Focus only controls descriptions that the application itself speaks. It does not affect:

- **A separate screen reader.** Your screen reader controls its own speech, even when it is talking about the same image. If you use one, some speech may continue after focus moves even with this option on.
- **Audio in videos.** The video player still controls this.

These differences matter most when two sources of speech are active at the same time.

### Where it's available

Pause on Focus is available in the **desktop application only**. The mobile version works the same way it did before.

### Reporting a problem

If a description keeps speaking after focus has visibly moved, please let us know. When you report it:

- **Tell us what moved focus**, such as a key press or command. This is more helpful than describing the image.
- **Tell us where the speech came from**, either the application or a separate screen reader, if you can tell. If you're not sure, please send the report anyway.

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, a new option for people who hear image descriptions while navigating with a keyboard.

Until now, once the application started speaking an image description, it kept speaking even after you moved keyboard focus to another control. **That is still the default.** Pause on Focus is for people who would rather have the description stop when they move on.

- **Moving keyboard focus to a different control pauses the image description** that is currently being spoken.

- **It works with descriptions you request yourself**, not only automatic ones.

**About the name:** "Pause" means the speech stops but the saved description is kept. It does not mean playback can pick up at the word where it stopped.

- **Video audio:** Sound inside a video is controlled by the video player and is not affected.

Keep these points in mind if you have more than one source of speech active at the same time.

If a description keeps playing after focus has visibly moved, please let us know. These details help most:

- **What you did to move focus.** This is more useful to us than sending the contents of the image.
- **Where the speech came from:** the application or a separate screen reader, if you can tell. You don't need to work this out before sending a report.

Until now, a description that had started speaking continued after keyboard focus moved to another control, and that is still the default. Pause on Focus is for people who want the description to stop when they move on. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

With Pause on Focus turned on, moving keyboard focus to a different control pauses the current image description. Returning focus to the image does not resume it automatically. To hear the description again, use the existing Read Description command, which plays it from the beginning. The option is called "pause" because the speech stops but the saved description is not deleted, not because playback can resume at the word where it stopped. The setting does not change the descriptions themselves.

Pause on Focus applies to descriptions spoken by the application. Speech from a separate screen reader is controlled by that screen reader, even when it is speaking about the same image. Turning on the option will therefore not necessarily stop all speech when focus moves. The option also has no effect on audio inside a video, which is still controlled by the video player. These differences may matter when two sources of speech are active.

If you turned off automatic image descriptions, they will still be off after you update, and Pause on Focus does not turn them on. The option can still be useful in that case, because it also pauses descriptions you request manually.

If a description keeps speaking after focus has visibly moved, please report it. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, include that, but you do not need to identify the source before reporting. Telling us which action moved focus is more useful than sending the contents of the image.

# New in this release: Pause on Focus

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, an option for people who use a keyboard to navigate and listen to spoken image descriptions. You'll find it in the **Reading** settings.

## What it does

By default, nothing changes. If an image description has started speaking and you move keyboard focus to another control, the description keeps going. Pause on Focus gives you the alternative.

With the option **turned on**:

- Moving keyboard focus to a different control pauses the image description that is speaking.
- Returning focus to the image does **not** resume it automatically.
- To hear the description again, use the existing **Read Description** command. It plays from the beginning.

"Pause" here means the speech stops and the saved description is kept. It does not mean playback picks up at the word where it stopped. The descriptions themselves are not changed.

## How it fits with your other settings

- **Automatic image descriptions:** If you previously turned these off, they stay off after updating. Pause on Focus does not turn them on.
- **Manually requested descriptions:** The option also pauses these, so it is useful even with automatic descriptions disabled.

## What it does not cover

Pause on Focus only affects descriptions spoken by this application. It will not necessarily stop all speech when focus moves:

- **Separate screen readers:** Speech from a screen reader is controlled by that screen reader, even when it is describing the same image.
- **Video audio:** Sound inside a video is controlled by the video player.

If two sources of speech are active at once, these limits may explain why you still hear something after focus moves.

## Availability

Pause on Focus is available in the **desktop application only**. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

## Reporting a problem

If a description keeps speaking after focus has visibly moved, please let us know. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or from a separate screen reader, include that, but you don't need to work it out before reporting. It helps most if you tell us which action moved focus. Please don't send the contents of the image.

response:
## Pause on Focus

This release adds an option called Pause on Focus to the Reading settings. It applies to spoken image descriptions when you navigate with a keyboard.

**Current behavior stays the default.** If a description has started speaking and you move keyboard focus to another control, the description keeps going. Pause on Focus is for people who would rather have it stop when they move on.

**With the option enabled**, moving keyboard focus to a different control pauses the current image description. Returning focus to the image does not resume it. To hear the description again, use the existing Read Description command, which starts from the beginning. "Pause" here means the speech stops and the saved description is kept. Playback cannot pick up at the word where it stopped. The option does not change the descriptions themselves.

**Automatic descriptions are unaffected.** If you turned them off earlier, they stay off after updating, and Pause on Focus does not turn them on. The option also pauses a description you request manually, so it is useful even with automatic descriptions disabled.

**What the option does not control:**
- Speech from a separate screen reader. That reader controls its own speech, even when it is describing the same image, so moving focus may not stop all speech.
- Audio inside a video, which stays under the video player's control.

This matters most when two sources of speech are active.

**Availability.** Pause on Focus is available in the desktop application only. The mobile version behaves as before.

**Reporting problems.** If a description keeps speaking after focus has visibly moved, please report it. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, include that, but you don't need to know before reporting. It is more useful to tell us what action moved focus than to send the contents of the image.

response:
The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before and four storms after a cover change. The three drains on the lower street received new covers; the three on the upper street retained their existing covers. Allocation was not random: crews selected the lower street because it had received more complaints.

Fixed cameras recorded the minutes water remained above a painted reference line at each drain during each storm. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero indicates no visible water above the line, not an absence of runoff. Across the twelve observations for each street in each period, mean duration fell from 18 to 10 minutes on the lower street and from 9 to 7 minutes on the upper street. The lower street therefore showed an eight-minute reduction, compared with a two-minute reduction on the upper street. This larger reduction can inform further study, but the comparison does not by itself establish an effect of the new covers.

Several factors limit interpretation. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. Neither street had a local gauge, and within-storm rainfall intensity was not measured. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the larger improvement on the lower street. Equally, cleaning cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets received it. These uncertainties, together with the nonrandom allocation of covers, leave the contribution of the cover change unresolved.

The camera records establish shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains during the later period. They do not establish increased drainage capacity, which was not directly measured, or fewer flooded properties, which was not measured at all. The pilot included no property-damage observations. Peak water depth could also change in a way that matters even if duration remained unchanged, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris quantities before cleaning. These measures would address some of the present ambiguities, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing conditions during these eight storms and assessing the practicality of the camera-based duration measure. Staff reported that every recording could be scored; whether different scorers assign the same duration remains untested.

response:
**Findings**

*What the pilot set out to test*

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover shortens the time water stands above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed across eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. The three drains on the lower street received new covers. The three drains on the upper street kept their existing covers. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so cover allocation was not random.

*What was measured*

A fixed camera at each drain recorded the number of minutes water remained above a painted reference line during each storm. A recorded duration of zero means no water was visible above the line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available for scoring.

Mean recorded duration, in minutes, across the twelve observations per street and period:

| Street | Before change | After change |
|---|---|---|
| Lower (covers changed) | 18 | 10 |
| Upper (covers retained) | 9 | 7 |

Durations fell at both sets of drains in the later period. The fall was larger on the street where covers were changed. That difference may help in deciding what to study next, but it does not by itself identify a cover effect.

*Why the comparison does not isolate a cover effect*

Two conditions changed alongside the covers, and neither can be separated from the cover change using the pilot's records.

- **Rainfall differed between periods.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier four. No gauge was installed on either street, and no within-storm intensity measurements exist. The pilot therefore cannot say how much of the shorter durations reflects lighter rain.
- **All six drains were cleaned on the day the covers were changed.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from every drain. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, the cleaning does not automatically explain why the lower street improved more. For the same reason, it cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets were cleaned. If the lower street had more debris to begin with, cleaning alone could account for part or all of the larger reduction there.

*What the measure does and does not capture*

The camera records show shorter durations above the reference line. This is a narrower result than it may appear.

- It is not a measurement of peak water depth. A change in peak depth could matter even where recorded duration did not change, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

The pilot does not establish whether the new cover shortens standing-water duration. The observed reduction on the lower street is consistent with a cover effect, with the effect of cleaning, with lighter rainfall, or with some combination. The design cannot distinguish among these.

One further uncertainty concerns the measure itself. Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. The pilot has not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the reliability of the camera-based measure is unconfirmed.

*Proposed follow-up*

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains, install local rainfall gauges to record intensity on each street, and record the quantity of debris at each drain before any cleaning. Those steps would address the allocation, rainfall, and cleaning ambiguities described above. Rotation alone would not make storms identical, so rainfall measurement would still be needed to interpret differences between periods.

The existing recordings retain two uses. They describe standing-water duration at these six drains across these eight storms. They also provide material for testing whether independent scorers produce consistent durations, which would establish whether the camera-based measure is practical for future work.

## Findings

### Design and allocation

The pilot compared two streets over eight storms: four before and four after a change to a different grate cover. Covers were changed at the three drains on the lower street. The three drains on the upper street kept their original covers and served as a comparison. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so the cover change was not randomly assigned, and the two streets may differ in ways the pilot did not measure.

### Measurement

A fixed camera recorded, for each drain during each storm, the number of minutes that water stood above a painted reference line. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero means no visible water above that line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. The measure therefore reflects only water above the reference line, not total inflow or drainage performance.

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. Scoring agreement between different scorers has not been tested, so the reliability of the duration measure is not yet established.

### Observed durations

On the lower street, the mean recorded duration across the twelve observations fell from 18 minutes before the cover change to 10 minutes after it. On the upper street, the mean fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. The reduction was larger on the street where covers were changed.

This comparison does not isolate a cover effect. The lower street had higher durations before the change, and the two streets were not assigned comparably. The difference in reductions is a description of the recordings, not an estimate of the cover's effect.

### Factors that could explain the change

Several factors were present during the same period and cannot be separated from the cover change with the current data:

- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. No gauge was installed on either street, and within-storm intensity was not measured, so local rainfall differences between streets and periods are unknown.
- **Cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because all six drains were cleaned, cleaning cannot account for the difference between the streets by itself. However, the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, so cleaning may still have interacted with the cover change in ways the pilot cannot detect.

### What was not measured

- Drainage capacity was not measured directly.
- Flooding of properties was not measured. The pilot has no property-damage observations.
- Peak water depth was not extracted from the images. A change in peak depth could matter even if recorded duration did not change, so the duration results do not establish whether depth changed.

The camera records show shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains in the later period. They do not establish the cause of that pattern, and they do not show any change in drainage capacity or flood outcomes.

### Unresolved questions

- Whether the cover change caused the reduction on the lower street, given non-random allocation and the differences in rainfall and cleaning.
- Whether the duration measure gives consistent results across different scorers.
- Whether changes in peak depth, drainage capacity, or flooding accompany the changes in duration.

### Proposed follow-up

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and leaf debris before cleaning. Rotation would address some of the present ambiguities, though it would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for testing whether the camera-based duration measure can be applied in practice.

## Findings

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water remained above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets during four storms before a cover change and four afterward. Covers changed at the three drains on the lower street; the upper street’s three drains kept their covers. Crews had received more complaints about the lower street, so cover allocation was not random.

A fixed camera recorded, for each drain and storm, the minutes water remained above a painted reference line. A recorded duration of zero means no visible water above the line, not that the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. On the lower street, the mean duration across the 12 observations fell from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes afterward. On the upper street, it fell from 9 to 7 minutes. The decrease was larger on the street where covers changed, but this comparison does not by itself show that the covers caused the difference.

Several factors complicate that comparison. The later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. There were no gauges on either street and no measurements of rainfall intensity within storms. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers changed. Because the initial amount of debris was not recorded, the cleaning cannot be ruled out as a factor in the larger decrease on the lower street, or dismissed because both streets were cleaned.

Recorded durations above the line fell in the later period at both sets of drains. The pilot did not measure drainage capacity, flooded properties, or property damage. Peak water depth was not extracted from the images; a change in peak depth could matter even if recorded duration stayed the same.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris before cleaning. These steps would address some of the current uncertainties, though rotating covers would not make storms identical. The existing recordings describe the eight observed storms and can help assess whether camera-based duration measurement is practical. Staff reported that every recording could be scored, but the pilot did not test whether different scorers would assign the same duration.

## Findings

### Pilot design

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water remains above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before a cover change and four storms after it. Covers were replaced at the three drains on the lower street; the three drains on the upper street kept their existing covers. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so the allocation of covers was not random.

### What was measured

For each drain in each storm, a fixed camera recorded the number of minutes during which water was visible above a painted reference line. A recorded duration of zero means that no water was visible above the line; it does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations (six drains × eight storms) were available.

| Street | Covers | Mean duration before change | Mean duration after change | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lower (3 drains) | Changed | 18 min | 10 min | −8 min |
| Upper (3 drains) | Unchanged | 9 min | 7 min | −2 min |

Each mean is based on twelve observations (three drains × four storms). Recorded duration fell on both streets in the later period, and the reduction was larger on the street where covers were changed.

The measurement captures duration above the reference line only. It does not measure:

- **Drainage capacity.** It was not measured directly, and shorter durations should not be read as evidence of increased capacity.
- **Flooding of properties.** It was not measured, and no property-damage observations were made during the pilot.
- **Peak water depth.** It was not extracted from the images. A change in peak depth could matter even where recorded duration did not change.

### Factors that limit interpretation

The larger reduction on the lower street does not by itself establish that the new covers caused it. Several conditions differed between periods or between streets:

- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the four earlier storms. No gauge was installed on either street, and there are no within-storm intensity measurements, so differences in local rainfall cannot be assessed.
- **Drain cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the initial quantity of leaves at each drain was not recorded, the cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the larger improvement on the lower street. Nor can it be dismissed merely because both streets were cleaned, since the streets may have started with different debris loads.
- **Non-random allocation.** The lower street was chosen on the basis of complaints and began with longer recorded durations (18 minutes against 9), so the two streets may not be comparable.

### Status of the measurement method

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. Whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording has not been tested.

### What remains unresolved

- Whether the new covers affect the duration of water above the pavement.
- How far lower rainfall and drain cleaning account for the reductions observed on both streets.
- Whether peak depth, drainage capacity or property flooding changed.
- Whether the camera-based duration measure is consistent across scorers.

### Possible follow-up

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains, record local rainfall intensity, and record debris before cleaning. That design would address some of the ambiguities above, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for further assessing whether the camera-based duration measure is practical, including a test of agreement between scorers.

## Findings

### Pilot design

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water remains above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during eight storms: four before a cover change and four after it. Covers were replaced at the three drains on the lower street. The three drains on the upper street kept their existing covers.

The lower street was chosen because crews had received more complaints there. Cover allocation was therefore not random, and the two streets may differ in ways that affect how their drains perform.

### What was measured

For each drain in each storm, a fixed camera recorded the number of minutes water stood above a painted reference line. All 48 drain-storm observations (six drains across eight storms) were available. A recorded duration of zero means no water was visible above the reference line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff.

This measure records duration above the line only. It is not a direct measure of drainage capacity. The pilot did not measure flooding of properties, and no property-damage observations were made. Peak water depth was not extracted from the images. A change in peak depth could matter even where recorded duration did not change, but the pilot cannot say whether depth changed.

### Observed durations

Mean recorded duration fell on both streets between the two periods. Each mean below covers 12 observations (three drains across four storms).

| Street | Covers | Before change | After change | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lower | Replaced | 18 min | 10 min | −8 min |
| Upper | Unchanged | 9 min | 7 min | −2 min |

The reduction was larger on the street where covers were replaced. The lower street also started from about twice the upper street's mean duration.

### Interpreting the difference between streets

The larger reduction on the lower street is consistent with a cover effect, but the pilot does not isolate one. Three factors limit interpretation.

- **Rainfall.** On average, the four later storms delivered less rain at the district gauge than the four earlier storms. This may contribute to the shorter durations on both streets. No gauge was installed on either street and no within-storm intensity was recorded. The pilot therefore cannot account for differences in rainfall between storms or between the two streets.
- **Cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. The amount of leaves before cleaning was not recorded, so the pilot cannot tell whether cleaning had a larger effect on one street than the other. Cleaning does not automatically explain the lower street's larger improvement. It also cannot be dismissed as irrelevant on the grounds that both streets were cleaned.
- **Street selection.** The lower street was selected on the basis of complaints, not at random, and started with longer durations. Differences between the streets that the pilot did not record may affect how much each one changed.

The difference between streets may help in deciding what to study next. On its own it does not identify a cover effect.

### Unresolved questions

- Whether the replacement cover shortens the time water stands above the reference line.
- How much of the reduction on either street reflects lighter rainfall or leaf clearing.
- Whether peak water depth changed.
- Whether drainage capacity changed, or whether there was any effect on flooding of properties.
- Whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording.

### Status of the duration measure

The existing recordings describe conditions at these six drains during these eight storms. They also show whether the camera-based duration measure is practical. Staff reported that every recording could be scored. Agreement between scorers has not been tested.

### Possible design for later study

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and the amount of debris present before cleaning. That would address some of the ambiguities described above. Rotation alone would not make storms identical.

The pilot made no observations of property damage. A change in peak water depth could matter even if the recorded duration did not change, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before and four storms after a cover change. Three drains on the lower street received new covers; three on the upper street retained their existing covers. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so allocation was not random.

A recorded duration of zero indicates no visible water above the line, rather than an absence of runoff. Across the 12 observations in each period on the lower street, mean duration fell from 18 to 10 minutes. On the upper street, it fell from 9 to 7 minutes. The lower street therefore recorded an eight-minute reduction, compared with a two-minute reduction on the upper street. This greater reduction provides a basis for further investigation but does not, by itself, identify an effect of the new covers.

Several factors limit interpretation. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the four earlier storms. Neither street had a local gauge, and within-storm rainfall intensity was not measured. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the initial quantities of leaves were not recorded, cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the greater improvement on the lower street. Nor can its contribution be dismissed because both streets were cleaned.

The measured finding is that water remained above the reference line for shorter durations at both sets of drains during the later storms. Drainage capacity was not directly measured, and the pilot collected no observations of flooded properties or property damage. Peak water depth was not extracted from the images; changes in peak depth could matter even where recorded duration remained unchanged.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris quantities before cleaning. These measures could address some of the current ambiguities, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing the eight observed storms and assessing the practicality of the camera-based duration measure. Staff reported that every recording could be scored, but agreement between different scorers has not been tested.

response:
# Findings

## What was measured

The pilot asked whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water stayed above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets during eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. The three drains on the lower street received the new covers. The three on the upper street kept their original covers. Cover allocation was not random. The lower street was chosen because crews had received more complaints there.

For each drain in each storm, a fixed camera recorded the minutes that water stood above a painted reference line. A duration of zero means no visible water above that line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations (6 drains × 8 storms) were available.

| Street | Cover change | Mean minutes above line, before (12 observations) | Mean minutes above line, after (12 observations) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lower | New covers | 18 | 10 | −8 |
| Upper | Original covers | 9 | 7 | −2 |

Recorded durations were shorter at both sets of drains in the later period, and the reduction was larger on the lower street. This is a description of the recordings. It may help in deciding what to study next, but it does not by itself identify an effect of the cover.

## What the measurements cannot explain

Several factors changed or varied alongside the covers, and the pilot cannot separate them:

- **Non-random allocation.** The lower street was selected because it had more complaints, and it also started with longer durations (18 minutes against 9). The two streets may differ in ways that affect both ponding and how they change over time, so the comparison between them is not a like-for-like test.
- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier four. Neither street had its own gauge, and the pilot has no within-storm intensity measurements. Lighter rain alone could produce shorter durations at both sets of drains, and we cannot say how much of the change it accounts for.
- **Simultaneous cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. The initial quantity of leaves was not recorded. We therefore cannot say that cleaning explains why the lower street improved more, and we cannot rule it out. Cleaning both streets does not make it irrelevant, because the lower street may have had more debris to remove.

## What was not measured

The camera records show shorter durations above the line. They should not be read as evidence of the following:

- **Drainage capacity.** It was not directly measured, so an increase in capacity is not established.
- **Flooded properties.** The pilot made no property-damage observations, and fewer flooded properties is not something these data can show.
- **Peak water depth.** A change in peak depth could matter even if duration did not change, but depth was not extracted from the images.

## Reliability of the duration measure

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. We have not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the consistency of the measure is unknown.

## Possible follow-up design

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and the amount of debris before cleaning. That would address some of the ambiguities above, though rotation alone would not make storms identical. Separately, a scorer-agreement check would show whether the camera-based duration measure is dependable.

## What the existing recordings can support

The recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for assessing whether camera-based duration is a practical measure. They do not establish that the new covers shortened ponding.

**Design and measurement**

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water stays above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets during four storms before a cover change and four storms after it. The covers were changed at the three drains on the lower street, and the three drains on the upper street kept theirs. Crews had received more complaints about the lower street, which is why it was chosen, so cover allocation was not random.

For each drain in each storm, a fixed camera recorded the minutes that water stood above a painted reference line. A duration of zero means no water was visible above the line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available.

**Observed durations**

On the lower street, the mean duration over the twelve observations fell from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes after. On the upper street it fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. The decline was larger on the street where covers were changed, which may help in deciding what to study next. Because allocation was not random, the comparison does not by itself identify an effect of the cover.

**Other explanations we cannot separate**

The district gauge recorded less rain on average in the four later storms than in the earlier four. Neither street had a gauge, and we have no within-storm intensity measurements, so lighter rain may account for part of the shorter durations on both streets. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. We did not record how many leaves had accumulated beforehand, so we cannot say whether cleaning contributed to the larger decline on the lower street. Cleaning both streets does not rule this out, since the amount removed may have differed between them.

**What the measurements do not show**

The recordings show shorter durations above the line at both sets of drains in the later period. They do not show increased drainage capacity, which we did not measure directly. They also say nothing about the number of flooded properties, which we did not measure at all, and the pilot has no property-damage observations. A change in peak water depth could matter even if the recorded duration did not change, but we did not extract peak depth from the images.

**Use of the existing recordings and follow-up**

The recordings can describe these eight storms and can be used to test whether the camera-based duration measure is practical. Staff reported that all recordings could be scored, but we have not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and the amount of debris before cleaning. This would address some of the ambiguities above, though rotation alone would not make the storms identical.

# Findings

## What was done

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets across eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. Covers were changed at the three drains on the lower street. The three drains on the upper street kept their existing covers. The lower street was chosen because crews had received more complaints there, so cover allocation was not random.

## What was measured

For each drain in each storm, a fixed camera recorded the minutes during which water was above a painted reference line. A duration of zero means no visible water above that line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations (six drains, eight storms) were available.

- **Lower street (changed covers):** mean duration across the twelve observations fell from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes afterward.
- **Upper street (unchanged covers):** mean duration fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes.

Recorded durations were therefore shorter at both sets of drains in the later period, and the fall was larger on the street where covers were changed.

The pilot did not measure drainage capacity, the number of flooded properties, or property damage. Peak water depth was not extracted from the images. A change in peak depth could matter even where recorded duration did not change, so the duration measure may not capture every relevant difference.

## What may explain the results, and what cannot yet be concluded

The larger fall on the lower street does not by itself identify a cover effect. Several factors are unresolved:

- **Allocation.** The lower street was selected because of complaint volume, not at random, so the two streets may differ in ways that affect drainage independently of the covers.
- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. This could account for some or all of the shorter durations at both streets. No gauge was installed on either street, and there are no within-storm intensity measurements, so the district figure cannot show what each street experienced.
- **Debris clearing.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the quantity of leaves beforehand was not recorded, we cannot say whether cleaning contributed more to the improvement on the lower street than on the upper street. Nor can it be set aside as irrelevant simply because both streets were cleaned: it may have contributed to the fall at both, and possibly unequally.

The comparison is therefore best read as a description of what happened in these eight storms, not as evidence of what the covers did. The shorter durations should also not be read as increased drainage capacity or as fewer flooded properties, since neither was measured.

## Measurement reliability

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. We have not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the consistency of the camera-based measure is unknown.

## Proposed follow-up

This section is a suggestion, not a finding. A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and the amount of debris before cleaning. This would address some of the ambiguities above, though rotation alone would not make storms identical. A test of agreement between scorers would show whether the duration measure is reliable.

The existing recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for assessing whether the camera-based duration measure is practical to apply.

response:
Returning keyboard focus to a cell puts the cursor back. Does it put the user back in context? This hypothetical study asked whether speaking the current row label after a note closes helps screen-reader users return to a table.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each of two versions. One spoke the row label when the note closed. The existing version returned focus to the same cell without the added cue. Six participants used the cue version first; six used the existing version first. The two task sets used different tables, and table assignments were reversed for half of each order group.

We timed the interval from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside that interval. We calculated each participant’s mean completion time for each version, then took the median of those twelve means. That median was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. The three-second gap is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test. These descriptive results do not establish a reliable speed benefit.

Did the cue help people feel oriented? Nine participants said it did in the closing interview. Four of those nine also described occasions when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. The same cue could help with orientation and interfere with listening. These reports describe participants’ experience; they are not a measured improvement in search performance.

The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype, but that does not tell us whether they wanted it enabled by default. We did not ask participants to choose a default.

The ordering scheme reduced the alignment between version and practice without removing every possible learning effect. A search strategy learned in the first task set may have carried into the second. The study also leaves two scope questions open: how less experienced users would respond, and how the cue would work in large tables. All participants were experienced, and the prototype tables fit within one screen.

For the product team, an orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. Added speech can also compete with ongoing speech. That competition needs attention even if a time difference eventually proves reliable. A next version could make the cue interruptible, then test whether users can get the location information without losing speech they still need. We did not implement or test that behavior here. The present timings cannot serve as evidence for it.

**Research summary: spoken row cue on note close**

Does a spoken row label help a screen-reader user get back to a table after reading a note? That was the question. We built a version that speaks the current row label when the note closes. The existing version returns keyboard focus to the same cell and says nothing extra.

**Who and how.** Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. The two task sets used different tables, and we reversed which table went with which version for half of each order group. We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note itself was not timed.

**What we measured.** The timing result is modest and should be read as a hint, not a finding.

| Measure | With cue | Without cue |
|---|---|---|
| Median of participant mean completion times | 38 s | 41 s |

That is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. The within-person picture:

| Personal mean time | Participants |
|---|---|
| Lower with cue | 7 |
| Higher with cue | 3 |
| Equal at recorded precision | 2 |

We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test. We logged time first because it was easy to log. Time was never the whole question.

**What people told us.** Nine of twelve said in the closing interview that the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described moments when the cue cut into speech they were still listening to. The remaining three reported no orientation benefit. None of the three asked us to remove the feature from the prototype. That is not the same as wanting it on by default. We did not ask anyone to choose a default, so we have no answer to that question.

**What this study cannot tell you.** The ordering scheme broke the full alignment of version and practice, but it did not remove every learning effect. Some participants may have learned a search strategy in the first task set and carried it into the second. We recruited only experienced users, so we do not know how less experienced users would respond. The tables fit on one screen in the prototype. Nothing here speaks to large tables.

**What it does suggest.** An orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. At the same time, added speech competed with speech the user was already hearing. That competition is a design problem in its own right. It stays a problem even if a time difference later proves reliable.

**Where the next test should go.** The obvious next version makes the cue interruptible. We did not build or test that behavior. The timings above are evidence about the uninterruptible cue only, and should not be presented as support for an interruptible one. The next study should ask what the user is attending to when the cue fires, and whether a cue they can cut off still orients them.

# Spoken Location Cue After Closing a Note: Research Summary

## Question

Does a spoken cue that announces the current row label help screen-reader users return to a table after they close a note? And if it does, what does the cue cost?

## Prototype and Design

We compared two versions:

- **Cue version:** When a note closes, the current row label is spoken.
- **Existing version:** Keyboard focus returns to the same cell, with no added cue.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. The two sets of tasks used different tables. For half of each order group, the assignment of tables to versions was reversed.

We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside the timed interval.

## Timing Results

- Median of participant-level mean completion times: **38 seconds** with the cue, **41 seconds** without it.
- This compares two medians of participant means. It is not the median of twelve within-person differences.
- Seven participants had a lower personal mean with the cue. Three had a higher mean. Two were equal at the recorded precision.
- We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test.

So the timing data points in one direction, but it does not establish a reliable difference. Seven of twelve is a split, not a pattern we can call settled.

## Orientation Feedback

In the closing interview, nine of twelve participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described moments when the cue interrupted speech they were still listening to.

The other three reported no orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype.

Two points to keep apart:

- Not asking for removal is not the same as wanting the cue on by default. Participants were not asked to choose a default, so we have no data on that.
- This is exploratory interview feedback. It is not a measured performance result.

## Limitations

- **Order effects:** Counterbalancing removed the complete alignment of version and practice, but not every learning effect. Some participants may have learned a search strategy in the first set of tasks that carried into the second.
- **Participants:** Less experienced users were not recruited. We don't know how they would respond.
- **Table size:** The tables fit on one screen in the prototype. The study says nothing about performance on large tables.

## Interpretation

The orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. The interruption reports show that added speech can compete with speech the user is already hearing. That competition is a design question regardless of whether the timing difference proves reliable.

## Next Steps
