**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) distinctly labeled garden plots in a circle. For \(0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) count the \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including neighbors across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), there is exactly one selection: the empty selection. The formula also gives \(1\), since
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now assume \(k\ge1\). We count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Each valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible marks, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) marked selections.

To count these another way, first choose the start plot in \(n\) ways. List the selected plots clockwise beginning there. Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, with \(g_k\) counting the gap back to the start. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots. The nonadjacency condition says that every gap is positive, and all the unselected plots belong to these gaps. Thus
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,\qquad g_i\ge1.
\]

To count these ordered gap tuples, arrange \(n-k\) objects in a row. Choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators. The resulting \(k\) nonempty blocks have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\), and each positive gap tuple determines exactly these separators. Hence there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
tuples. For \(k=1\), choosing no separators gives the one required block.

A start label and a gap tuple uniquely reconstruct a marked selection: moving clockwise, leave \(g_i\) plots unselected after selected plot \(i\), then reach the next selected plot. Because the gaps and selected plots total \(n\), this process makes exactly one circuit and returns to the start. Every gap is positive, including the final gap, so the selection is valid around the entire circle. Conversely, every marked selection gives exactly one such start and tuple.

Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly \(k\) times, once for each possible marked selected plot. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n(n-k-1)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is \(1\), which the argument allows. We never identify selections under rotation: the plot labels remain fixed throughout. \(\square\)

\[

\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,
\qquad g_i\ge 1.

\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}

gap tuples. For \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain the single group of size \(n-1\).

\[
k+(g_1+\cdots+g_k)=n
\]
plots, completing exactly one circuit. Conversely, each marked selection determines its start label and gap tuple. Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) removes the \(k\) possible marks on each selection. This is legitimate because \(k\ge 1\). Expanding the factorials then gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(n-k>0\) and \(n-2k\ge 0\). If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap has size one, which the counting includes. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have fixed, distinct labels. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For \(0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) count the \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including neighbors across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the empty selection is the only selection. The formula also gives \(1\), since \(\binom n0=1\).

Now assume \(k\ge1\). We count **marked selections**: valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Every valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible marks, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) marked selections.

We can also construct them by choosing a start and recording the gaps between selected plots. There are \(n\) choices for the start label. Beginning there and moving clockwise, number the selected plots \(1,\ldots,k\). Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, with the last gap returning to the start. For \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

The no-neighbor condition says that every gap is positive, including the last one. Since exactly \(n-k\) plots are unselected,
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,\qquad g_i\ge1.
\]
To count these ordered gap lists, arrange \(n-k\) objects in a row. Choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators. The resulting \(k\) nonempty groups have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\), and every allowed gap list determines exactly those separators. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap lists. When \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain the one possible gap list.

A start label and a gap list uniquely determine a marked selection: select the start, then move clockwise, leaving the prescribed number of unselected plots before each next selected plot. The gaps and selected plots together occupy
\[
(n-k)+k=n
\]
plots, so the final gap returns exactly to the start. Positivity of every gap ensures that no selected plots are neighbors. Conversely, every marked selection gives exactly one start label and one gap list.

Therefore,
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly \(k\) times, once for each possible mark, and \(k>0\). Hence
\[
A(n,k)=\frac nk\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Using the factorial definition of the binomial coefficients,
\[
\frac nk\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n(n-k-1)!}{k!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
Here \(n-2k\ge0\) and \(n-k>0\), so all expressions are defined.

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is \(1\), which is allowed. Throughout, the labels remain fixed: we remove only the choice of mark, and do not identify selections under rotation. \(\square\)

\[

\qquad g_i\ge 1.
\]

\[

\]

\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

\[

&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\

\end{aligned}

response:
**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two selected plots are neighbors, where the plot with the largest label and the plot with the smallest label count as neighbors because the circle closes. Then
$$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.$$

**Proof.**

*The case $k = 0$.* There is exactly one selection of zero plots, the empty selection, and it has no two neighboring plots selected because it has no plots at all. So $A(n,0) = 1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0} = 1$, which agrees. From now on assume $k \ge 1$.

*Stage 1: what we count instead of selections.* It is awkward to count valid selections directly, because the circle has no natural place to begin. So we count a slightly larger set. A **marked selection** is a valid $k$-element selection together with a choice of one of its selected plots, which we call the start. Let $P$ be the set of all marked selections.

Every valid selection has exactly $k$ selected plots, so it can be marked in exactly $k$ ways, and different selections give different marked selections. Grouping the elements of $P$ by their underlying selection therefore splits $P$ into $A(n,k)$ groups of exactly $k$ elements each. Hence
$$|P| = k \cdot A(n,k). \tag{1}$$

*Stage 2: describing a marked selection by its start and its gaps.* Fix a marked selection. Starting at the start plot and walking clockwise, we meet the selected plots in some order; call them plot $1$ (the start), plot $2$, and so on up to plot $k$. For each $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots we pass between selected plot $i$ and the next selected plot clockwise. For $i = k$ the "next" selected plot is plot $1$ again, so $g_k$ counts the unselected plots passed on the way back around to the start. When $k = 1$ there is only one gap, and $g_1 = n - 1$ counts every other plot on the circle.

Two facts about these gaps:

- **Each $g_i \ge 1$.** If some $g_i$ were $0$, then selected plot $i$ and the next selected plot would be adjacent on the circle, which the selection forbids. This applies to $g_k$ as well, and that is exactly where the circular boundary condition is used: the gap from plot $k$ back to plot $1$ may cross from the largest label to the smallest, and the rule that these are neighbors is what forces $g_k \ge 1$.
- **$g_1 + g_2 + \cdots + g_k = n - k$.** Walking once around the circle from the start, we pass every plot exactly once. The $k$ selected plots are not counted in any gap, and each of the $n - k$ unselected plots lies in exactly one gap, namely the gap after the most recent selected plot. So the gaps together account for all $n - k$ unselected plots.

So each marked selection yields a pair consisting of a start label (one of the $n$ plots) and an ordered $k$-tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n - k$.

*Stage 3: this description is reversible.* Conversely, suppose we are given a start label $s$ and an ordered $k$-tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n - k$. Place a selected plot at $s$, then move clockwise $g_1 + 1$ plots and select the plot there, then move clockwise $g_2 + 1$ more plots and select, and so on. The total distance traveled after all $k$ steps is
$$(g_1 + 1) + (g_2 + 1) + \cdots + (g_k + 1) = (n - k) + k = n,$$
which is exactly once around the circle, so the $k$-th step lands back on $s$ and no earlier step does (each partial sum is strictly between $0$ and $n$). Thus we have selected exactly $k$ distinct plots. Consecutive selected plots are separated by $g_i \ge 1$ unselected plots, including the final pair across the closing of the circle, so the selection is valid. Marking $s$ as the start gives a marked selection, and reading off its gaps returns exactly $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$, while reading off its start returns $s$.

So marked selections correspond exactly, one to one, with pairs (start label, gap tuple). Counting one set counts the other.

*Stage 4: counting the pairs.* The start label can be any of the $n$ plots. For a given start label, the allowed gap tuples are all ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers summing to $n - k$, and this collection does not depend on which start label was chosen. By the multiplication principle,
$$|P| = n \cdot (\text{number of ordered } k\text{-tuples of positive integers summing to } n-k). \tag{2}$$

To count these tuples, draw $n - k$ dots in a row. Between consecutive dots there are $n - k - 1$ spaces. Choose $k - 1$ of these spaces and draw a bar in each. The bars cut the row into $k$ blocks of dots, read left to right; each block contains at least one dot because bars occupy distinct spaces between dots, and the block sizes add to $n - k$. So each choice of $k - 1$ spaces gives a tuple of the required kind. Conversely, a tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ tells us to place bars after the $g_1$-th dot, after the $(g_1 + g_2)$-th dot, and so on; these are $k - 1$ distinct spaces, and they reproduce the tuple. So the tuples are in one-to-one correspondence with $(k-1)$-element subsets of a set of $n - k - 1$ spaces, and their number is
$$\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$
This requires $k - 1 \le n - k - 1$, that is $k \le n/2$, which is exactly our hypothesis. At the extreme $k = n/2$ (for even $n$) there is only one tuple, namely all gaps equal to $1$, and indeed $\binom{k-1}{k-1} = 1$; a selection with every gap equal to $1$ is allowed since no two selected plots touch.

*Stage 5: solving for $A(n,k)$.* Combining (1) and (2),
$$k \cdot A(n,k) = n \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$
Since $k \ge 1$, we may divide both sides by $k$. This division is legitimate precisely because of Stage 1: $P$ was split into $A(n,k)$ groups of equal size $k$, so $A(n,k)$ is the integer $|P|/k$. Thus
$$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

*Stage 6: matching the stated form.* Write both expressions in factorials. Note that $n - k \ge 1$ and $n - 2k \ge 0$, so all factorials below are defined. On one hand,
$$\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1} = \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!} = \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},$$
using $k \cdot (k-1)! = k!$. On the other hand,
$$\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k} = \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!} = \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},$$
using $(n-k)! = (n-k)\cdot(n-k-1)!$. The two are equal, which proves the claim.

*Remark on the circle.* No division by $n$ for rotations appears in this argument. The plots carry distinct fixed labels, so two selections that differ by rotating the circle are different selections and are meant to be counted separately. The circle enters only through the requirement that the final gap $g_k$, which wraps around to the start, be at least $1$. $\blacksquare$

*Counting marked selections another way.* Take a marked selection and walk clockwise around the circle from the start. We meet the $k$ selected plots in some order. Call the start selected plot $1$, the next selected plot we meet plot $2$, and so on up to plot $k$. For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between selected plot $i$ and the next selected plot clockwise. For $i = k$ the next selected plot is plot $1$ again, so $g_k$ counts the unselected plots between the last selected plot and the start, across the boundary. For $k=1$ there is only one selected plot, and $g_1 = n-1$ counts every other plot on the way around back to the start.

Two facts about the tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$:

- Each $g_i \ge 1$. If some $g_i$ were $0$, selected plot $i$ and the next selected plot would be neighbors, which the selection forbids. This applies to $g_k$ too, which is exactly the condition across the circular boundary.
- The $g_i$ sum to $n-k$. Walking once around the circle we pass every plot exactly once: the $k$ selected plots and the $g_1 + \dots + g_k$ unselected ones. So $k + g_1 + \dots + g_k = n$.

Conversely, suppose we are given a start label $s$ (one of the $n$ plots) and a tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$. We recover a marked selection: select plot $s$, move clockwise past $g_1$ plots and select the next one, move past $g_2$ plots and select the next one, and so on. After selecting the $k$-th plot and moving past $g_k$ more plots, we have passed $k + (n-k) = n$ plots in total and are back at $s$, so the construction closes up consistently. Every gap is at least $1$, so no two selected plots are neighbors, including the pair on either side of the boundary. Marking $s$ as the start gives a marked selection, and reading off its gaps returns the tuple we began with.

So marked selections correspond exactly to pairs (start label, gap tuple), and

$$
k \cdot A(n,k) = n \cdot (\text{number of tuples } (g_1,\dots,g_k) \text{ of positive integers with } g_1 + \dots + g_k = n-k).
$$

*Counting the gap tuples.* Draw $n-k$ dots in a row. Between consecutive dots there are $n-k-1$ spaces. Choose $k-1$ of these spaces and draw a bar in each. The bars cut the row into $k$ blocks of consecutive dots, each block nonempty because the bars sit in distinct spaces between dots. Reading the block sizes from left to right gives a tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n-k$. Conversely, such a tuple tells us where to put the bars: after the first $g_1$ dots, then after the next $g_2$ dots, and so on, and these positions are distinct spaces because each $g_i \ge 1$. So the tuples are in one-to-one correspondence with the ways to choose $k-1$ of the $n-k-1$ spaces, and there are

$$
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
$$

of them. This choice makes sense because $k \le n/2$ gives $k-1 \le n-k-1$. (For $k=1$ we choose no spaces, giving the single tuple $(n-1)$.)

*Putting the counts together and dividing.* We now have

$$
k \cdot A(n,k) = n \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Since $k \ge 1$, we may divide both sides by $k$. The division is legitimate because the left side is an exact count: every valid selection was counted precisely $k$ times among the marked selections, no more and no fewer. Hence

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Finally we rewrite this in the form claimed. Writing out the binomial coefficient with factorials, and using $n - 2k \ge 0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
&= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!} \\
&= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!} \qquad\text{since } k\,(k-1)! = k! \\
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!} \qquad\text{since } (n-k)\,(n-k-1)! = (n-k)! \\
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.** When $n$ is even and $k = n/2$, the gaps sum to $n/2$ with $n/2$ parts, so every gap equals $1$: the selected plots alternate with unselected ones all the way around. This is allowed, and the count gives $A(n, n/2) = \frac{n}{n/2}\binom{n/2}{n/2} = 2$, the two alternating patterns.

The factor $n$ in the argument is the number of choices for the start label. It is not a quotient by rotations. The plots carry distinct fixed labels, so rotating a selection generally produces a different selection, and we never identify such selections with one another.

**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two selected plots are neighbors, where the plot with the largest label and the plot with the smallest label count as neighbors because they meet across the circular boundary. Then
$$
A(n,k) \;=\; \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.** First take $k=0$. There is exactly one selection with no plots, the empty selection, and it has no two neighboring plots selected, so $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives
$$
\frac{n}{n-0}\binom{n}{0} \;=\; 1 \cdot 1 \;=\; 1,
$$
so the claim holds. From now on assume $k \ge 1$.

**What we count.** Call a *marked selection* a pair $(S,p)$ where $S$ is a valid selection of $k$ plots and $p$ is one plot of $S$ that we single out as the start. We count the marked selections in two ways.

**First count.** Each valid selection $S$ has exactly $k$ plots, so it can be marked in exactly $k$ ways. Different selections give different marked selections, and so do different marks on the same selection. Therefore
$$
\#\{\text{marked selections}\} \;=\; k\,A(n,k).
$$

**Second count.** Fix a marked selection $(S,p)$. Starting at $p$ and walking clockwise, we meet the plots of $S$ in some order $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$ with $p_1 = p$, and then return to $p_1$. Let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots we pass strictly between $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ for $i = 1, \dots, k-1$, and let $g_k$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $p_k$ and $p_1$ on the way back to the start. When $k=1$ there is only $g_1$, and it counts all $n-1$ plots other than the start.

Two facts hold for these gaps.

- Each $g_i \ge 1$. If some $g_i$ were $0$, then $p_i$ and the next selected plot would be neighbors, which the selection forbids. The gap $g_k$ is the one that crosses the circular boundary, so the boundary rule is exactly what forces $g_k \ge 1$.
- $g_1 + g_2 + \dots + g_k = n-k$. Walking once around the circle visits every plot exactly once. The $k$ selected plots are the $p_i$, and every unselected plot lies in exactly one gap. So the gaps together contain all $n-k$ unselected plots.

Thus every marked selection gives a start label $p$ together with a $k$-tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n-k$.

**Recovering the marked selection.** Conversely, suppose we are given a label $p$ and positive integers $g_1,\dots,g_k$ summing to $n-k$. Place $p_1 = p$, then walk clockwise $g_1$ plots past $p_1$ and select the next plot as $p_2$, then walk $g_2$ plots past $p_2$ and select the next plot as $p_3$, and so on through $p_k$. Walking $g_k$ further plots past $p_k$ and then one more step brings us back exactly to $p_1$, because the total number of steps is
$$
(g_1 + 1) + (g_2 + 1) + \dots + (g_k + 1) \;=\; (n-k) + k \;=\; n,
$$
one full lap. So the construction closes up correctly, the $k$ plots $p_1,\dots,p_k$ are distinct, and no two are neighbors because every gap is at least $1$, including the gap $g_k$ across the boundary. Marking $p_1$ gives a marked selection, and reading its gaps returns exactly $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Different pairs $(p; g_1,\dots,g_k)$ give different marked selections, since either the start differs or the gaps differ. So marked selections correspond exactly to pairs consisting of a start label and a gap tuple.

**Counting the gap tuples.** There are $n$ choices for the start label. It remains to count $k$-tuples of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Draw $n-k$ dots in a row. Between consecutive dots there are $n-k-1$ spaces. Choose $k-1$ of these spaces and cut the row there. This splits the row into $k$ consecutive blocks, each containing at least one dot, and the block sizes read left to right form a $k$-tuple of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Conversely, a tuple of positive integers $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ with sum $n-k$ tells us to cut after dot $g_1$, after dot $g_1+g_2$, and so on, which picks out exactly $k-1$ of the spaces. So gap tuples correspond exactly to choices of $k-1$ spaces out of $n-k-1$, and their number is
$$
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
This makes sense because $k \le n/2$ gives $k-1 \le n-k-1$. In the boundary case $k = n/2$ with $n$ even, we must cut at every one of the $n/2-1$ spaces, so the only tuple is $(1,1,\dots,1)$, every gap is exactly one plot, and the binomial coefficient equals $1$.

Combining the start choice with the gap tuple,
$$
\#\{\text{marked selections}\} \;=\; n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

**Equating the two counts.** Both expressions count the same finite set, so
$$
k\,A(n,k) \;=\; n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
Since $k \ge 1$, we may divide both sides by $k$. This division is legitimate because the first count showed that every valid selection appears exactly $k$ times among the marked selections, so dividing the total by $k$ recovers the number of selections. We get
$$
A(n,k) \;=\; \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

**Rewriting the binomial coefficient.** Expanding the factorials,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
&= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)\,(n-k-1)!}{k\,(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The second line multiplies numerator and denominator by $n-k$, and the third uses $(n-k)(n-k-1)! = (n-k)!$ and $k\,(k-1)! = k!$. This is the claimed formula.

**Remark on rotations.** The plots carry distinct fixed labels, so rotating a selection around the circle generally produces a different selection, and we never divide by $n$. The only division in the argument is by $k$, and it accounts for the $k$ ways of marking a start in a single selection, not for any symmetry of the circle. $\blacksquare$

# Revised Proof: Non-Adjacent Selections on a Labeled Circle

**Setting.** Label the plots $1,\dots,n$ clockwise around a circle, with $n\ge 3$. Plot $i$ is adjacent to $i+1$, indices taken mod $n$, so plot $n$ is adjacent to plot $1$. For $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that no two plots of $S$ are adjacent, including the pair $\{n,1\}$. We prove

$$A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\,\binom{n-k}{k}.$$

Since $k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, we have $n-k\ge k\ge 0$ and $n-k\ge 1$, so the denominator is nonzero and the binomial coefficient is an ordinary one.

---

**Case $k=0$ (empty selection).** The only $0$-element subset is $\varnothing$. It contains no pair of plots, so it is valid, and $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1\cdot 1=1$. The two agree.

**Case $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.** The rest of the proof assumes $k\ge 1$.

**Step 1: Count marked selections two ways.** Let
$$P=\{(S,s): S \text{ is a valid } k\text{-selection},\ s\in S\}.$$
Here $s$ is a "start," a chosen selected plot.

- *By selection:* each valid $S$ has exactly $k$ choices of $s$. So $|P|=k\,A(n,k)$.
- *By start:* we count $P$ differently in Steps 2–4.

The division by $k$ is legitimate because each valid $S$ contributes exactly $k$ pairs to $P$. The fibers of the projection $(S,s)\mapsto S$ all have size $k\ge 1$, so $A(n,k)=|P|/k$ exactly.

**Step 2: Encode a pair by its gap sequence.** Fix $(S,s)\in P$. Starting at $s$ and moving clockwise, list the selected plots as $p_1=s,p_2,\dots,p_k$ in clockwise order. For $i=1,\dots,k$, let $p_{k+1}=p_1$, and define

$$g_i=\text{the number of unselected plots strictly between } p_i \text{ and } p_{i+1} \text{ going clockwise.}$$

When $k=1$, $p_2=p_1$ and $g_1$ counts all $n-1$ other plots, which are all unselected.

The gaps have two properties:

- **(a) Each $g_i\ge 1$.** The plots $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are distinct selected plots, so they are not adjacent. Hence at least one plot lies strictly between them clockwise. For $k=1$, $g_1=n-1\ge 2$ because $n\ge 3$.
- **(b) $\sum_i g_i=n-k$.** The $k$ gaps are disjoint and together contain every unselected plot exactly once.

Let $G$ be the set of ordered $k$-tuples $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Step 2 defines a map $(S,s)\mapsto(s,g)$ from $P$ to $[n]\times G$.

**Step 3: This map is a bijection.** Define $\Phi:[n]\times G\to P$ as follows. Given $s$ and $g=(g_1,\dots,g_k)\in G$, set the clockwise offsets
$$d_1=0,\qquad d_{i+1}=d_i+(g_i+1)\quad (i=1,\dots,k-1),$$
and let $p_i=s+d_i \pmod n$, with $S=\{p_1,\dots,p_k\}$.

*Well-defined.* Since each $g_i+1\ge 2$, the offsets are strictly increasing. Also $d_k=\sum_{i<k}(g_i+1)=(n-k)+k-(g_k+1)=n-(g_k+1)<n$, so the offsets $d_1,\dots,d_k$ lie in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and are distinct. Thus the $p_i$ are $k$ distinct plots, and $s=p_1\in S$.

*Valid.* Take two distinct selected plots $a,b$. The clockwise distance from $a$ to $b$ is a sum of one or more terms $g_j+1\ge 2$, and the same holds for the clockwise distance from $b$ to $a$. Neither distance equals $1$, so $a$ and $b$ are not adjacent. This covers the wraparound pair as well.

*Inverse.* Given $(S,s)\in P$, the gap sequence of Step 2 satisfies $d_i=$ clockwise distance from $s$ to $p_i$, and $\Phi$ rebuilds exactly $S$ from it. Conversely, $\Phi(s,g)$ has start $s$ and gap sequence $g$, because its offsets are exactly the $d_i$ above. So $\Phi$ and the Step 2 map are mutually inverse.

Therefore $|P|=n\,|G|$. The factor $n$ is the number of possible start labels.

**Step 4: Count $G$.** Put $m=n-k$. Map a tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)\in G$ to the cut set $\{c_1,\dots,c_{k-1}\}$, where $c_j=g_1+\cdots+g_j$. Since every $g_j\ge 1$, we have $0<c_1<\cdots<c_{k-1}<m$, so this is a $(k-1)$-subset of $\{1,\dots,m-1\}$. The inverse takes $g_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$ with $c_0=0$ and $c_k=m$, which gives positive parts summing to $m$. So
$$|G|=\binom{m-1}{k-1}=\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$
This is the stars-and-bars count: a row of $m$ unselected plots has $m-1$ internal gaps, and $k-1$ of them are cut.

**Step 5: Combine.** From Steps 1, 3, and 4,
$$k\,A(n,k)=|P|=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},\qquad\text{so}\qquad A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

**Step 6: Convert to the stated form.** Since $n-k\ge k\ge1$, the binomial coefficients are defined. Using factorials,
$$\binom{n-k}{k}=\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},\qquad \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}=\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}.$$
The ratio is
$$\frac{\binom{n-k}{k}}{\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}}=\frac{(n-k)!}{(n-k-1)!}\cdot\frac{(k-1)!}{k!}=\frac{n-k}{k},$$
so $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}=\frac{k}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}$. Substituting into Step 5,
$$A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{k}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.\qquad\blacksquare$$

---

**Remarks and checks.**

- **Why no rotation quotient.** $A(n,k)$ counts subsets of *labeled* plots, so distinct rotations of a configuration are distinct subsets and are counted separately. The only division in the proof is the division by $k$ in Step 1, which is justified by the exact fiber size.
- **Boundary case $k=n/2$ ($n$ even).** Here $n-k=k$, so the only composition is $(1,\dots,1)$ and $|G|=1$. The formula gives $A=n/k=2$. This matches the two diagonal selections $\{1,3\},\{2,4\}$ when $n=4$.
- **Example $n=5$, $k=2$.** Here $m=3$ and $G=\{(1,2),(2,1)\}$, so $|P|=5\cdot 2=10$ and $A=10/2=5$. The formula gives $\frac{5}{3}\binom{3}{2}=5$. The five valid pairs are $\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,4\},\{2,5\},\{3,5\}$.
- **Range of $k$.** The restriction $k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is used in Step 6 to keep $n-k\ge k$. For larger $k$ the count is $0$, and the displayed formula should not be applied there without checking.

**Claim.** Let $n \ge 3$ labeled plots be arranged in a circle, and let $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of plots that contain no two neighboring plots, where plot $n$ and plot $1$ count as neighbors. Then
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*Case $k=0$.* The only selection is the empty set, which has no selected plot. So $A(n,0)=1$. The right-hand side is $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$, so the formula holds. The empty selection has no plot that can be marked as a start, so it cannot enter the counting below and must be handled separately.

*Case $k\ge 1$.* Let $P$ be the set of pairs $(S,p)$, where $S$ is a valid $k$-selection and $p \in S$ is a marked selected plot. Each valid selection has exactly $k$ choices of marked plot, so
$$
|P| = k\,A(n,k).
$$

We now count $P$ in a second way. Fix the label $p$ of the marked plot. Since the plots have distinct labels, the $n$ possible values of $p$ give disjoint sets of pairs, so $|P|$ is the sum over these $n$ values.

For a fixed $p$, walk clockwise from $p$ and list the selected plots in order as $x_1=p, x_2, \dots, x_k$. Let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $x_i$ and the next selected plot, where $x_{k+1}$ means $x_1=p$ again. When $k=1$, $g_1$ counts the $n-1$ unselected plots between $p$ and itself going around the circle, so $g_1=n-1$.

Two facts about the gaps follow.

- Each $g_i \ge 1$, because no two neighboring plots are both selected.
- $g_1+\dots+g_k = n-k$, because the $k$ selected plots and the $g_i$ unselected plots together make up all $n$ plots.

**The map is a bijection.** Send $(S,p)$ to the pair consisting of $p$ and the gap tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Conversely, given $p$ and a tuple of positive integers $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ summing to $n-k$, start at $p$, skip $g_1$ plots clockwise, mark the next plot as $x_2$, skip $g_2$ plots, and continue. After $k$ such steps the walk has covered $n$ plots and returns to $p$. The $k$ marked plots are distinct because each step moves past at least one unselected plot. Reading the gaps off this selection returns the original tuple, and building the selection from the tuple returns the original $S$. So the correspondence is one-to-one in both directions.

**Counting the tuples.** We need the number of ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Write $n-k$ as a row of $n-k$ unit objects. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between adjacent objects. Choosing $k-1$ of these spaces as cut points splits the row into $k$ nonempty blocks, and each block has a size that is a positive integer. Different cut sets give different tuples, so the count is $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$. This is valid because $k\ge 1$ and $k\le n/2$ give $0 \le k-1 \le n-k-1$.

Therefore, for each of the $n$ labels $p$, there are $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ valid pairs, and
$$
k\,A(n,k) = |P| = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

**Dividing by $k$.** Since $k\ge 1$, we can divide both sides by $k$:
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
This division is legitimate because $k$ is a fixed positive integer and we are solving an equation. It does not quotient out rotations. The plots have fixed distinct labels, so two selections that differ by a rotation are different sets and are both counted.

**Simplifying.** Since $n-2k\ge 0$, all factorials below are defined:
$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
Also,
$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},
$$
where dividing by $n-k$ is valid because $n-k \ge n/2 > 0$. The two expressions are equal, so
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remark on $k=n/2$.** When $n$ is even and $k=n/2$, the gaps sum to $n-k=k$ and each must be at least $1$. So every gap equals $1$, which is allowed. This matches the count: $\binom{k-1}{k-1}=1$.

**Claim.** Label the $n \ge 3$ plots $1, \dots, n$ around a circle, with plot $n$ adjacent to plot $1$. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets $S$ of plots such that no two plots in $S$ are adjacent, where adjacency includes the pair $\{n,1\}$. Then

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*Case $k=0$.* The only $0$-element selection is the empty set, so $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$, which agrees.

*Case $k\ge 1$.* Let $P$ be the set of pairs $(S,s)$ where $S$ is a valid $k$-selection and $s\in S$ is a marked plot. Each selection has $k$ choices for $s$, so

$$
|P| = k\,A(n,k).
$$

For each $(S,s)\in P$, walk clockwise from $s$. Let $p_1=s,\ p_2,\dots,p_k$ be the selected plots in the order met, and set $p_{k+1}=p_1$. Let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$, for $i=1,\dots,k$. Two facts follow:

- Each $g_i\ge 1$. If $g_i=0$, then $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ would be adjacent selected plots.
- $\sum_{i=1}^k g_i = n-k$, because the $n-k$ unselected plots are split among the $k$ gaps.

When $k=1$, the single gap contains all $n-1$ other plots, so $g_1=n-1$.

Let $T$ be the set of ordered tuples $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$. The map

$$
\Phi(S,s) = (s, g_1,\dots,g_k)
$$

sends $P$ into $\{1,\dots,n\}\times T$. It is a bijection. To invert it, start at $s$ and place the selected plots at clockwise offsets

$$
d_1=0,\qquad d_{i+1}=d_i+g_i+1 \quad (i=1,\dots,k-1).
$$

The offsets increase strictly and $d_k = n-(g_k+1)<n$, so they lie in one lap and are distinct. Consecutive selected offsets differ by $g_i+1\ge 2$, and the wraparound gap from $d_k$ back to $n$ is also $g_k+1\ge 2$. So the resulting set is a valid selection with $s$ selected, and walking from $s$ recovers exactly the tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Since the sum of $(g_i+1)$ over all $i$ is $(n-k)+k=n$, the walk closes after exactly one lap. Hence $\Phi$ is a bijection, and

$$
|P| = n\,|T|.
$$

*Counting $T$.* An element of $T$ is a composition of $n-k$ into $k$ positive parts. Write $n-k$ units in a row. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between consecutive units. Cutting the row into $k$ consecutive blocks of sizes $g_1,\dots,g_k$ means choosing $k-1$ of these spaces as cut points. Each choice gives exactly one tuple, and each tuple gives exactly one choice. This is valid because $k\le n-k$, so $k-1\le n-k-1$. Therefore

$$
|T| = \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Combining the counts,

$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Since $k\ge 1$, we may divide by $k$:

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Final identity.* Since $k\le n/2$, we have $n-2k\ge 0$, so all factorials below are defined. Also $n-k\ge 1$, so dividing by $n-k$ is legitimate. Expanding both sides:

$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},
$$

$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$

The two expressions are equal, which gives

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remarks.**

- At $k=n/2$ for even $n$, $n-k=k$, so the sum of $k$ positive gaps equals $k$. The only tuple is $(1,\dots,1)$, and $\binom{k-1}{k-1}=1$. Every gap is a single unselected plot, which is allowed. For example, with $n=4$ and $k=2$, the selections are $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$, and the formula gives $\frac{4}{2}\binom{2}{2}=2$.
- No division by $n$ accounts for rotations. The plots carry fixed distinct labels, so each selection is counted once as a set of labeled plots, and the marked start $s$ is a label rather than a rotation class.

\[

\]
The range \(k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) ensures \(n-k\ge k\), so these binomial coefficients are defined. When \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, which is allowed. The plots have distinct fixed labels, so no quotient by rotations is taken.

\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge1\). Count pairs consisting of a valid selection and one of its selected plots marked as the start. Each selection gives \(k\) such pairs, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) pairs.

Starting there and moving clockwise, let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). If \(k=1\), this gap consists of all the other plots before returning to the start. Each \(g_i\) is positive because neighboring plots cannot both be selected, and the gaps contain all \(n-k\) unselected plots. Thus
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]

The number of ordered lists of \(k\) positive integers with this sum is \(\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\): represent \(n-k\) as a row of objects and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) spaces between them as separators. The resulting \(k\) groups give the gap sizes. Each start plot and gap list determines exactly one marked selection, including when the gaps are all one. Hence
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},
\qquad
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Expanding the factorials gives
\[
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
The division by \(k\) is legitimate because each valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible choices of the marked plot. The plots have fixed labels, so rotations are not identified. \(\square\)

# Counting Non-Adjacent Selections Around a Circle

**Setting.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle, numbered $1, 2, \dots, n$ clockwise. Two plots are *neighbors* if their labels differ by $1$, or if they are plots $n$ and $1$, which meet across the circular boundary. Each plot therefore has exactly two neighbors. The condition $n \ge 3$ guarantees that these two neighbors are distinct.

A *selection* is a set of plots. Because every plot carries its own fixed label, two selections are the same only when they contain exactly the same labels. Rotating a selection generally produces a *different* selection, so we never identify selections up to rotation.

**Claim.** For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections in which no two selected plots are neighbors. Then
$$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.$$

Since $k \le n/2 < n$, the denominator $n-k$ is positive, so the right-hand side is always defined.

---

## Proof

### Case $k = 0$: the empty selection

Exactly one selection has no plots: the empty set. It contains no pair of selected plots at all, so it satisfies the no-neighbors condition automatically. Hence $A(n,0) = 1$.

The formula gives $\dfrac{n}{n-0}\dbinom{n}{0} = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$, which agrees.

The empty case must be handled separately. The argument below marks one selected plot and later divides by $k$, and neither step makes sense when $k = 0$.

From now on assume $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

### Stage 1: What we count — marked selections

Define a **marked selection** as a pair $(S, s)$, where $S$ is a valid $k$-element selection and $s$ is one of the plots in $S$, designated as the *start*.

We count marked selections in two ways.

**First count.** Each valid selection $S$ has exactly $k$ elements, so it can be marked in exactly $k$ ways. Different selections give different pairs. Therefore
$$\#\{\text{marked selections}\} = k \cdot A(n,k).$$

### Stage 2: Encoding a marked selection by a start and a gap tuple

Given a marked selection $(S, s)$, walk clockwise from $s$. Call the selected plots in the order you meet them $p_1 = s, p_2, \dots, p_k$, and then you return to $p_1$.

For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of *unselected* plots strictly between $p_i$ and the next selected plot clockwise. The next selected plot is $p_{i+1}$, and for $i = k$ it is $p_1$ again.

When $k = 1$, there is only $p_1$. The single gap $g_1$ counts all the other $n-1$ plots passed on the way around back to $p_1$.

The gap tuple has two properties.

1. **Each $g_i \ge 1$.** If some $g_i = 0$, then $p_i$ and the next selected plot would be neighbors. For $i = k$, this covers the wrap-around pair. For $k = 1$, we have $g_1 = n - 1 \ge 2$.
2. **$g_1 + \cdots + g_k = n - k$.** Going once around the circle visits each of the $n$ plots exactly once. Exactly $k$ of them are selected, and each of the other $n-k$ lies in exactly one gap.

So every marked selection yields a pair consisting of:
- a start label $s \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, and
- an ordered tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$.

**This encoding is a bijection.** Conversely, take any start label $s$ and any such tuple. Select plot $s$. Step clockwise $g_1 + 1$ places and select that plot. Then step $g_2 + 1$ places and select that plot, and so on. After all $k$ steps you have moved
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k}(g_i + 1) = (n-k) + k = n$$
places, which is exactly once around. So you land back on $s$ and do not overlap any earlier choice. This construction has three consequences:
- It produces $k$ distinct plots.
- No two of them are neighbors, because every gap, including the wrap-around one, is at least $1$.
- Marking $s$ gives a marked selection whose encoding is the $(s, g)$ we started with.

Decoding and then encoding, or encoding and then decoding, returns what we began with. Hence
$$\#\{\text{marked selections}\} = n \cdot C,$$
where $C$ is the number of ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers summing to $n-k$. The factor $n$ appears because every label is a legitimate start, and the gap tuple's possibilities do not depend on which start was chosen.

### Stage 3: Counting the gap tuples

**Claim:** $C = \dbinom{n-k-1}{k-1}$.

Line up $n-k$ identical tokens in a row:
$$\bullet\ \bullet\ \bullet\ \cdots\ \bullet$$
There are $n-k-1$ *internal* spaces, one between each adjacent pair of tokens. Choose $k-1$ of these spaces and place a separator in each. The separators cut the row into $k$ consecutive blocks, read left to right, and we let $g_i$ be the size of the $i$-th block.

- Each block is nonempty, because separators sit only in internal spaces and at most one sits in each space. So each $g_i \ge 1$.
- The block sizes sum to $n-k$.

Conversely, a tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$ determines where the separators go: after the first $g_1$ tokens, after the next $g_2$, and so on. That gives $k-1$ distinct internal spaces. Choices of separator positions and gap tuples therefore correspond one-to-one, and
$$C = \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

This count is valid in the extreme cases as well.
- **$k = 1$:** we choose $0$ of $n-2$ spaces. There is $\binom{n-2}{0} = 1$ way, matching the single tuple $(n-1)$.
- **$k = n/2$ with $n$ even:** we choose $k-1$ of $k-1$ spaces. There is $1$ way, matching the single tuple $(1, 1, \dots, 1)$. This is the alternating selection, in which every gap is exactly one plot. It is valid, including across the boundary.

In general $k \le n/2$ gives $k - 1 \le n-k-1$, so the binomial coefficient counts a genuine choice.

### Stage 4: Equating the counts and dividing

The two counts of marked selections must agree:
$$k \cdot A(n,k) = n \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

**Why division by $k$ is legitimate.** Every valid selection is counted *exactly* $k$ times on the left, once for each choice of marked plot. It is never counted fewer or more times, because all such selections have exactly $k$ elements. Since $k \ge 1$, we may divide by $k$:
$$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

### Stage 5: Rewriting in the stated form

Expand the binomial coefficient using factorials. This is valid because $0 \le k-1 \le n-k-1$.
$$\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.$$

Multiply the numerator and denominator by $n-k$, which is positive:
$$= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.$$

Together with the case $k = 0$, this proves the claim for every $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Sanity check.** Take $n = 6$ and $k = 3$. The formula gives $\tfrac{6}{3}\binom{3}{3} = 2$. These two selections are $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,4,6\}$. They are rotations of each other, but they count as two different selections because the plots are labeled.

response:
**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two neighboring plots are both selected. This includes the pair of plots that meet across the circular boundary. Then

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.** Number the plots $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ clockwise, so that plot $n-1$ is next to plot $0$. Since $k \le n/2 < n$, the denominator $n-k$ is positive.

*The empty selection.* If $k = 0$, the only selection is the empty one. It has no neighboring selected plots, so $A(n,0) = 1$. The formula also gives

$$
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0} = 1.
$$

From now on assume $k \ge 1$.

*Counting marked selections in two ways.* A *marked selection* is a valid selection together with one of its selected plots, which we call the start. Each valid selection has exactly $k$ selected plots, so it can be marked in exactly $k$ ways. The number of marked selections is therefore

$$
k\,A(n,k).
$$

We now count marked selections another way. Fix a marked selection and call its selected plots $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$, in clockwise order starting from the start $p_1$. For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $p_i$ and the next selected plot clockwise. For $i = k$, the next selected plot is $p_1$ again, so $g_k$ counts the unselected plots across the circular boundary. When $k = 1$, $g_1$ counts all the other plots before the circle returns to the start, so $g_1 = n-1$.

Two selected plots are neighbors exactly when the gap between them is $0$. The selection is valid, including at the circular boundary, if and only if every gap is at least $1$. Every plot is either one of the $k$ selected plots or lies in exactly one gap, so

$$
g_1 + g_2 + \cdots + g_k = n - k, \qquad g_i \ge 1 .
$$

So each marked selection determines a pair: the label of its start, which is one of $n$ values, and an ordered tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n-k$.

Conversely, any such pair determines exactly one marked selection. Select the start plot $s$. Then move clockwise past $g_1$ plots and select the next plot. Continue past $g_2$ plots and select the next one, and so on. After placing $k$ selected plots and passing $g_1 + \cdots + g_k = n-k$ unselected plots, we have used all $n$ plots and returned to $s$. The selected plots are therefore distinct, and all gaps are positive. So the selection is valid, and its gap tuple read from $s$ is the given one. The two constructions undo each other, so marked selections correspond one-to-one with pairs (start label, gap tuple).

*Counting the gap tuples.* Write $m = n - k$. We count ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers summing to $m$. Place $m$ identical objects in a row. There are $m - 1$ spaces between adjacent objects. Choose $k-1$ of these spaces and put a separator in each. This cuts the row into $k$ consecutive nonempty blocks, and their sizes read left to right form a tuple of positive integers summing to $m$. Every such tuple arises from exactly one choice of separators: put the separators after the first $g_1$ objects, after the next $g_2$, and so on. Since $k \le n/2$, we have $m - 1 = n-k-1 \ge k-1$, so the choice is possible. The number of tuples is

$$
\binom{m-1}{k-1} = \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

When $n$ is even and $k = n/2$, this count is $\binom{k-1}{k-1} = 1$. The only tuple has every gap equal to $1$, which is allowed, and it gives the alternating selections.

*Combining the counts.* The start label and the gap tuple are chosen independently, so the number of marked selections is $n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$. Equating the two counts gives

$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Since $k \ge 1$, we may divide by $k$. The division is legitimate because each valid selection was counted exactly $k$ times, once for each choice of start:

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Rewriting the binomial.* Using $n - 2k \ge 0$ and expanding the factorials,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
&= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},\\[4pt]
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two expressions agree, so

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

The plots have distinct fixed labels, so two selections that differ by a rotation are different selections. For this reason we do not divide by the number of rotations. $\blacksquare$

**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of ways to select $k$ plots so that no two selected plots are neighbors. This includes the two plots that meet across the circular boundary. Then

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

Since $k \le n/2 < n$, the denominator $n-k$ is positive.

**Proof.**

*The empty selection.* If $k = 0$, the only selection is the empty one, and it has no neighboring pair. So $A(n,0) = 1$. The formula gives

$$
\frac{n}{n-0}\binom{n}{0} = 1,
$$

so the claim holds. From now on assume $k \ge 1$.

*What we count.* We count *marked selections*. A marked selection is a valid selection together with one of its $k$ selected plots chosen as a start. Each valid selection has exactly $k$ selected plots, so it can be marked in exactly $k$ ways. Therefore

$$
\#\{\text{marked selections}\} = k\,A(n,k).
$$

We now count the same objects a second way.

*Describing a marked selection by gaps.* Begin at the start plot and move clockwise. Call the selected plots $1, 2, \dots, k$ in the order they are reached, so selected plot 1 is the start. For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots between selected plot $i$ and the next selected plot. For $i = k$, the next selected plot is the start again, so $g_k$ counts the plots crossed while wrapping around the circle. When $k = 1$, this means $g_1$ counts all the other plots before we return to the start.

Two facts about the gaps follow:

- Each $g_i \ge 1$. A gap of $0$ would make two selected plots neighbors. The gap $g_k$ is the one that checks the pair across the circular boundary.
- Every plot is either selected or lies in exactly one gap, so
$$
k + g_1 + g_2 + \cdots + g_k = n,
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad
g_1 + \cdots + g_k = n-k.
$$

*The correspondence.* A marked selection determines a start plot, which can be any of the $n$ labeled plots, and an ordered tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n-k$.

Conversely, take any start plot and any such tuple. Select the start, skip $g_1$ plots clockwise, select the next plot, skip $g_2$ plots, and continue. After selecting $k$ plots and skipping $g_1 + \cdots + g_k = n-k$ plots, we have passed exactly $n$ plots, so we arrive back at the start. The selected plots are distinct, and since every gap is at least $1$, no two of them are neighbors, including across the boundary. The procedure therefore produces a valid marked selection, and its gap tuple is the one we started from.

These two constructions undo each other. So the marked selections correspond one-to-one with the pairs (start plot, gap tuple).

*Counting the gap tuples.* We count ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers summing to $n-k$. Put $n-k$ identical objects in a row. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between adjacent objects. Choosing $k-1$ of these spaces as separators cuts the row into $k$ nonempty blocks. Read from left to right, their sizes are $g_1, \dots, g_k$. Every such tuple arises from exactly one choice of separators, so there are

$$
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
$$

tuples. This needs $k-1 \le n-k-1$, which holds because $k \le n/2$. For $k=1$ there are no separators, the only tuple is $g_1 = n-1$, and $\binom{n-2}{0} = 1$ agrees.

*Comparing the two counts.* The start plot can be chosen in $n$ ways and the tuple in $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ ways, independently. So

$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Because $k \ge 1$, we may divide by $k$. The division is exact, because each valid selection was counted exactly $k$ times, once for each choice of start:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&= \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!} \\
&= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!} \\
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The third equality uses $k\,(k-1)! = k!$. The fourth multiplies numerator and denominator by $n-k$ and uses $(n-k)(n-k-1)! = (n-k)!$.

*Remarks on the edge cases.* When $n$ is even and $k = n/2$, the gaps sum to $n-k = k$ with each gap at least $1$, so every gap equals $1$. This means alternating plots are selected, which is allowed. We do not divide by the $n$ rotations of the circle. The plots carry distinct fixed labels, so rotating a selection generally gives a different selection, and the only overcounting in the argument is the factor $k$ from choosing the start. $\blacksquare$

response:
**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two selected plots are neighbors. This includes the pair of plots that meet across the circular boundary. Then
$$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.$$

**Proof.**

*Setup.* Label the plots $1, 2, \dots, n$ clockwise. The neighbors of plot $j$ are plots $j-1$ and $j+1$. Plots $n$ and $1$ are also neighbors, because they meet across the circular boundary. Since $n \ge 3$, every plot has two different neighbors. Call a selection *valid* if no two of its selected plots are neighbors. Because $k \le n/2$, we have $n-k \ge n/2 > 0$, so the right-hand side never divides by zero.

*The empty selection ($k = 0$).* There is exactly one $0$-element selection, the empty selection. It is valid because it contains no pair of plots. So $A(n,0) = 1$, and the formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0} = 1$.

We handle this case separately because the argument below marks one selected plot, and the empty selection has nothing to mark. For $k = 0$ the argument would only produce $0 \cdot A(n,0) = 0$, which says nothing about $A(n,0)$. Dividing by $k$ would also be impossible.

From now on, $1 \le k \le n/2$.

*Stage 1: What we count.* A *marked selection* is a valid $k$-element selection with one of its selected plots designated as the *start*. We count marked selections in two ways.

First way: choose the valid selection ($A(n,k)$ ways), then choose the start among its $k$ selected plots ($k$ ways). Different choices produce different marked selections. So there are
$$k\,A(n,k)$$
marked selections.

*Stage 2: Recording a marked selection by its gaps.* Take a marked selection with start $s$. Walk clockwise once around the circle from $s$, and name the selected plots in the order you meet them: $p_1 = s, p_2, \dots, p_k$. For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $p_i$ and the next selected plot. The next selected plot after $p_k$ is $p_1 = s$ again. When $k = 1$ there is only one gap: $g_1$ counts all the other plots passed before returning to $s$, so $g_1 = n-1$.

The gaps have two properties.

- **Sum.** The walk passes every plot exactly once before returning to $s$. Each plot is either one of the $k$ selected plots or lies in exactly one gap. Hence $k + g_1 + \dots + g_k = n$, that is,
 $$g_1 + \dots + g_k = n-k.$$
- **Positivity.** For $k \ge 2$, two selected plots are neighbors exactly when one immediately follows the other clockwise, which happens exactly when some gap is $0$. So the selection is valid if and only if every $g_i \ge 1$. For $k = 1$, validity is automatic, and indeed $g_1 = n-1 \ge 2$.

 The walk goes all the way around the circle, so it includes the step from plot $n$ to plot $1$. The boundary pair is therefore checked by the gap condition exactly like every other neighboring pair. This is where the cyclic setting enters the count.

So the gap list $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ is an ordered list of positive integers with sum $n-k$.

*Stage 3: The gaps lose no information.* Now go the other way. Start from any start label $s$ (one of the $n$ plots) and any ordered list $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Build a selection as follows:

1. Put $p_1 = s$.
2. For $i = 1, \dots, k-1$, let $p_{i+1}$ be the plot $g_i + 1$ steps clockwise from $p_i$. In other words, skip $g_i$ plots and select the next one.

Then $p_i$ lies
$$d_i = (i-1) + g_1 + \dots + g_{i-1}$$
steps clockwise from $s$. These distances satisfy $0 = d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_k$ and
$$d_k = (k-1) + (n-k-g_k) = n-1-g_k \le n-2.$$

So the $d_i$ are distinct numbers among $0, 1, \dots, n-1$. This means the $p_i$ are $k$ distinct plots, met in the order $p_1, \dots, p_k$ when walking clockwise from $s$. Between $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ there are exactly $g_i$ unselected plots. From $p_k$ clockwise back to $s$ there are $n-1-d_k = g_k$ unselected plots. Every gap is positive, so by Stage 2 the selection is valid. Its gap list read from $s$ is exactly $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$.

In the other direction, reading off the gaps of a marked selection and then rebuilding returns the same selection. The rebuilt plots sit at the same clockwise distances from $s$ as the original ones.

Therefore marked selections correspond one-to-one with pairs of the form
$$(\text{start label},\ \text{ordered list of } k \text{ positive integers with sum } n-k).$$

*Stage 4: Counting the pairs.* There are $n$ choices of start label. The set of allowed lists does not depend on which plot is the start, so by the product rule it remains to count the lists.

Line up $n-k$ identical objects in a row. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between neighboring objects. Choose $k-1$ of these spaces and put one separator in each. This cuts the row into $k$ blocks, read left to right. Every block is nonempty, because no two separators share a space and no separator sits at either end. The block sizes form an ordered list of $k$ positive integers with sum $n-k$.

Conversely, a list $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ arises from exactly one choice of separators. Place them after the first $g_1$ objects, after the first $g_1 + g_2$ objects, and so on, up to after the first $g_1 + \dots + g_{k-1}$ objects. Because each $g_i \ge 1$, these partial sums are strictly increasing and lie between $1$ and $n-k-g_k \le n-k-1$. So they name $k-1$ distinct internal spaces.

Hence there are $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ lists. Since $k \le n/2$, we have $n-k-1 \ge k-1 \ge 0$, so this is an ordinary binomial coefficient. For $k = 1$ it equals $\binom{n-2}{0} = 1$, which matches the single list $(n-1)$.

Second way: there are
$$n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$$
marked selections.

*Stage 5: Comparing and dividing.* The two counts must agree:
$$k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

Dividing by $k$ is legitimate here. First, $k \ge 1$. Second, in the count $k\,A(n,k)$, every valid selection appears exactly $k$ times, once for each of its selected plots. No selection is counted more or fewer times. Dividing by $k$ therefore removes the overcount exactly:
$$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

To reach the stated form, expand the factorials. Since $1 \le k \le n/2$, the numbers $k-1$, $n-k-1$ and $n-2k$ are all nonnegative. Using $k\,(k-1)! = k!$,
$$\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1} = \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!} = \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.$$
Using $(n-k)! = (n-k)\,(n-k-1)!$, with $n-k > 0$,
$$\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k} = \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!} = \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.$$

The two expressions are equal, so $A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}$ for $1 \le k \le n/2$. Together with the case $k = 0$, this proves the claim. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.**

1. *The extreme case.* Suppose $n$ is even and $k = n/2$. Then the $k$ gaps are positive integers with sum $n-k = k$, so every gap equals $1$, and selected and unselected plots alternate. This is allowed, because gaps only need to be at least $1$. In Stage 5, $n-2k = 0$ and $0! = 1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n/2}\binom{n/2}{n/2} = 2$. These two selections are the even-labeled plots and the odd-labeled plots.

2. *No division by rotations.* The factor $n$ counts choices of start label. It is not a symmetry to be divided out. The plots have distinct, fixed labels, so two selections that differ by a rotation are different selections, and $A(n,k)$ counts both.

 Even if one wanted to count selections up to rotation, dividing by $n$ would be wrong. The alternating selection in Remark 1 has only $2$ distinct rotations, not $n$. The only division in the proof is by $k$, and it is exact for the reason given in Stage 5.

response:
**Claim.** Arrange $n\ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two neighboring plots are selected, including the pair that meets across the circular boundary. Then

$$
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.** We first treat $k=0$. The only $0$-element selection is the empty one. It contains no pair of selected plots, so it satisfies the condition, and $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives

$$
\frac{n}{n-0}\binom{n-0}{0}=1\cdot 1=1.
$$

Now assume $k\ge 1$. We count one collection of objects in two ways. A *marked selection* is a valid $k$-element selection together with one of its selected plots, which we call the start.

*First count.* Each of the $A(n,k)$ valid selections has $k$ selected plots, and any of them can be the start. So the number of marked selections is

$$
k\,A(n,k).
$$

*Second count.* We describe a marked selection by its start and the sizes of the gaps between its selected plots. Begin at the start and move clockwise around the circle. Call the selected plots $p_1,\dots,p_k$ in the order we meet them, so $p_1$ is the start. For $i=1,\dots,k-1$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots between $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$. Let $g_k$ be the number of unselected plots between $p_k$ and the return to the start. For $k=1$ there is only $g_1$, and it counts all the other $n-1$ plots before returning to the start.

These numbers have two properties.

1. Each $g_i$ is a positive integer. If $g_i=0$ for some $i<k$, then $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ would be neighbors. If $g_k=0$, then $p_k$ and the start would be neighbors. When $k=1$, $g_1=n-1\ge 2$.
2. Each of the $n-k$ unselected plots lies in exactly one gap, so
$$
g_1+g_2+\dots+g_k=n-k.
$$

So a marked selection determines a start, which is one of the $n$ plots, and an ordered tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$.

Conversely, take any plot $s$ and any such tuple. Select $s$. Move clockwise past $g_1$ plots and select the next plot. Then move past $g_2$ plots and select the next one, and continue until $p_k$ has been selected. Moving past another $g_k$ plots brings us back to $s$, because the walk has then covered

$$
k+(g_1+\dots+g_k)=k+(n-k)=n
$$

plots, which is exactly once around the circle. Hence the $k$ selected plots are distinct. Two selected plots that were neighbors would be consecutive in clockwise order with no plot between them, which would give a gap of zero. Every gap, including the one from $p_k$ back to $s$, contains at least one plot, so no two selected plots are neighbors. The result is a valid marked selection with start $s$, and reading its gaps clockwise from $s$ returns $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Rebuilding a marked selection from its own start and gaps also returns that marked selection. Therefore each pair of a start and a tuple gives exactly one marked selection, and each marked selection comes from exactly one such pair.

It remains to count the tuples. Line up $n-k$ objects in a row. There are $n-k-1$ internal spaces, one between each pair of adjacent objects, and we number them $1,\dots,n-k-1$ from left to right. Placing separators in $k-1$ of these spaces cuts the row into $k$ nonempty blocks, and the block sizes, read from left to right, form an ordered tuple of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Every such tuple comes from exactly one choice of spaces, namely

$$
g_1,\quad g_1+g_2,\quad \dots,\quad g_1+\dots+g_{k-1}.
$$

These numbers are strictly increasing because each $g_i\ge 1$. The first is at least $1$, and the last equals $n-k-g_k\le n-k-1$, so they are $k-1$ distinct internal spaces. When $k=1$ no separators are placed, and the only tuple is $(n-1)$. The number of tuples is therefore the number of ways to choose $k-1$ of the $n-k-1$ internal spaces, which is

$$
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

At $k=n/2$ for even $n$, we have $n-k-1=k-1$, so every space receives a separator and every gap is one. This is allowed, since only a gap of zero is excluded.

The start and the tuple can be chosen independently, so the second count is

$$
n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

We do not divide by $n$ to account for rotations. The plots have distinct fixed labels, so the $n$ choices of start are genuinely different, and selections that differ by a rotation are counted separately in $A(n,k)$.

Both counts describe the same marked selections, so

$$
k\,A(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Since $k\ge 1$, we may divide by $k$:

$$
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

This division is why the empty selection needed separate treatment. When $k=0$ there is no plot to mark, so the first count is $0$ and says nothing about $A(n,0)$.

Finally, $1\le k\le n/2$ gives $n-2k\ge 0$ and $n-k\ge n/2>0$. So the factorials below are of nonnegative integers, and dividing by $n-k$ is legitimate. Expanding the factorials,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
&=\frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first equality uses $(n-k-1)-(k-1)=n-2k$. The second uses $k\,(k-1)!=k!$. The third multiplies the numerator and denominator by $n-k$ and uses $(n-k)\,(n-k-1)!=(n-k)!$. The last is the definition of $\binom{n-k}{k}$, which applies because $n-k-k=n-2k$.

response:
**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots with no two neighboring plots selected, including the pair that meets across the circular boundary. Then

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*The empty selection.* If $k = 0$, there is exactly one selection, the empty one, and it contains no pair of neighbors. So $A(n,0) = 1$, and the formula gives

$$
\frac{n}{n-0}\binom{n}{0} = 1.
$$

The argument below marks one selected plot and ends by dividing by $k$, so it cannot be used when nothing is selected. From now on, assume $k \ge 1$.

*What we count.* We count pairs consisting of a valid selection and one of its selected plots, which we mark as the start. A valid selection has exactly $k$ selected plots, and any of them can be the start, so each valid selection appears in exactly $k$ pairs. The number of pairs is therefore

$$
k\,A(n,k).
$$

We now count the same pairs a second way, by recording where the start is and how the selected plots are spaced around the circle.

*Recording a marked selection.* There are $n$ possibilities for the label of the start. Moving clockwise from the start, number the selected plots $1, 2, \dots, k$ in the order we reach them, so the start is selected plot $1$. For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots between selected plot $i$ and the next selected plot clockwise. For $i = k$, the next selected plot is the start again. When $k = 1$, this means $g_1$ counts all the other plots before we return to the start, so $g_1 = n-1$.

Each unselected plot lies in exactly one of these gaps, so

$$
g_1 + g_2 + \cdots + g_k = n-k.
$$

If two selected plots are neighbors, then going clockwise from one of them we reach the other immediately. The other is then the next selected plot, and the gap between them is $0$. Conversely, $g_i = 0$ means that selected plot $i$ and the next selected plot are neighbors. Because $g_k$ is the gap leading from the last selected plot back to the start, the gaps cover the whole circle, so this includes the pair that meets across the circular boundary. A selection is therefore valid exactly when every $g_i$ is a positive integer.

Conversely, take any start label and any positive integers $g_1, \dots, g_k$ with sum $n-k$. Select the start, skip $g_1$ plots clockwise and select the next plot, skip $g_2$ plots and select the next, and continue in this way. After skipping $g_k$ plots, we have passed $k + (n-k) = n$ distinct plots, so the next plot is the start. This gives a marked selection of exactly $k$ plots with gaps $g_1, \dots, g_k$, and it is valid because every gap is positive. Building a selection from a start and a tuple, and recording the start and gaps of a marked selection, undo each other. So a start and a tuple uniquely give a marked selection, and conversely.

The plots have distinct fixed labels, so a selection and a rotation of it around the circle are different selections. The $n$ choices of start therefore all count separately, and there is no rotation to divide out.

*Counting the gap tuples.* It remains to count ordered tuples $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Place $n-k$ objects in a row. There are $n-k-1$ internal spaces between neighboring objects, and since $k \le n/2$, there are at least $k-1$ of them. Choose $k-1$ internal spaces and put one separator in each. The separators cut the row into $k$ blocks, and each block is nonempty because no two separators share a space and no separator sits at either end of the row. Letting $g_i$ be the number of objects in the $i$th block from the left gives a tuple of positive integers with sum $n-k$.

Conversely, a tuple determines the separators. They go after the first $g_1$ objects, after the first $g_1 + g_2$ objects, and so on up to the first $g_1 + \cdots + g_{k-1}$ objects. Since every $g_i \ge 1$, these are distinct internal spaces. Hence the number of tuples is

$$
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

For $k = 1$ there are no separators, $\binom{n-2}{0} = 1$, and the single tuple is $g_1 = n-1$.

When $n$ is even and $k = n/2$, the $k$ gaps sum to $n-k = k$ and each is at least $1$, so every gap is one. Gaps of one are allowed, so this case is included in the count.

*Combining the counts.* Each pair is determined by one of the $n$ start labels together with one gap tuple, so counting the pairs both ways gives

$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Each valid selection was counted exactly $k$ times on the left, and $k \ge 1$, so we may divide by $k$:

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

To reach the stated form, we expand the factorials. Since $k \le n/2$, we have $n - 2k \ge 0$, so the factorials below are defined, and $n-k \ge n/2 > 0$, so the factor $n-k$ can be cancelled:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{n-k}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&= \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The second line uses $(n-k)! = (n-k)\,(n-k-1)!$ and $k! = k\,(k-1)!$. The third uses $(n-k-1) - (k-1) = n-2k$. Therefore

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}. \qquad \blacksquare
$$

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) distinctly labeled garden plots in a circle. For \(0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) count the \(k\)-element selections with no neighboring plots selected, including neighbors across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), there is exactly one selection: the empty selection. The formula also gives \(1\), since
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom n0=1.
\]

Now assume \(k\ge1\). Count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Each valid selection has exactly \(k\) choices for this mark, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) marked selections.

We can also construct a marked selection by first choosing its start plot, in \(n\) ways. Beginning there, number the selected plots clockwise. Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, with the last gap returning to the start. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

The no-neighbors condition says that every \(g_i\) is positive. Since the gaps contain all the unselected plots exactly once,
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]
To count these ordered gap lists, put \(n-k\) objects in a row and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators. The resulting \(k\) nonempty groups have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\), and every positive gap list arises uniquely this way. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap lists. For \(k=1\), choosing no separators gives the single required gap.

A start plot and a gap list determine a unique marked selection: move clockwise, leaving \(g_i\) unselected plots after each selected plot before reaching the next. The \(k\) selected plots and the \(n-k\) gap plots fill exactly one circuit, so the last gap closes at the start. Conversely, reading the gaps of a marked selection recovers that start and list. Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly \(k\) times, once for each selected plot that could be marked. Hence
\[
A(n,k)=\frac nk\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac nk\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), all gaps equal \(1\), which the construction allows. No division by rotations is needed: the labels occupy fixed positions, and choosing a different start is precisely the marking already accounted for. \(\square\)

gap tuples. For \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain the single group of size \(n-1\).

A start and a gap tuple determine exactly one marked selection: move clockwise from the start, leaving \(g_i\) unselected plots before placing the next selected plot. Because
\[

\]
this construction goes exactly once around the circle and returns to the start. Recovering the start and gaps from the marked selection reverses the construction. Therefore,
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly once for each of its \(k\) selected plots. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n(n-k-1)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, which the construction allows. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have fixed, distinct labels, so selections using different labels are different selections. \(\square\)

\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the empty selection is the only selection. The formula also gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now assume \(k\ge1\). We count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Every valid selection has exactly \(k\) choices for this mark, so the number of marked selections is
\[
kA(n,k).
\]

We can also construct a marked selection by choosing its start and the gaps between its selected plots. There are \(n\) choices for the start. Beginning there, number the selected plots \(1,\ldots,k\) in clockwise order, and let \(g_i\) count the unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot. The last gap returns to the start, so it includes the circular boundary. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

The condition on neighbors says that every gap is positive. Since there are \(n-k\) unselected plots altogether,
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,
\qquad g_i\ge1.
\]
To count these ordered gap tuples, place \(n-k\) objects in a row. Choosing \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators divides the row into \(k\) nonempty blocks, whose sizes are \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\). Conversely, each such tuple determines those separator positions. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap tuples. For \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain the single gap \(g_1=n-1\).

A chosen start and gap tuple determine a unique marked selection: move clockwise from the start, leaving \(g_i\) plots unselected after selected plot \(i\). Because
\[
k+\sum_{i=1}^k g_i=n,
\]
this construction goes exactly once around the circle and returns to the start. Conversely, a marked selection determines its start and every gap. Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly once for each of its \(k\) possible marks. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, so this case is included. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have distinct fixed labels, and the only extra choice we introduced was the marked start. \(\square\)
