# Map Archive: Trial Change to Retrieval

For the next six weeks, the map archive will trial a different arrangement for retrieving material. The reading room will keep its usual opening times. The change affects retrieval, not access. Access has sometimes been taken to mean that every item can be brought upstairs immediately, and during the trial that will not be the case.

## How to request a map

- **Requests received before noon** will be collected together and retrieved at two o'clock.
- **There will be no second afternoon retrieval** during the trial.
- **Include a shelfmark.** A request needs a shelfmark to join the retrieval.

You do not need to arrive before noon. It is the request that must arrive by then, not you. If you have requested a map in advance, you can come later in the day. If you arrive later without a request, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves, and you can submit a request for the next opening day.

## Requests without a shelfmark

Requests without a shelfmark will be held while staff help you identify the item. Once it is identified, the request will join the next retrieval. That may not be on the day the request was first received.

## Fragile maps

Maps already identified as fragile need a support prepared by the conservation team. The team will contact you with an appointment, and the two o'clock retrieval does not apply to these appointments.

The catalogue shows which maps are affected. Occasionally an item is found to need support only when staff retrieve it. In that case, staff will contact you.

## Why we are doing this

The trial is intended to reduce interruptions in the store. It is not a reduction in opening hours. Before deciding whether to continue, we will count delayed requests and review reader comments. A comment card will be available at the desk throughout the trial, and we welcome your views.

The amber indicator on the curing-line monitor appeared just after washdown on three of the last five morning shifts. It means the humidity probe’s reading is outside the range accepted by the controller; it does not establish whether the room is too humid or the probe’s reading is unreliable. The other display, often called the “backup,” measures temperature only, so a normal reading there cannot resolve a humidity question.

On all three mornings, the amber indicator cleared within twelve minutes. Operators wiped moisture from the outside of the probe housing on two mornings; on the third, nobody touched it. These observations are consistent with moisture around the housing, but they do not establish that wiping cleared the warning. The housing is not the sensing element. Wiping is recorded here as an observation, not as a recommended remedy.

For now, record when the indicator appears, when it clears, and whether washdown has finished. Do not open the housing. If the indicator remains amber after fifteen minutes, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may request a handheld humidity check using the unit kept in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading does not give standing permission to restart; the shift lead must make that decision.

Maintenance has been asked to inspect the seal at the next planned stop. This request does not establish that the seal has failed. Continue recording mornings when no warning appears by marking the “no warning” box beside the log’s time fields. Recording both warnings and mornings without warnings is necessary to show how often the pattern occurs.

response:
Shift handover note: amber indicator on the curing-line monitor

What has been observed. On three of the last five morning shifts, the amber indicator on the curing-line monitor came on shortly after washdown. On each of those three mornings it cleared within twelve minutes. On two of the mornings the operator wiped moisture from the outside of the probe housing before it cleared. On the third morning nobody touched the probe and it cleared anyway. We do not yet have a record of the mornings on which no warning appeared, which matters for the reason given at the end of this note.

What the indicator means. The amber indicator shows that the humidity probe is reporting a value outside the range the controller accepts. It does not tell us which of two things is happening: the room may actually be too humid, or the probe may be giving an unreliable reading. The second display, the one people have been calling the backup, measures temperature only. A normal number on that display therefore says nothing about humidity and cannot settle the question either way.

Our working explanation, and its limits. The pattern fits moisture collecting around the probe housing after washdown. That is a plausible explanation, not a confirmed one. The fact that the warning cleared after wiping on two mornings does not show that wiping cleared it, because it also cleared on a morning when nobody wiped anything. The housing is also not the sensing element, so moisture on the outside of it may or may not affect the reading. This note records the wiping because it happened, not because it is the remedy. Please do not treat it as one.

What to do for now. Each time the indicator appears, record the time it came on, the time it cleared, and whether washdown had finished when it appeared. Do not open the housing. If the indicator is still amber fifteen minutes after it came on, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may ask for a handheld humidity check. The handheld unit is kept in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading is information for the lead, not permission to restart. The decision to restart belongs to the shift lead in every case.

What is already in motion. We have asked maintenance to inspect the probe seal at the next planned stop. That request is a precaution. It does not mean the seal has failed, and nobody should treat it as a finding.

One more request. Please also record the mornings on which no warning appears. The log has a 'no warning' box beside the time fields for this purpose. A log that contains only the mornings with warnings cannot tell us how often the pattern actually occurs, and without that we cannot judge whether the explanation above is right.

On two of those mornings the operator wiped moisture from the outside of the probe housing. On the third morning nobody touched the probe.

The room may really be too humid, or the probe may be giving an unreliable reading. The second display, which people have been calling the backup, cannot answer that question either. It measures temperature only, so a normal number there tells us nothing about humidity.

**Our working explanation, and its limits.** What we have seen fits the idea that moisture is collecting around the probe housing after washdown. It does not show that wiping the housing cleared the warning. On the morning nobody wiped it, the indicator cleared anyway. Also, the housing is not the sensing element itself. For these reasons the wiping is recorded here as something that happened, not recommended as a fix. We have also asked maintenance to inspect the seal at the next planned stop. That request is a check on one possible cause. It does not mean the seal has failed.

**What you need to do.** Each morning, record the time the indicator appears, the time it clears, and whether washdown had finished. Do not open the probe housing. If the indicator is still amber after fifteen minutes, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may ask for a check with the handheld humidity unit, which is kept in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading does not by itself give permission to restart. That decision belongs to the shift lead.

Please also log the mornings when no warning appears, using the "no warning" box beside the time fields. A log that lists only warnings cannot tell us how often the pattern actually happens.

For that reason this note records the wiping without recommending it as a remedy. Maintenance has been asked to inspect the seal at the next planned stop. That request is not a finding that the seal has failed.

**What is required now.** Record the time the indicator appears, the time it clears, and whether washdown has finished. Do not open the housing. If the indicator is still amber after fifteen minutes, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may ask for a handheld humidity check, and the handheld unit is kept in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading is not a standing permission to restart. That decision belongs to the shift lead.

**Keep logging the quiet mornings.** Please also record mornings on which no warning appears. A list containing only warnings cannot show how often the pattern occurs. The log has a "no warning" box beside the time fields for this purpose.

The listening gallery offers two ways to hear the recorded accounts. You can use the fixed headphones beside each case, or borrow a receiver at the welcome desk to listen through the room’s induction loop. Receivers are free, and no booking is needed. We have six receivers, so one may not be available immediately.

Every recording also has a printed transcript in the drawer beneath its case. The transcripts describe sounds that matter to the account, such as a bell or a pause interrupted by machinery, but not every background sound. Large-print copies are available at the welcome desk. You are welcome to take them into the gallery; please return them before leaving.

At half past each hour, a three-minute sound sequence plays through the room’s speakers. A light above the entrance comes on one minute before it begins. If you would rather avoid the sequence, you can leave through either doorway and return afterward. The recordings at the cases pause during the sequence, then resume from where they stopped.

On Wednesday mornings, from opening until noon, the speaker sequence is switched off. The case recordings and induction loop remain available. These mornings are quieter, but we cannot promise silence: people still talk, doors open, and school groups sometimes visit.

You are welcome to ask a gallery host for help with the equipment or for a seat. Hosts can explain the available options, though they cannot reserve a receiver or keep the room quiet for an individual visit. If you prefer to read before coming, you can request the same transcripts from the visitor team.

response:
The listening gallery offers two ways to hear the recorded accounts. You can use the fixed headphones beside each case or borrow a receiver from the welcome desk to listen through the room’s induction loop. The receiver is free, and you don’t need to book one. We have six receivers, so one may not be available straight away.

A printed transcript of each recording is in the drawer beneath its case. Transcripts describe sounds that matter to the account, such as a bell or a pause interrupted by machinery, but not every background sound. Large-print copies are available from the welcome desk and may be taken into the gallery. Please return them before you leave.

At half past each hour, the room plays a three-minute sound sequence through its speakers. A light above the entrance comes on one minute before it starts. If you’d rather avoid the sequence, you can leave through either doorway and return afterward. The recordings at the cases pause during the sequence and resume from where they stopped.

On Wednesday mornings, from opening until noon, the speaker sequence is switched off. The case recordings and induction loop remain available. These mornings are quieter, but we can’t promise silence: people still talk, doors open, and school groups sometimes visit.

You’re welcome to ask a gallery host for help with the equipment or for a seat. Hosts can explain the available options, but they can’t reserve a receiver or keep the room quiet for an individual visit. If you’d prefer to read before coming, you can request the same transcripts from the visitor team.

response:
Rain can alter acoustic recordings as well as animal calling, complicating comparisons between wet and dry surveys. This pilot examined whether a rain shield changed the output of a fixed call detector. It did not estimate animal abundance; calling activity itself is an ecological outcome only when it matches the question being asked.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, with shielded and exposed positions assigned by coin toss within each patch. The recorders operated simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, yielding 144 paired windows: 48 classified as wet and 96 as dry from field logs. Weather was observed, not assigned. A window was positive if the detector marked at least one target call, using the same detector settings throughout.

During wet windows, the recorders agreed in 29 of 48 pairs; twelve pairs were positive only on the shielded recorder and seven only on the exposed recorder. During dry windows, they agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement includes both jointly positive and jointly negative pairs, which were not separated in this summary. The agreement counts therefore cannot be interpreted as the number of windows containing calls.

The excess of shield-only over exposed-only positives during wet windows is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. The direction of discordance was reversed during dry windows. These descriptive patterns do not establish that shielding recovered genuine calls: without independent call labels, we cannot determine whether discordant detections reflect true calls or detector errors. Nor do the results establish that rain reduced calling. Weather was not experimentally assigned, and repeated windows within patches mean that the 144 paired windows are not 144 independent ecological replicates.

The paired comparison identifies a measurement issue to resolve before using these recordings to infer ecological trends. A future study could include blinded human labeling to assess detection validity and more patches to broaden replication. For now, the data describe disagreement between shielded and exposed recordings within the observed weather categories, while leaving its biological interpretation open.

response:
Rain can alter a recording as well as animal calling, complicating comparisons between wet and dry surveys. This pilot examined whether a rain shield changed the output of a fixed call detector. It did not estimate animal abundance; calling activity itself is an ecological outcome only when it matches the study question.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed, with shield status assigned to the two positions by a coin toss. The devices recorded simultaneously, and detector settings remained fixed. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, yielding 144 paired windows. Field logs classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry; weather was not experimentally assigned. A recording was classified as positive when the detector marked at least one target call.

In wet conditions, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. Of the discordant pairs, twelve were positive only on the shielded device and seven only on the exposed device. In dry conditions, the devices agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only positives and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement includes both joint positives and joint negatives, which were not separated in this summary. The agreement counts therefore cannot be interpreted as counts of windows containing calls.

The direction of discordance differed between the observed weather categories: shield-only positives exceeded exposed-only positives in wet windows, whereas exposed-only positives slightly exceeded shield-only positives in dry windows. Without independent call labeling, however, it cannot show whether the additional positives represented genuine calls or detection errors. Nor does it establish that rain reduced calling. Weather was observational, and repeated windows within patches mean that the 144 paired windows were not 144 independent ecological replicates.

The pilot thus identifies a measurement question that should be addressed before these recordings are used to infer ecological trends. Blinded human labeling could help distinguish genuine calls from detection errors, and sampling more patches could broaden the comparison. For the present data, the supported conclusion is descriptive: the paired devices showed different patterns of discordance in wet and dry windows, while the biological interpretation remains unresolved.

**Results and discussion (revised)**

Rain can change a recording before it changes the behaviour of the animals being recorded. A difference between wet and dry surveys may therefore reflect the measurement rather than the calling, and only calling is the ecological quantity of interest. This pilot asked a narrower question: does a rain shield change the output of one fixed call detector? We did not attempt to estimate the number of animals.

**Design.** In each of twelve habitat patches we deployed two recorders, one shielded and one exposed. Position within a patch was assigned by coin toss, and the two devices recorded simultaneously. From each patch we analysed twelve paired ten-minute windows, for 144 paired windows in total. Using the field log, we classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry. Weather was observed, not assigned. A window was scored positive when the detector marked at least one target call, and detector settings were held constant throughout.

**Device agreement.** Agreement here means both devices positive or both negative. We have not separated these two kinds of agreement, so the agreement counts should not be read as the number of windows containing calls.

| Condition | Paired windows | Devices agree | Shield-only positive | Exposed-only positive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wet | 48 | 29 | 12 | 7 |
| Dry | 96 | 84 | 5 | 7 |

Under rain, disagreement was more common and was skewed toward the shielded device. In dry windows, disagreement was rarer and showed no such skew.

**Interpretation.** The excess of shield-only over exposed-only positives in wet windows is consistent with shielding altering detector output under rain. It does not show that the shield recovered genuine calls, because no independent labelling of calls was performed. It also does not show that rain reduced calling. Because windows were repeated within patches, the 144 pairs are not 144 independent ecological replicates. These limitations constrain what the data can say, but they do not undermine the paired comparison as evidence about where the two devices disagree.

**Implications.** The pilot identifies a measurement question that should be resolved before these recordings are used to estimate an ecological trend. A follow-up study would add blinded human labelling of calls and more patches. That study has not been run. For the present data we can report the direction of discordance and its dependence on observed weather category, while leaving the biological interpretation open.

This matters when we compare wet and dry surveys, because a difference in the call count could come from the recording. It could also be a change in calling, which is the ecological quantity of interest only if the question concerns calling. Our pilot therefore asked whether a rain shield changes the output of one fixed call detector. We did not attempt to estimate the number of animals.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed. In each patch, a coin toss assigned the shielded and exposed recorders to the two positions, and the two devices recorded simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, for 144 paired windows in total. Weather was not assigned. Using the field log, we classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry. A window was positive when the detector marked at least one target call, and the detector settings were the same throughout.

In wet windows, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. The shielded device alone was positive in twelve pairs and the exposed device alone in seven. In dry windows, they agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement covers pairs in which both devices were positive as well as pairs in which neither was. This summary does not separate the two, so the agreement counts should not be read as the number of windows with calls.

In wet windows, shield-only positives outnumbered exposed-only positives. This is consistent with the shield changing detector output under rain. It does not establish that the shield recovered genuine calls, because calls were not independently labeled. Nor does it establish that rain reduced calling. In addition, the windows are repeated within patches, so the 144 paired windows should not be treated as 144 independent ecological replicates. These limitations matter, but they do not make the paired comparison uninformative about disagreement between the devices.

The pilot identifies a measurement question to examine before these recordings are used to study an ecological trend. response:
Rain can affect acoustic recordings as well as animal calling, complicating comparisons between wet and dry surveys. This pilot examined whether a rain shield changed the output of a fixed call detector. It did not estimate animal abundance or distinguish changes in recording performance from changes in calling activity.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed, with the two positions assigned by coin toss within each patch. The devices recorded simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, yielding 144 paired windows: 48 classified as wet and 96 as dry from field logs. Weather was observed, not assigned. A window was classified as positive when the detector marked at least one target call; detector settings remained constant throughout.

During wet windows, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. The shielded device alone was positive in twelve pairs, and the exposed device alone in seven. During dry windows, the devices agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only positives and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement includes both jointly positive and jointly negative pairs, which were not separated in this summary. The agreement counts therefore cannot be interpreted as the number of windows containing calls.

The direction of discordance differed between the observed weather categories: shield-only positives exceeded exposed-only positives in wet windows, whereas exposed-only positives slightly exceeded shield-only positives in dry windows. This pattern is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. Because windows were repeated within patches, the 144 paired windows should not be treated as independent ecological replicates; the study included twelve patches.

The pilot identifies a measurement issue to resolve before using these recordings to infer ecological trends. A future study could include blinded human labeling and more patches to assess detection accuracy and the consistency of the pattern. For the present data, the paired comparison describes disagreement and its direction within observed weather categories, while leaving the biological interpretation open.

response:
## Results and discussion

Rain can affect a recording before it affects the animals being recorded. This matters when comparing wet and dry surveys, because a change in detections could reflect the recording, the calling, or both. Calling is the ecological quantity of interest only if the question concerns calling. This pilot asked a narrower question: does a rain shield change the output of one fixed call detector? We did not try to estimate the number of animals.

**Design.** We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed. A coin toss assigned the two positions within each patch, and the devices recorded simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, giving 144 paired windows. The field log classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry. Weather was not assigned, so the wet/dry contrast is observational. A window was scored positive if the detector marked at least one target call, and detector settings were identical throughout.

**Results.** Table 1 gives the paired outcomes by weather category.

| Weather | Pairs | Devices agreed | Shield-only positive | Exposed-only positive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wet | 48 | 29 | 12 | 7 |
| Dry | 96 | 84 | 5 | 7 |

Disagreement was thus 19 of 48 pairs in wet windows and 12 of 96 in dry windows. In wet windows, shield-only positives exceeded exposed-only positives (12 vs. 7). In dry windows the direction was slightly reversed (5 vs. 7). "Agreed" combines pairs in which both devices were positive with pairs in which neither was, and we have not separated these here. The agreement counts therefore cannot be read as the number of windows containing calls.

**Interpretation.** The wet-window excess of shield-only over exposed-only positives is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. Several limits apply:

- No independent labeling of calls was done, so the data cannot show that the shield recovered genuine calls rather than, for example, producing different false positives.
- The data do not show that rain reduced calling. Both devices sat in the same patch at the same time, and the comparison concerns how they differ in detector output, not how much the animals called.
- The 144 windows are repeated measures within twelve patches and are not independent ecological replicates. The effective sample is closer to the number of patches, and the discordant counts are small.
- Weather was not assigned, so wet and dry windows may differ in other ways, such as time of day or patch. The contrast between the wet and dry patterns is descriptive and should not be treated as an estimated interaction.

These limits do not make the paired comparison uninformative about disagreement. Randomizing shield position within patches means that systematic differences between the two devices within a patch are unlikely to stem from position alone.

**Implications.** The pilot identifies a measurement question to resolve before these recordings are used for an ecological trend. A follow-up could add blinded human labeling of calls, report both-positive and both-negative agreement separately, and include more patches. That study has not been run. For the present data, we report the direction of discordance and its dependence on the observed weather categories, and we leave the biological interpretation open.

response:
**Results and Discussion**

Rain can degrade a recording before it affects the animals being counted. This matters when wet and dry surveys are compared, because a change in the count could reflect a change in calling. That change is the ecological quantity of interest only if the question concerns calling. Our pilot asked a narrower question: does a rain shield change the output of one fixed call detector? We did not attempt to estimate the number of animals.

**Design.** We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed. A coin toss assigned the two positions within each patch, and the devices recorded simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, giving 144 paired windows. From the field log, 48 windows were classified as wet and 96 as dry. Weather was not assigned, so the wet/dry contrast is observational. A window was scored positive when the detector marked at least one target call, and detector settings were identical throughout.

**Results.** In wet windows, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. The shielded device alone was positive in 12 pairs and the exposed device alone in 7. In dry windows, the devices agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with 5 shield-only and 7 exposed-only positives.

Agreement here combines pairs in which both devices were positive with pairs in which neither was. We have not separated these two kinds of agreement, so the agreement counts must not be read as the number of windows containing calls.

**Discussion.** In wet conditions, shield-only positives outnumbered exposed-only positives (12 vs. 7). In dry conditions the discordant pairs were balanced slightly the other way (5 vs. 7). This pattern is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain.

Several limits constrain the interpretation:

- No independent labeling of calls was performed, so the result does not show that the shield recovered genuine calls.
- It does not show that rain reduced calling.
- Windows within patches are repeated measures, so 144 is not the number of independent ecological replicates.
- Because weather was not assigned, wet and dry windows may differ in other respects.

These limitations do not make the paired comparison uninformative about disagreement between devices. They restrict what the disagreement can be taken to mean.

The pilot therefore identifies a measurement question to resolve before these recordings are used for an ecological trend. A next study could add blinded human labeling and more patches, but it has not been run. For the present data, we can report the direction of discordance and how it differs between the observed weather categories. The biological interpretation remains open.

Of the 600 households invited to our library-use survey, 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Among these respondents, 252 reported using a library in the previous month: 70 percent. This figure described the initial respondents, as the preliminary note stated. It did not establish the percentage among all invited households, although it was sometimes interpreted that way.

The telephone follow-up added information from 90 of the 240 initial nonrespondents. Interviewers stopped when they reached the budgeted total of 90 completed interviews. These households were not a simple random sample of the initial nonrespondents: inclusion depended on whether interviewers could reach them and whether they agreed to participate. Of the 90, 42 reported library use in the previous month, or approximately 46.7 percent.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, or approximately 65.3 percent. The decline from 70 to 65.3 percent shows how the descriptive result changed when the follow-up households joined the respondent pool. The follow-up respondents reported library use less often than the initial respondents. Although both stages used the same question and reference month, households were not randomly assigned to questionnaire or telephone modes. We therefore cannot separate differences between the people reached from any effect of how the question was administered.

The follow-up broadened the observed group, but it did not establish that nonresponse had been corrected. No weights or imputed responses were used, and 150 households still provided no response. We do not know whether those households resemble either responding group. Treating the combined percentage as an estimate for all 600 invitees would require assumptions that this study did not evaluate.

The report should retain the results from both stages and present 65.3 percent as the percentage among all responding households. This preserves the follow-up’s concrete contribution—additional responses that changed the observed result—while making clear that library use among all invited households remains unknown.

response:
**What the follow-up changed**

The preliminary note reported that 70 percent of respondents had used a library in the previous month. That figure was accurate for the people who returned the initial questionnaire. In later discussion it was sometimes read as a figure for all invited households, which it never was.

The stages of the survey are summarized below.

| Stage | Households | Reported library use | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Invited | 600 | unknown | unknown |
| Returned initial questionnaire | 360 | 252 | 70.0% |
| Reached by telephone follow-up | 90 | 42 | 46.7% |
| All responding households combined | 450 | 294 | 65.3% |
| Still no response | 150 | unknown | unknown |

The telephone follow-up approached the 240 households that had not returned the questionnaire. The budget allowed 90 completed interviews, and interviewers stopped once that number was reached. The 90 households were therefore not a random draw from the 240. Whether a household could be reached, and whether it agreed to take part, both shaped who ended up in the group. The follow-up used the same question and the same reference month as the questionnaire, but households were not randomly assigned to one mode or the other.

Combining the two stages moves the observed share from 70 percent to about 65 percent. That shift is a fact about the pool of people who answered. It shows that the households reached by telephone reported library use less often than the households that returned the questionnaire. This is the concrete information the follow-up added, and it is worth reporting on its own terms.

**What remains unknown**

The combined figure is not an estimate for all 600 invited households. A quarter of them, 150, still gave no answer, and nothing in the data shows whether they resemble the questionnaire respondents, the telephone respondents, or neither. The follow-up also cannot separate two possible explanations for the lower telephone figure. The people reached by telephone may differ from the people who mailed back the questionnaire, or the telephone mode itself may elicit different answers. Both could be true, and the design does not distinguish them.

It is tempting to call the follow-up an adjustment for nonresponse, since it reached people who were missing from the first calculation. In a descriptive sense it did widen the observed group. In the statistical sense, however, an adjustment would mean the remaining nonresponse has been corrected for, and that claim would rest on assumptions that were not evaluated here. No weights were applied and no responses were imputed. The combined figure is simply a larger observed group, not a corrected population estimate.

**How the report should present this**

The report should keep both stages visible rather than replacing the first percentage with the combined one as if it were final. The value of the follow-up lies in showing how much the result moved when a different set of households answered. The combined figure should be accompanied by a plain statement of what is still unknown about the 150 silent households. That statement should sit alongside the result, not bury it.

**What the Follow-Up Changed, and What It Did Not**

Our survey of library use invited 600 households. Of these, 360 returned the initial questionnaire, and 252 of those 360 reported using a library in the previous month. That is 70 percent, and it was the figure circulated in the preliminary note. The note correctly presented it as a description of respondents. In later discussion, however, it was sometimes treated as if it described all invited households. It does not. It tells us about the 360 households that answered, not the 600 that were asked.

To learn more about the 240 households that did not return the questionnaire, we contacted them by telephone. The budget allowed 90 completed interviews. Interviewers worked through their contact attempts and stopped when they reached 90. This group was therefore not a random draw from the 240 nonrespondents. Who ended up in it depended on which households could be reached and which agreed to take part. Of the 90 interviewed households, 42 reported library use in the previous month, about 46.7 percent.

When the 360 questionnaires and 90 interviews are combined, 294 of 450 responding households reported library use, about 65.3 percent. This drop from 70 to 65.3 percent reflects a change in who is counted among respondents. It shows that the households reached by telephone reported library use less often than the households that returned the first questionnaire.

Three things remain unknown:

- **The rate among all 600 invited households.** Even after the follow-up, 150 households gave no response. We have no information about their library use, and we do not know whether they resemble the initial respondents, the telephone respondents, or neither.
- **Whether the gap reflects the people or the method.** Both stages asked the same question about the same reference month. Households were not randomly assigned to questionnaire or telephone, though. The lower rate in the follow-up could come from differences between the kinds of households reached, from people answering differently on the phone than on paper, or from both. These data cannot separate the two.
- **Whether the remaining nonresponse has been corrected.** The follow-up broadens the group we observed, because it includes households missing from the first calculation. That does not mean it corrects for nonresponse in a statistical sense. Making that claim would require assumptions about the remaining 150 households that we have not tested. We applied no weighting and filled in no missing answers.

For these reasons, the report should present both figures: 70 percent among initial respondents and about 65.3 percent among all respondents after follow-up. The combined figure should not replace the first as a final estimate for all invited households. The value of the follow-up lies in showing how much the result moved once another group answered. The combined figure should be accompanied by a plain statement that the 150 households still unheard from could move it further, in a direction we cannot predict.

# What the Follow-Up Changed, and What Remains Unknown

A percentage based on early returns can look like it answers more than it does. In our survey of library use, we invited 600 households, and 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Of those 360, 252 reported using a library in the previous month, or 70 percent. The preliminary note reported this figure as a description of the households that responded, which is accurate. In later discussion, however, it was sometimes treated as a description of all 600 invited households. It is not. The 70 percent figure tells us nothing directly about the 240 households that did not return the questionnaire.

To learn more about those 240 households, we contacted them by telephone. The budget covered 90 completed interviews, so interviewers kept making contact attempts until 90 interviews were finished and then stopped. As a result, the 90 households were not a random draw from the 240. Two things decided who was included: whether an interviewer managed to reach a household, and whether that household agreed to take part. Of the 90 households interviewed, 42 reported library use in the previous month, about 46.7 percent. The telephone interview used the same question and the same reference month as the questionnaire. However, the two groups answered in different ways, one by returning a questionnaire and the other by speaking with an interviewer. We did not randomly assign households to one way of answering or the other.

Combining the two groups gives the following picture:

| Group | Households | Reported library use in previous month | Percent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial questionnaire respondents | 360 | 252 | 70.0 |
| Telephone follow-up respondents | 90 | 42 | about 46.7 |
| All respondents combined | 450 | 294 | about 65.3 |
| No response at either stage | 150 | unknown | unknown |
| All invited households | 600 | unknown | unknown |

The move from 70 to 65.3 percent reflects a change in which households are being counted. It is evidence that the households reached by telephone reported library use less often than the households that returned the questionnaire. The follow-up does not answer two other questions.

First, it does not tell us how common library use is among all 600 invited households. The 65.3 percent figure describes the 450 households that responded at either stage. The remaining 150 households still gave us no answer.

Second, it does not tell us why the two groups differ. The telephone respondents differ from the questionnaire respondents in two ways at once: they are different households, and they answered by a different method. Because we did not randomly assign the method of answering, we cannot separate the two. Some of the gap could reflect real differences in library use between the households, and some could reflect how people answer when speaking with an interviewer. The data do not show how much of the gap comes from each.

It might seem natural to call the follow-up an adjustment for nonresponse, since it brings in households missing from the first calculation. In a plain descriptive sense, that is fair: the group we observe is larger and now includes some households that did not respond at first. In the stricter statistical sense, though, calling it an adjustment would imply that the remaining nonresponse had been corrected for. That claim would depend on assumptions about the 150 households that never responded, and we have not evaluated those assumptions. We did not give any responses extra weight to stand in for missing households, and we did not fill in estimated answers for households that gave none.

The report should therefore present both stages rather than replacing the 70 percent figure with 65.3 percent as if the second were a final estimate for all invited households. The value of the follow-up lies in the comparison: it shows how far the result moved once another group of households answered. We still do not know whether the 150 remaining households resemble the questionnaire respondents, the telephone respondents, or neither. That uncertainty should be stated alongside the combined figure, without obscuring the concrete information the follow-up added.

# What the Follow-Up Changes and What Remains Unknown

An early return rate can look like an answer to a question it has not answered. In our survey of library use, 600 households were invited and 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Of those 360, 252 reported using a library in the previous month, which is 70 percent of initial respondents. This figure appeared in the preliminary note, which described it as a finding about respondents. In later discussion it was sometimes treated as a description of all invited households, and that reading is not supported.

**What the follow-up added.** We approached the 240 initial nonrespondents by telephone. The follow-up budget covered 90 completed interviews, and interviewers worked through contact attempts until 90 were done. The 90 households are therefore not a simple random sample of the 240. Which households entered the group depended on whether interviewers could reach them and whether they agreed to take part. Forty-two of the 90 reported library use in the previous month, about 46.7 percent. The question and reference month were the same as in the questionnaire, but mode was not randomly assigned.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, about 65.3 percent. The shift from 70 to 65.3 percent is a change in the observed respondent pool. It shows that the initial respondents and the reached follow-up respondents differed in what they reported, and this is the concrete information the follow-up contributed.

**What the follow-up does not settle.** The combined figure does not tell us the prevalence among all 600 invitees, because 150 households still gave no response. It also cannot separate two explanations for the gap between 70 and 46.7 percent. One is a telephone-mode effect on how people answered. The other is a real difference between the people who answered by questionnaire and the people reached by phone. Without random assignment of mode, the two are entangled.

**Not an adjustment for nonresponse.** We considered describing the follow-up as an adjustment for nonresponse. In a descriptive sense it does broaden the observed group by including people absent from the first calculation. In the statistical sense, though, saying the remaining nonresponse has been corrected would require assumptions that we have not evaluated. No weights or imputed responses were used, and the combined figure should not be read as a corrected estimate.

**Recommendation for reporting.** The report should keep both stages visible rather than replacing the first percentage with a supposedly final population estimate:

| Stage | Households | Reported library use | Percent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial questionnaire | 360 | 252 | 70.0 |
| Telephone follow-up | 90 | 42 | about 46.7 |
| Combined respondents | 450 | 294 | about 65.3 |
| No response | 150 | unknown | unknown |

We do not know whether the 150 remaining households resemble either responding group. The combined figure should be accompanied by a plain statement of that uncertainty. The statement should not obscure what the follow-up showed: the descriptive result moved noticeably once a different group answered.

response:
The persistence rule was motivated by the concern that a single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault. It requires two threshold crossings within a cycle before raising an alarm, whereas the comparison rule uses a higher threshold and alarms after one crossing. Both thresholds and the persistence requirement were fixed using a separate setup recording; the evaluation recordings were not used to select them. Because the persistence rule also uses a lower threshold, the comparison evaluates two fixed rules rather than isolating the effect of persistence.

The held-out bench set comprised 120 machine cycles from one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 with no induced fault. Each rule produced at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule alarmed in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and eight of the 90 no-fault cycles; the comparison rule alarmed in 21 fault cycles and three no-fault cycles. Thus, the persistence rule detected more induced faults but also alarmed more often in cycles designated no-fault. This designation means only that no fault was induced: the machine was not dismantled after every cycle to exclude all possible defects.

Eighteen fault cycles triggered both rules. Within this shared subset, the mean time from logged fault onset to the first alarm was 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Comparing delays on the same cycles avoids differences arising from the composition of the detected sets. However, it excludes faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both, so the delay result applies only to shared detections.

The observed benefit therefore differs from the rule’s motivation. Although persistence was introduced to address transient spikes, this experiment showed higher detection of induced faults at the cost of more alarms in no-fault cycles. Neither the rule’s construction nor these results establish better false-alarm control.

These recordings evaluate two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. No preferred rule was selected because that choice depends on the relative costs of missing a fault and interrupting a cycle, neither of which was measured.

Here is the revised passage.

---

The persistence rule was introduced to address a specific problem: a single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault. The rule therefore uses a lower threshold and requires two threshold crossings within a cycle before it raises an alarm. The comparison rule uses a higher threshold and alarms after one crossing. Both thresholds and the two-crossing requirement were fixed in advance from a separate setup recording; the evaluation recordings played no part in choosing them. It is tempting to describe the new rule simply as a way to reduce false alarms. That description is incomplete, because the lower threshold does not only filter alarms. It also changes which cycles are capable of producing one. The persistence condition and the lower threshold pull in opposite directions, and the rule's construction alone does not settle which effect dominates. The results below are read with that in mind.

The held-out bench set contains 120 machine cycles recorded on one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 with no induced fault. Each rule produces at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule alarms in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and in eight of the 90 no-fault cycles. The comparison rule alarms in 21 of the 30 fault cycles and in three of the 90 no-fault cycles. In this set, then, the persistence rule detects more of the induced faults and also alarms more often in the cycles designated no-fault. The designation carries a caveat. "No-fault" means only that no fault was induced. We did not dismantle the machine after every cycle, so an undetected defect in some of these cycles cannot be excluded.

Eighteen fault cycles trigger both rules. On those eighteen cycles, the mean time from the logged fault onset to the first alarm is 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Restricting the delay comparison to shared detections ensures that both delays are measured on the same cycles rather than on two different sets. The restriction has a cost. It leaves out the faults detected by only one rule and the faults missed by both. The delay result is therefore conditional on that shared subset and should not be read as a property of either rule across all 30 fault cycles.

The gap between motivation and outcome needs to remain visible in how this rule is reported. The rule was motivated by transient spikes. Its observed benefit in this experiment was higher detection of induced faults, obtained at the cost of more alarms in no-fault cycles. These results do not separate the effect of the two-crossing requirement from the effect of the lower threshold, and they do not show improved false-alarm control. A low threshold combined with a persistence condition is not, by its construction alone, evidence of better false-alarm control. It has to be demonstrated, and in this set it was not.

These recordings test two fixed rules under one bench arrangement on one machine. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. We have not selected a preferred rule. The acceptable tradeoff between a missed fault and an interrupted cycle depends on the cost of each, and neither cost was measured in this work.

A single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault, so we introduced a persistence rule that requires two threshold crossings within a cycle before it raises an alarm. We compare it with a rule that uses a higher threshold and alarms after one crossing. Both thresholds and the persistence requirement were fixed using a separate setup recording, and the evaluation recordings were not used to choose them.

The held-out bench set contains 120 machine cycles from one machine. A valve fault was induced in 30 of them and not in the other 90. Here "no-fault" means only that no fault was induced. We did not dismantle the machine after every cycle to exclude every possible defect. Each rule produces at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule alarms in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and eight of the 90 no-fault cycles. The comparison rule alarms in 21 fault cycles and three no-fault cycles. On this set, the persistence rule detects more of the induced faults but also alarms more often in the no-fault cycles.

We introduced the persistence rule because of transient spikes, and it is tempting to describe it as a way to reduce false alarms. But its lower threshold also changes which cycles can produce an alarm, and a low threshold combined with a persistence condition is not, by its construction alone, evidence of better false-alarm control. In this experiment, the observed benefit was instead higher detection of induced faults, at the cost of more alarms in no-fault cycles.

Eighteen fault cycles trigger both rules. On these cycles, the mean time from the logged fault onset to the first alarm is 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Restricting the delay comparison to shared detections avoids comparing delays on different sets of cycles, but it leaves out faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both. The delay result is conditional on this shared subset.

These recordings test two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. We have not selected a preferred rule, because the acceptable tradeoff depends on the cost of a missed fault and the cost of interrupting a cycle, and those costs were not measured.

**Evaluation of the persistence rule against a single-crossing comparison**

The persistence rule trades more false-alarm-prone behavior for greater fault detection on this bench set. It did not demonstrate better false-alarm control, which was its original motivation.

**Design.** We introduced the persistence rule because a single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault. It raises an alarm only after two threshold crossings within a cycle. The comparison rule uses a higher threshold and alarms after one crossing. The lower threshold of the persistence rule also changes which cycles can produce an alarm, so the rule is not simply a filter on the comparison's alarms. We fixed both thresholds and the persistence requirement using a separate setup recording; the evaluation recordings played no part in choosing them.

**Data.** The held-out bench set contains 120 cycles from one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 without. Each rule produces at most one alarm per cycle. "No-fault" means only that no fault was induced; we did not dismantle the machine after every cycle to exclude every possible defect.

**Detection and alarms.**

| Rule | Alarms in 30 fault cycles | Alarms in 90 no-fault cycles |
|---|---|---|
| Persistence | 24 | 8 |
| Comparison | 21 | 3 |

The persistence rule detects three more induced faults (24 versus 21) but alarms in five more no-fault cycles (8 versus 3). Both effects appear in the same set, so the result is a tradeoff, not an improvement on every measure.

**Delay.** Eighteen fault cycles trigger both rules. On those cycles, the mean time from logged fault onset to first alarm is 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison. Restricting the comparison to shared detections avoids averaging delays over different cycles, but it excludes faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both. The delay result therefore applies only to this shared subset.

**Interpretation.** The rule was motivated by transient spikes, yet its observed benefit was higher detection of induced faults, at the cost of more alarms in no-fault cycles. This difference between motivation and outcome should stay visible: a low threshold combined with a persistence condition is not, by construction alone, evidence of better false-alarm control.

**Limits.** These recordings test two fixed rules under one bench arrangement on one machine. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. We have not selected a preferred rule, because the acceptable tradeoff depends on the cost of a missed fault relative to the cost of interrupting a cycle, and neither cost was measured.

response:
A single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault, so we introduced a persistence rule that raises an alarm only after two threshold crossings within a cycle. The comparison rule alarms after one crossing, but at a higher threshold. We fixed both thresholds and the persistence requirement using a separate setup recording, not the evaluation recordings. The persistence rule is motivated by transient spikes, but it should not be read simply as a way to reduce false alarms. Its lower threshold also changes which cycles can produce an alarm, and a low threshold combined with a persistence condition is not, by construction, evidence of better false-alarm control.

The held-out bench set contains 120 cycles from one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 with no induced fault. Here "no-fault" means only that no fault was induced. We did not dismantle the machine after each cycle to exclude every possible defect. Each rule produces at most one alarm per cycle.

| Rule | Alarms in 30 fault cycles | Alarms in 90 no-fault cycles |
|---|---|---|
| Persistence | 24 | 8 |
| Comparison | 21 | 3 |

The persistence rule therefore detects more of the induced faults in this set, and it also alarms more often in the no-fault cycles. The benefit we observed was higher detection, at the cost of more alarms in no-fault cycles. It was not a reduction in false alarms.

Eighteen fault cycles trigger both rules. On those cycles, the mean time from the logged fault onset to the first alarm is 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Restricting the delay comparison to shared detections avoids comparing delays on different sets of cycles. It also leaves out faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both, so the delay result holds only for this shared subset.

These recordings test two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. We have not selected a preferred rule, because the acceptable tradeoff depends on the cost of a missed fault and the cost of interrupting a cycle, and we did not measure either cost.

response:
We started by counting filled date fields because they seemed a simple way to measure completeness. But a year in the field was not enough. It also needed to be supported by the card. An empty field could mean that the date was unreadable, that there was no date, or that someone had missed it. Before using completeness as a measure, we needed to separate those possibilities.

We chose eighty catalogue cards from one drawer that had not yet been entered into the digital index. Two staff members transcribed each card independently. They could enter a year, mark the date as absent, or mark it as unreadable. The instructions did not allow them to infer a year. We later inspected the cards together and recorded a reference decision for each one. This gave us an internally reconciled record for the trial, rather than an independent external check of the dates.

In that record, fifty cards had a readable year, eighteen had no date, and twelve had an unreadable date. The first transcriber entered the reference year on forty-seven of the fifty readable cards and marked the other three as unreadable. The second entered the reference year on forty-nine and marked one as unreadable. Neither entered a year on any of the thirty cards recorded as having an absent or unreadable date. On those thirty cards, the transcribers agreed with each other about whether the date was absent or unreadable on twenty-six. We have not counted how often each transcriber agreed with the reconciled decision on that distinction.

Counting only cards with a year would make both transcribers’ work look substantially incomplete. Yet for thirty cards, the instructions required an entry other than a year. That count would also leave out the four disagreements about why no year was entered. Those differences matter to the next person using the record. A reader trying to find a document’s date needs to know something different from a conservator considering whether another imaging method might help.

We chose the drawer for convenience, so these counts describe this trial only. They do not estimate error across the collection. They suggest that we should report readable-year transcription separately from decisions about absent or unreadable dates. That would make clearer what we had counted. Whether it would help people retrieve items later remains untested.

response:
We started the transcription trial with a question about completeness. It turned out to be a question about what we meant by the word. The index has a field for a date, and a filled field is easy to count. A date in the field is not the same as a date the item supports. An empty field can mean the date was illegible, or that there was no date, or that someone skipped it. Counting filled fields alone mixes those three kinds of work together.

We took eighty catalogue cards from one drawer that had not yet gone into the digital index. Two staff members transcribed each card on their own. For each card they could enter a year, mark the date as absent, or mark it as unreadable. The instructions did not allow a guessed year. Afterwards we looked at the cards together and recorded a reference decision for each one. That was an internal reconciliation. Nobody outside the trial checked the dates.

The reconciled record has fifty cards with a readable year, eighteen with no date, and twelve with a date we could not read. The first transcriber entered the reference year on forty-seven of the fifty readable cards and marked the other three unreadable. The second entered it on forty-nine and marked one unreadable. Neither entered a year on any of the thirty cards the reconciled record classed as absent or unreadable. On those thirty, their absent-or-unreadable calls matched each other on twenty-six. We have not yet tabulated how each of them compared with the reconciled decision on that distinction.

If we judged the index only by how many cards carried a year, both transcribers would look as though they had left a good deal undone. That reading would ignore the cards where the procedure told them to enter something other than a year. It would also hide the four cases where they disagreed about why no year was entered. Those distinctions matter later. A reader who wants a document's date has one problem. A conservator deciding whether another imaging method might recover the date has a different one.

We chose the drawer because it was convenient. The counts describe this trial and nothing more. They do not estimate error across the collection. What they suggest is that our reporting should treat readable-year transcription separately from the classification of missing or unreadable dates. Whether that change helps anyone find things later is a separate question, and we have not tested it.

response:
The committee should choose the handling replica for the navigation exhibit this season because it better fits the exhibit’s current question: how does a reading change when an instrument is tilted? Visitors cannot tilt the original. The replica would let them investigate that question directly, although whether the proposed activity helps them understand it remains to be tested.

The original’s availability on loan is a real opportunity, and one that may not recur. It offers something the replica cannot: a material connection to the instrument’s working history. A maker’s correction remains visible on its scale, providing a basis for an account of repair and adaptation. A photograph would not give every visitor the same experience as standing beside the object. These strengths support considering the original, but they do not establish that it best serves the exhibit we have designed. Our current text concerns reading and error. Making repair central would require a change in direction and a different use of the season’s remaining preparation time.

Cost supports the choice of the replica without deciding it. The loan would cost 18,000 units from the exhibit budget, including transport, insurance, and a sealed case. The replica would cost 7,000 units, including replacement parts for the season. Both fit the allocated budget, and neither quote is a complete estimate of staff time. The reason to prefer the replica is therefore what visitors would be permitted to do, not that the loan is unaffordable. Its lower quoted cost would also leave more resources available for testing the activity.

That testing is necessary. The replica’s moving parts could distract visitors from the question, or visitors could turn them without noticing the scale. A visitor trial has not yet happened, so we should not claim that handling has already improved understanding. The recommendation rests on the replica’s fit with the intended activity, not on a demonstrated teaching benefit.

Choosing the replica now would preserve the exhibit’s focus while leaving resources to test how well the activity works. response:
We recommend repeating the pond survey this season before describing this year’s lower count as a population decline. These recommendations are consistent: we can act promptly to improve the evidence while remaining cautious about what the existing count means.

Last year’s team visited each of eight ponds twice at dusk. This year’s team visited the same ponds once at midday and recorded fewer animals overall. No adjustment has been made for the differences in visit frequency or time of day, and the records do not contain enough information to reconstruct the missed dusk visits. The lower total is an observation that warrants attention, but the difference between the totals does not establish whether, or by how much, the population has declined.

The pending drainage proposal adds urgency to the monitoring decision. It concerns three of the surveyed ponds, and the advisory meeting is next month. Because drainage has not begun, the proposal does not explain this year’s lower count. It does, however, make information about the ponds’ condition relevant to an upcoming decision. That urgency does not make the two surveys more comparable.

We recommend two dusk visits to each pond, using last year’s recording sheet. Matching those features would reduce an avoidable source of ambiguity and make the new observations more comparable with last year’s. Weather and detectability would still vary, however. The repeat survey would neither isolate the effect of drainage nor provide a population census. Its immediate purpose is to improve the evidence available to the meeting.

If the repeat survey cannot be completed before the meeting, the advisory note should report the lower observed total together with the differences in survey effort and timing, and identify the planned work as pending. The current record supports neither a confident estimate of decline nor a confident assurance of stability. The monitoring request should be judged by its value to the pending decision, without requiring either conclusion in advance.

# Position Statement: Repeat Pond Survey Before the Advisory Meeting

## Recommendation

We make two recommendations:

1. Do not describe the lower count as a population decline until the survey has been repeated.
2. Repeat the survey this season.

These have sometimes been heard as opposites, because asking for another survey can sound like asking everyone to wait. They are compatible. A repeat survey is something we can do now, while the existing count remains difficult to interpret.

## Why the current count is hard to interpret

The two surveys were carried out differently:

- **Last year:** each of eight ponds was visited twice, at dusk.
- **This year:** the same ponds were visited once, at midday.

This year's total was lower. However, no adjustment has been made for the difference in visit frequency or time of day. The records also do not contain enough information to reconstruct the missed dusk visits.

The lower count is a genuine observation. But the difference between the two totals cannot be read as the size of a population change.

## Why the timing matters

There is still a reason to take the observation seriously. A drainage proposal concerns three of the surveyed ponds, and the advisory meeting is next month.

The proposal does not show why the count was lower, especially since drainage has not begun. It does make the condition of the ponds relevant to a decision that will be made soon. The timing creates a need for information. It does not make the two surveys any more comparable.

## What the repeat survey would and would not do

We recommend two dusk visits to each pond, using last year's recording sheet. Matching these features of the earlier survey would make the new observations more comparable with last year's.

The repeat survey would **not**:

- remove variation from weather or detectability, which will still differ between years;
- isolate the effect of drainage; or
- produce a population census.

Its immediate purpose is narrower. It would remove one avoidable source of ambiguity from the evidence available to the meeting.

## If the repeat cannot be completed in time

The advisory note should report the lower observed total alongside the differences in survey effort and timing. It can also describe the planned survey as pending.

The current record supports neither a confident estimate of decline nor a confident assurance of stability.

## How to judge this request

The monitoring request should be judged by whether it improves the basis for the pending decision. It should not be judged by whether it supplies either conclusion in advance.

response:
**Position statement: pond survey and the drainage proposal**

We recommend repeating the pond survey this season, and we recommend not describing this year's lower count as a population decline until that is done. Caution about the count and urgency about the survey can sound like opposing positions, and a request for another survey can sound like a request to wait. But a repeat survey is something we can do now, while the existing count remains hard to interpret.

**What the current record shows**

Last year's team visited each of eight ponds twice at dusk. This year's team visited the same ponds once, at midday. The total number of animals recorded was lower this year. No adjustment has been made for the number of visits or the time of day, and the records do not contain enough information to reconstruct the missed dusk visits.

The lower count is therefore an observation. It is not a measure of population change, because the size of any change cannot be read from the difference between two totals gathered under different conditions.

**Why the observation still matters**

A drainage proposal concerns three of the surveyed ponds, and the advisory meeting is next month. The proposal does not explain why the count was lower, particularly because the drainage has not begun. It does make the condition of the ponds relevant to a decision that will be made soon. That timing creates a need for better information, but it does not make the two surveys comparable.

**What we recommend**

We recommend two dusk visits to each pond, using the earlier recording sheet. Matching these features of last year's survey would make the new observations more comparable with the old ones, although weather and detectability would still vary. The repeat would not isolate the effect of drainage, and it would not be a population census. Its immediate purpose is narrower: to remove one avoidable ambiguity from the evidence available to the meeting.

The advisory note should report the lower observed total together with the difference in survey effort and timing, and it should describe the planned repeat survey as pending. The current record supports neither a confident estimate of decline nor a confident assurance of stability.

The monitoring request should be judged by whether it improves the pending decision, not by whether it supplies either conclusion in advance.

response:
We propose revising the short discovery labels attached to twenty digitized collections. Some labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without explaining whose categories they were. The scanned inventories would remain available exactly as they are. This distinction matters: changing the archive’s present description of a collection is different from changing the historical document. Yet discovery labels are also part of how the archive represents its collections. Revising them therefore requires justification, even when the source documents remain untouched.

The case for revision begins with two ways readers reach the material. A reader following a quotation from an inventory benefits from finding the same words in the catalogue. The existing labels provide that consistency, and its value for retrieval should be preserved. A reader who has not seen the inventory, however, may reasonably understand the label as the archive’s present description. Repeating an old heading without context can thus help one reader find a collection while misleading another about how the archive describes it. Both needs deserve attention.

We propose using a current descriptive label, adding a note identifying the original heading, and retaining that heading as a searchable alternative. The historical words would remain a route into the collection without standing alone as its present description. Search results would display the current label; the note would be visible when a reader opened the catalogue record. Neither the words in the historical document nor access to the old inventory would change.

A reasonable objection is that a replacement label interprets the collection. It does. But selecting an inventory heading as the main discovery label also interprets the collection, even when that selection appears simply to copy the source. The question is therefore how well the label describes the material and how clearly it shows its relationship to the historical wording. A new label should describe the contents at the level the collection supports, and the accompanying note should make that relationship visible. This standard does not establish that our drafts meet it: labels have been drafted for all twenty collections, but readers and subject specialists have not yet reviewed them.

There is also a practical objection: contextual notes can make a short catalogue harder to scan. Keeping the note inside the record preserves brevity in search results, but it means a reader may not immediately see the historical wording. Retaining that wording as searchable helps preserve retrieval from quotations; it does not eliminate the tradeoff over what readers see first.

These limits support a trial rather than wider adoption. We recommend testing the proposal with the twenty collections, followed by checks of both successful and failed searches. We have no evidence yet that it will improve retrieval. The trial would test whether this approach can provide context while preserving a route from historical quotations. Expanding the policy before that check would go beyond what the present case supports.

response:
**Revised draft**

We propose revising the short discovery labels attached to twenty digitized collections. A discovery label is the text a reader sees before opening a record, and it helps that reader decide which collection to open. Several of these labels currently repeat terms from old inventory headings without saying whose categories those were. The scanned inventories themselves would remain available exactly as they are. The proposal changes nothing in the historical record. It changes only the archive's present description of the collection, and that description is not mere packaging, because it is part of how the archive represents the material to readers who have not yet seen it.

The existing labels have a genuine advantage. They are consistent with the old headings, so a reader who follows a quotation from an inventory can find the same words in the catalogue. That retrieval benefit is real and should not be given up. But the same repetition carries a cost for a different reader. Someone who has not seen the inventory has no way to know that the label is a historical heading rather than the archive's current view. For that reader, the label can read as endorsement of categories the archive does not hold. Repeating the heading is therefore faithful to one route into the material and misleading on another. Neither route is imaginary, and a sound policy has to serve both.

The proposal keeps both routes open. Each collection would receive a current descriptive label, a note identifying the original heading, and the original heading retained as a searchable alternative. The quoted words would still lead a searcher to the collection. They would simply no longer stand alone as the collection's present description. Search results would show the current label, and the note would appear when a reader opens the record. Nothing would be removed from the historical document, and the old inventory would remain as available as it is now.

The first objection is that any replacement label interprets the collection. We agree, and the point cuts both ways. Choosing an inventory heading as the main label is also an interpretive act, even though it looks like copying. The decision to repeat a heading is a decision about how the collection should be presented. Acknowledging this does not make every replacement equally good. A new label should describe the contents at the level of detail the collection actually supports, and the accompanying note should make the relationship to the old wording visible rather than hiding it. We have drafted labels for the twenty collections on those terms. They have not yet been reviewed by readers or subject specialists, and that review is part of what the trial below is for.

The second objection follows from accepting the first. If the note is what makes the relationship to the old wording visible, then placing it where readers will see it matters. Adding notes to every search result would make a short catalogue harder to scan. The proposal therefore keeps the note inside the record. The cost of that choice is that a reader scanning results may not see the historical wording immediately, though the retained searchable heading means such a reader can still arrive at the collection by the old words. This is a tradeoff between scannability and immediate context, not a complete resolution of the two needs.

Because the proposal rests on claims about how readers actually use labels and notes, it should be tested before it is extended. We recommend a limited trial with the twenty collections, followed by checks of both successful searches and failed searches. We have no evidence yet that the trial will improve retrieval, and we do not claim that it will. Its purpose is narrower: to test whether this arrangement provides context for one kind of reader while preserving a route for the other. Expanding the policy before that check would outrun the present case for it.
