It is not a reason to treat the machines as free just because we already own them. If the pool is worth continuing, we need to know what it costs us.

**Who can ask, and who gets a machine.** I favour opening the pool to every customer with a repair booked. A universal rule means nobody has to establish hardship before they can ask about a loan, and it is simple for staff to apply. But being able to ask is not the same as getting a machine. Two things can stop a loan even for an eligible household: the available machines may not fit the space or connect safely, and there may be more requests than machines. Eligibility cannot guarantee suitability, so we need a practical check before any delivery. If demand exceeds six machines, we need an allocation rule agreed before launch. This statement does not settle that rule, and that decision should not be left to whoever happens to be on shift.

**Delivery-fee assistance.** I would offer this according to need, and I would keep it a separate decision from the eligibility rule. Assistance requires a conversation about circumstances, which the opening rule deliberately avoids. Combining the two would make the first test harder than it needs to be, and it would blur what we learn about each. Running them side by side lets us see whether the fee is a barrier without making hardship the price of asking.

**Running costs.** The older loan machines may cost more to run than some of the machines being repaired. That objection is real, and it matters most for people already struggling with bills, who would bear any extra cost. A short loan is a possible bridge, not proof that running costs don't matter. For each available machine we should give the household whatever running information we have, so the choice is informed. We should also be honest when we don't know. Households should be able to decline a loan without it affecting their repair.

**Review.** At the end of twelve weeks, the cooperative should review actual use, staff time, and reported difficulties before deciding whether to continue. That includes any difficulty with fit, running costs, or fee assistance. We do not have those results yet, and this proposal doesn't claim to know what they will show.

We should try a loan pool for households waiting for a washing-machine repair. At present the workshop can diagnose a machine quickly and still leave its owner waiting for a part. The pool would address that wait. It would not shorten the supplier's delivery time, and we should not advertise it as doing so. The aim is to see whether we can make the wait easier to bear without promising anything the workshop cannot deliver.

Six refurbished machines are available for a twelve-week trial, and transport insurance for the trial has been approved. We have not yet costed the staff time for delivery, collection, and cleaning between loans. That is a reason to keep the trial small and to record that time. It is not a reason to treat the machines as free because we already own them. A loan will also not suit a household whose space cannot fit the available machine or cannot connect it safely, so being eligible does not mean a loan is right for everyone.

I favour opening the pool to every customer with a repair booked, and offering delivery-fee assistance according to need. These are two separate decisions. If we asked people to show hardship before they could even ask about a loan, the first decision would become harder than it needs to be. Fee assistance would still involve a separate conversation. If demand exceeds six machines, we will need an allocation rule agreed before launch. This statement does not settle that rule.

The older loan machines may cost more to run than some of the machines being repaired. That objection is real, especially for people already struggling with bills. A short loan can bridge the wait, but it does not make running costs unimportant. For each available machine we should give the household the running-cost information we have and let them decide. After twelve weeks, the cooperative should review actual use, staff time, and reported difficulties before deciding whether to continue. We do not have those results yet.

response:
I favour returning the cooperative’s one-off surplus through an equal credit on every household account. The choice is about how we share a common benefit, and we should be clear about the fairness principle behind it.

All figures here are hypothetical and cover one year. With a £1,200 surplus and 100 household accounts, each account would receive a £12 credit. The alternative is to spread the surplus across the year’s total water use of 20,000 cubic metres, reducing the volumetric charge by £0.06 per cubic metre. Both options return exactly £1,200, but they distribute it differently:

| Annual household water use | Return through a £0.06-per-cubic-metre reduction | Equal account credit |
|---|---:|---:|
| 40 cubic metres | £2.40 | £12 |
| 300 cubic metres | £18.00 | £12 |

The strongest case for the volumetric reduction is straightforward: households that bought more water paid more in volume charges, so they would receive more back. That is a reasonable principle for a refund. It is not an arithmetic mistake or an inherently unfair position.

My preference rests on a different principle: treating this particular surplus as a common benefit of a member-owned service. It has not been traced to an error on any account, so I favour sharing it equally across accounts rather than returning it in proportion to water purchases.

An equal credit means the same cash amount for each account, not the same percentage reduction in every bill. Nor is it targeted help for those in greatest need. Accounts can serve different numbers of people, and equal treatment of accounts does not establish equal benefit per person.

The credit also leaves the charge for each additional cubic metre unchanged. That preserves the current price schedule; it does not demonstrate a conservation effect. We have not estimated whether a temporary rate reduction would change use.

The case for a £12 credit is therefore specific: it shares a one-off common surplus equally across household accounts without changing the usage rate.

response:
**Returning this year's surplus: why I favour an equal £12 credit**

The cooperative has a one-off surplus of £1,200 to return to members. We have 100 household accounts. I recommend a £12 credit on each account.

The alternative under discussion is a reduction in the volumetric charge. Members used 20,000 cubic metres this year in total, so spreading £1,200 across that volume gives a reduction of £0.06 per cubic metre.

Both approaches return the same £1,200 on these figures. They differ in who receives it.

**What each household would receive**

| Household's annual use | Equal credit | Volumetric reduction |
|---|---|---|
| 40 cubic metres | £12.00 | £2.40 |
| 300 cubic metres | £12.00 | £18.00 |

Under the volumetric reduction, a household's share rises with the water it bought. Under the equal credit, every account receives the same amount.

**Why I prefer the credit**

The surplus was earned by a member-owned service. I think of it as a common benefit, and a common benefit is most naturally shared equally among accounts. The credit also leaves the price of an additional cubic metre exactly as it is now, so no usage rate has to be revised to return the money.

Two things the credit does not do. It does not give every household the same percentage reduction in its bill, because bills and water use differ. And it is not targeted help. This proposal contains no information about members' incomes or household sizes. A low-use account is not necessarily a low-income household, and a high-use account may serve more people. I am not claiming that a £12 credit reaches those in greatest need.

**The case for the volumetric option**

The strongest argument for the volumetric reduction is this: households that bought more water paid more in volume charges, so returning money in proportion to purchases looks like a refund. That is a reasonable principle, and it would be the right one if the surplus were the correction of an identified overcharge.

It has not been traced to an error on any account. That is why I treat it as a common benefit rather than a refund. The choice between the two options is a choice between these two fairness principles. Neither one is arithmetically confused, and we should say plainly which principle we are adopting.

One further point. Some may suppose that keeping the volumetric price unchanged helps conservation. We have not estimated whether a temporary price reduction would change anyone's use, so I make no such claim. The credit simply preserves the current price schedule.

**In short**

The case for the £12 credit is modest but sufficient. For a one-off common surplus, it treats every account equally and does not require revising the usage rate to do so.

# Returning the Surplus: Equal Credits or a Lower Rate?

The cooperative has a one-off surplus of £1,200 to return to members. The figures below are hypothetical annual figures. There are two ways to return it, and on these figures both return exactly £1,200. That they add to the same total does not mean they answer the same question about fairness.

**Option A: an equal credit.** Divide the surplus across the 100 household accounts: £1,200 ÷ 100 = **£12 per account**.

**Option B: a lower volumetric charge.** Divide the surplus across this year's 20,000 cubic metres: £1,200 ÷ 20,000 = **£0.06 less per cubic metre**.

Here is what each option means for two households:

| Household use | Option A: equal credit | Option B: £0.06 off each m³ |
|---|---|---|
| 40 m³ | £12.00 | £2.40 |
| 300 m³ | £12.00 | £18.00 |

Under Option A, both households receive £12. Under Option B, the 300 m³ household receives 7.5 times as much as the 40 m³ household.

## Why I prefer the credit

I favour Option A because it treats this surplus as a common benefit of a member-owned service. Each account gets an equal share. The credit also leaves the price of an additional cubic metre unchanged.

An equal credit does not mean every household sees the same percentage reduction. Bills and water use differ, so £12 is a larger proportion of a small bill than of a large one.

## The case for the volumetric option

The strongest argument for Option B is that households which bought more water also paid more in volume charges. Returning money in proportion to purchases therefore looks like a refund. That is a reasonable principle.

My disagreement is about what this surplus is. It has not been traced to an overcharge on any account. I treat it as a shared benefit, not as the correction of an identified overcharge. The two options rest on different principles:

- **Proportional to purchases:** each account receives back in line with what it paid through volume charges.
- **Equal share:** each account receives the same amount of a common surplus.

Both principles are defensible. We should state which one we choose and why, rather than dismissing the other as arithmetically confused.

## What the credit does not do

An equal credit is not targeted help. This proposal includes no income or household-size information. A low-use account is not necessarily a low-income household, and a high-use account may serve more people. I am not claiming that £12 reaches those in greatest need.

I have also not estimated whether a temporary cut in the volume price would change how much water members use. Keeping the marginal price unchanged preserves the current price schedule. It does not show a conservation effect in either direction.

The case for the credit is modest but sufficient. It gives equal treatment to accounts for a one-off common surplus, and it does not require revising the usage rate to accomplish that.

# Why I favour an equal £12 credit for every account

*All figures are illustrative annual amounts.*

The cooperative has a one-off surplus of £1,200 to return to members. I propose we do it by placing a **£12 credit on each of our 100 household accounts**.

The other option under discussion is to reduce this year's volumetric charge. Members used 20,000 cubic metres this year, so returning £1,200 that way would mean **£0.06 off every cubic metre**.

## Same total, different shares

Both options return exactly £1,200. What differs is how it is divided.

| Household's annual use | Equal credit | Volume reduction (£0.06/m³) |
|---|---|---|
| 40 m³ | £12.00 | £2.40 |
| 200 m³ (the average account) | £12.00 | £12.00 |
| 300 m³ | £12.00 | £18.00 |

The average account uses 200 cubic metres (20,000 ÷ 100). At that level both options give the same £12. A household using less than average receives more from the credit, and a household using more than average receives more from the volume reduction.

Adding up to the same total does not mean the two options answer the same question about fairness.

## Why I prefer the credit

I have two reasons:

1. **It shares a common benefit equally.** The surplus was earned by a service all members own together. An equal credit gives each account an equal share of it.
2. **It leaves the price of water unchanged.** The cost of each additional cubic metre stays where it is.

The credit does not give every household the same *percentage* off its bill. Bills differ because water use differs, so £12 is a larger share of a small bill than of a large one.

## The case for the other option

The strongest argument for the volume reduction is this: households that bought more water paid more in volume charges, so returning money in proportion to purchases looks like a refund. That is a reasonable principle.

Where I differ is on what this surplus is. It has not been traced to an error on any account. I see it as a common benefit to be shared, not as the correction of an identified overcharge. Whichever principle we adopt, we should say plainly which one we are choosing, rather than suggesting the other side has its arithmetic wrong.

## What I am not claiming

- **The credit is not targeted help.** This proposal contains no information about household incomes or household sizes. A low-use account is not necessarily a low-income household, and a high-use account may serve more people. I am not claiming that a £12 credit reaches those in greatest need.
- **The credit is not a conservation measure.** We have not estimated whether a temporary cut in the volume price would change how much water members use. Leaving the per-cubic-metre price alone keeps the current price schedule in place, but it does not show any conservation effect.

## In short

The case for the credit is modest but sufficient. This is a one-off surplus that belongs to all members, so each account should receive an equal share, and we can return it without revising the usage rate.

response:
# Share the surplus equally: why I favour a £12 credit

The cooperative has a one-off surplus of £1,200 to return to its 100 household accounts. There are two main options. All figures below are hypothetical annual figures.

- **An equal credit:** £12 on every account.
- **A volumetric reduction:** lower the charge on this year's total of 20,000 cubic metres by £0.06 per cubic metre.

On these figures both options return the same £1,200. But adding up to the same total does not mean they answer the same question about fairness. I favour the equal credit.

## What each option means for a household

| Annual use | Equal credit | Volumetric reduction |
|---|---|---|
| 40 m³ | £12.00 | £2.40 |
| 300 m³ | £12.00 | £18.00 |

Under the volumetric option, the larger user receives much more than the smaller one. Under the credit, both receive the same.

## Why I prefer the credit

The surplus was earned by a member-owned service. I think of it as a common benefit, so each account should get an equal share. The credit also leaves the price of an additional cubic metre unchanged.

I am not claiming that every household would see the same percentage reduction in its bill. Bills and water use differ, so the percentages will too. The claim is only that each account receives an equal share.

## The strongest case for the other side

The best argument for the volumetric option is that people who bought more water paid more in volume charges. Returning money in proportion to purchases then looks like a refund. That is a reasonable principle, and I do not think those who hold it are confused about arithmetic.

My preference rests on a different view of this surplus. It has not been traced to an error on any account, so I do not see it as the correction of an identified overcharge. I see it as a shared gain. The disagreement is over which principle to apply, and we should say openly which one we choose.

## What this argument does not claim

- **It is not targeted help.** This proposal has no information on income or household size. A low-use account is not necessarily a low-income household, and a high-use account may serve more people. I am not claiming that £12 reaches those in greatest need.
- **It makes no claim about conservation.** We have not estimated whether a temporary volume-price reduction would change use. Leaving the marginal price alone preserves the current price schedule. It does not show a conservation effect.

## Conclusion

The case for the credit is modest but sufficient: equal treatment of accounts for a one-off common surplus, without revising the usage rate to accomplish it.

**Proposal: rotate six of eight shoreline sectors per visit**

I propose that on each visit we survey six of the eight shoreline sectors, rotating which two are left out, and that we apply the same observation protocol in every sector we reach.

**Why the current schedule does not work**

Our present daylight window allows six sectors at the required pace. The visit logs show what happens when we try to fit in eight: the notes from the last stops are rushed. In practice, the final sectors already receive a different kind of visit from the first ones. The schedule promises eight full surveys and delivers six full surveys and two hurried ones. It would be more honest, and more useful for the record, to plan for what we can actually do.

**The coordinator's objection, and why it carries weight**

The coordinator wants every sector covered on every visit, because a missed sector can contain a short-lived nesting event. This is a serious point. Rotation would create planned gaps, and the logs cannot tell us how many events those gaps would miss. The rushed visits are still visits, and it would be wrong to pretend they provide no information.

I do not want to overstate my case. The choice is between different losses, not between a complete record and an empty one. Full coverage with weak notes at the end of the day loses detail in every sector that comes last. Rotation loses whatever happens in two sectors on any given day. My argument is that the second loss is at least visible and planned, while the first is diffuse and already recorded in the logs as a problem.

**Why splitting the team is not an answer for next month**

One suggestion is to split the team into pairs and run two routes. We already work in pairs under the group's shoreline safety protocol, and only two trained observers are available on these visits. Splitting them would change that protocol. A second trained pair would change the scheduling calculation, but none is available for the coming month. This remains a useful future option. It does not help with the next four visits.

**What I propose for the next four visits**

1. **Publish the rotation in advance.** Everyone knows which two sectors are omitted on each date before the visit begins.
2. **Give each sector three visits across the month.** Four visits of six sectors provide twenty-four sector visits, which is exactly enough for three per sector.
3. **Mark unvisited sectors explicitly in the record.** A planned absence should be distinguishable from a visit on which no nest was recorded. It is still an absence, and the record should say so.
4. **Review at the end of the month.** We check whether the notes were more complete than under the current schedule and whether additional staffing has become possible.

That review will not recover events missed during gaps. It will let us reconsider the schedule with a clearer account of what we actually did, rather than a schedule that only works on paper.

# Proposal: Rotating Six-Sector Coverage for the Next Four Visits

## Proposal

For the next four visits, we should survey six of the eight shoreline sectors on each visit, rotating which two are skipped. Every sector we reach gets the same observation protocol. The rotation should be published in advance. Each sector should be visited three times across the month, and unvisited sectors should be marked explicitly in the record.

## Why change the current schedule

Our daylight window allows six sectors at the required pace. Fitting in eight has led to rushed notes at the last stops, as the visit logs record. A schedule that works only if the final sectors get a different kind of visit from the first ones is not really an eight-sector schedule. I think we should stop writing it as one.

## The strongest objection

The coordinator wants every sector covered on every visit, because a missed sector can contain a short-lived nesting event. I take this seriously. Rotation creates planned gaps, and the logs cannot tell us how many events those gaps would miss. I am not claiming the cost is small.

The rushed visits are still visits, though, and they do provide some information. The choice is between different losses, not between a complete record and an empty one. Rotation risks missing events in the sectors we skip. The current approach risks lower-quality observations in the sectors we rush, and the logs show this is already happening.

## Why not split into two routes

Splitting the team into pairs would let us cover more ground. But we already work in pairs under the group's shoreline safety protocol, and only two trained observers are available on these visits. Splitting them would change that protocol. A second trained pair could change the scheduling calculation, but none is available for the coming month. It is a useful future option, not an answer for the next four visits.

## Feasibility

Four visits at six sectors each give 24 sector visits. Eight sectors at three visits each also come to 24, so the rotation fits exactly, with each sector skipped once.

## What the record will show

Because the rotation is published in advance and unvisited sectors are marked, a planned absence can be told apart from a visit on which no nest was recorded. It remains an absence, and any analysis should treat it that way.

## End-of-month review

At the end of the month we should review whether the notes were more complete and whether additional staffing has become possible. The review cannot recover events missed during the gaps. It would let us reconsider the schedule, including the coordinator's preferred full coverage, with a clearer account of what we actually did.

Consider an idealized recorder with \(n\) labeled memory slots, numbered \(0,\ldots,n-1\), where \(n\) is a positive integer. Starting at slot \(a\), with \(0\le a<n\), the recorder advances by a fixed integer \(s\ge0\) after every write. Its slot after \(k\) advances is
\[
x_k=(a+ks)\bmod n,\qquad k\ge0.
\]
This schedule is a mathematical model, not a measured hardware property. A return occurs when \(x_k=a\) for a positive integer \(k\); resemblance between numerical representatives does not constitute a return.

Let \(g=\gcd(n,s)\), with \(\gcd(n,0)=n\). The least positive return time is exactly
\[
\boxed{\frac{n}{g}}.
\]
The reachable slots are exactly those congruent to \(a\) modulo \(g\), and the labeled slots form \(g\) disjoint cycles.

To prove the return-time claim, write \(n=gn'\) and \(s=gs'\). Then \(\gcd(n',s')=1\). A return after \(k\) advances occurs precisely when
\[
n\mid ks,
\]
or, equivalently, when \(n'\mid ks'\). Coprimality forces \(n'\mid k\): choose integers \(u,v\) such that \(un'+vs'=1\), and multiply by \(k\) to obtain
\[
k=ukn'+vks'.
\]
The first term on the right is divisible by \(n'\), and the second is also divisible by \(n'\) whenever \(n'\mid ks'\). Thus \(k\) must be a multiple of \(n'\). Conversely, \(k=n'\) gives a return, so the least positive return time is \(n'=n/g\).

The first \(n'\) visited slots, \(x_0,\ldots,x_{n'-1}\), are distinct. Otherwise, equality at indices \(i<j<n'\) would imply \(n\mid(j-i)s\), giving a positive return time smaller than \(n'\). Every visited slot is congruent to \(a\) modulo \(g\), since both the advance \(s\) and the modulus \(n\) are multiples of \(g\). There are exactly \(n/g=n'\) labeled slots in this congruence class, so these distinct visits exhaust it. The \(g\) congruence classes partition all slots, each forming one cycle.

When \(s=0\), the return time is one and every cycle consists of a single slot. When \(n=1\), slot zero is the only slot, regardless of \(s\). The argument never divides by \(s\), does not require \(s<n\), and does not count rotations of the labeled slots as new schedules.

\[

\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad

\[

\[

\[

\[

## Schedule Return Period and Reachable Slots

This appendix treats the recorder as an idealized model. The slot numbers, step size, and return times below are properties of the model, not measurements of any hardware.

**Setup.** The recorder has $n$ labeled slots, numbered $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, where $n \ge 1$. It starts at slot $a$ with $0 \le a < n$. After each write it advances by a fixed integer step $s \ge 0$. After $k$ steps, the position is $x_k \equiv a + ks \pmod n$, for $k \ge 0$. A *return* is a positive $k$ with $x_k = a$. This means the slot index equals $a$ exactly, not merely that two integer representatives happen to look alike.

Let $g = \gcd(n, s)$, with the convention $\gcd(n, 0) = n$.

**Claims.**
1. The least positive return time is $n/g$.
2. The visited slots are exactly the slots congruent to $a$ modulo $g$.
3. There are $g$ disjoint cycles, one for each congruence class modulo $g$.

**Proof.**

*Reduction to coprime form.* Write $n = g n'$ and $s = g s'$. Then $\gcd(n', s') = 1$. A return after $k$ steps means $x_k = a$, which holds exactly when $n \mid ks$. Dividing both sides by $g$, this is equivalent to $n' \mid ks'$.

*Coprimality forces $n' \mid k$.* Since $\gcd(n', s') = 1$, Bézout's identity gives integers $u, v$ with $u n' + v s' = 1$. Multiply by $k$:
$$k = (u n')k + v(s'k).$$
Suppose $n' \mid ks'$. Then $n'$ divides $v(s'k)$. It also divides $(u n')k$ trivially. So $n'$ divides $k$.

*The return time is $n'$.* Conversely, if $n' \mid k$, then $n \mid ks$, so $k$ is a return. Taking $k = n'$ gives $x_{n'} = a + n's = a + ns' \equiv a$, so a return occurs at $n' = n/g$. No smaller positive $k$ works, because every positive multiple of $n'$ is at least $n'$. This proves claim 1.

*The first $n'$ visited slots are distinct.* Suppose $x_i = x_j$ for some $0 \le i < j < n'$. Then $(j - i)s \equiv 0 \pmod n$. This means $x_{j-i} = a$, so $j - i$ is a positive return time. But $0 < j - i < n'$, which contradicts the minimality just shown. Hence the $n'$ slots $x_0, \dots, x_{n'-1}$ are distinct.

*The visited slots are the slots congruent to $a$ modulo $g$.* Since $g$ divides both $s$ and $n$, every $x_k = a + ks$ satisfies $x_k \equiv a \pmod g$. There are exactly $n/g = n'$ slots in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with that congruence. The $n'$ distinct visited slots from the previous step therefore exhaust them. This proves claim 2.

*Cycles.* The $g$ congruence classes modulo $g$ partition the $n$ slots into $g$ disjoint sets, each of size $n/g$. Starting from any slot in a class, the recorder visits all of that class and returns after $n/g$ steps. Each class is therefore one cycle, which proves claim 3.

**Edge cases.**
- If $s = 0$, then $g = n$ and $n' = 1$. The return time is $1$, and every cycle is a single slot.
- If $n = 1$, the only slot is $0$, regardless of $s$.

**Scope of the argument.** The argument does not divide by $s$, does not assume $s < n$, and does not treat rotations of the labeled slots as a new schedule.

## Return Times and Reachable Slots of the Recorder Schedule

This section analyzes an idealized arithmetic model of slot selection. It is not a measured property of any hardware.

**Setup.** Let $n$ be a positive integer, and label the memory slots $0,1,\dots,n-1$. Fix a starting slot $a$ with $0\le a<n$ and a fixed integer advance $s\ge 0$. The recorder advances by $s$ after each write. For $k\ge 0$, let $x_k$ be the residue of $a+ks$ modulo $n$, so $x_k\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and $x_0=a$.

A *return* is an index $k\ge 1$ with $x_k=a$. This is a congruence condition on residues modulo $n$. It does not depend on whether the integers $a$ and $a+ks$ look similar.

Let $g=\gcd(n,s)$, with $\gcd(n,0)=n$. We prove three claims:

1. The least positive return time is $n/g$.
2. The visited slots are exactly the slots congruent to $a$ modulo $g$.
3. Across all starting slots, the schedule splits into $g$ disjoint cycles.

**Step 1: Characterize returns.** For $k\ge 1$,

$$
x_k=a \iff a+ks\equiv a \pmod n \iff n\mid ks.
$$

**Step 2: Reduce to coprime form.** Write

$$
n=g\,n', \qquad s=g\,s'.
$$

Since $g$ is the greatest common divisor of $n$ and $s$, the integers $n'$ and $s'$ are coprime. If $s=0$, then $g=n$, $n'=1$, $s'=0$, and $\gcd(1,0)=1$ still holds. Dividing by $g$ gives

$$
n\mid ks \iff g n'\mid g k s' \iff n'\mid k s'.
$$

$$
k=u k\,n'+v\,(k s').
$$

Suppose $n'\mid ks'$. Then both terms on the right are divisible by $n'$, so $n'\mid k$. Conversely, if $k=n'$, then $ks'=n's'$ is divisible by $n'$.

Therefore the positive return times are exactly the positive multiples of $n'$. The least one is $n'$, so

$$
R=n'=\frac{n}{g}.
$$

Since this computation did not use $a$, every starting slot has return time $n/g$.

**Step 4: Identify the visited slots.** Since $g\mid n$ and $g\mid s$, we have $a+ks\equiv a\pmod g$ for every $k$. So every visited slot lies in the class

$$
C_a=\{r : 0\le r<n,\ r\equiv a \pmod g\}.
$$

Because $g\mid n$, this class has exactly $n/g$ elements.

Now consider the first $n/g$ visited slots $x_0,\dots,x_{n/g-1}$. Suppose $x_i=x_j$ for some $0\le i<j<n/g$. Then

$$
a+is\equiv a+js \pmod n,
$$

so $(j-i)s\equiv 0\pmod n$. This means $x_{j-i}=a$. But $0<j-i<n/g=R$, which contradicts the minimality of $R$. Hence $x_0,\dots,x_{n/g-1}$ are $n/g$ distinct elements of $C_a$. Since $C_a$ has exactly $n/g$ elements, these visited slots are all of $C_a$.

The same argument applies to any starting slot $b\in C_a$. Its return time is also $n/g$, and its visited slots form the class $C_b=C_a$. So the orbit of every slot in $C_a$ is $C_a$ itself.

**Step 5: Count the cycles.** The $g$ residue classes modulo $g$ partition $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$. By Step 4, each class is the orbit of each of its members. So the schedule consists of $g$ disjoint cycles, each of length $n/g$.

**Edge cases.**

- If $s=0$, then $g=n$, so $n/g=1$. The return time is $1$, and each class is a single slot. Every cycle is a fixed point.
- If $n=1$, the only slot is $0$. Then $g=1$, the return time is $1$, and the schedule has one cycle regardless of $s$.

**Remarks on the argument.** The proof divides only by $g$ and by $n'$. It never divides by $s$, and it does not assume $s<n$, because all reasoning is carried out modulo $n$. **Schedule Return Period and Reachable Slots**

A recorder has $n$ labeled memory slots, numbered $0$ through $n-1$, where $n$ is a positive integer. It starts at slot $a$, with $0 \le a < n$. After each write, it advances by a fixed integer $s \ge 0$. For $k \ge 0$, let $x_k$ denote the residue of $a + ks$ modulo $n$, so $x_0 = a$. A *return* is an index $k > 0$ with $x_k = a$. This compares residues modulo $n$, not integer representatives.

Let $g = \gcd(n, s)$, with $\gcd(n, 0) = n$. We claim:

1. The least positive return time is $n/g$.
2. The visited slots are exactly the slots congruent to $a$ modulo $g$.
3. There are $g$ disjoint cycles, one for each congruence class modulo $g$.

**Return time.** Write $n = gn'$ and $s = gs'$, where $\gcd(n', s') = 1$. Then

$$
x_k = a \iff n \mid ks \iff gn' \mid gks' \iff n' \mid ks'.
$$

So a return after $k$ steps occurs exactly when $n' \mid ks'$. We show this forces $n' \mid k$. Since $n'$ and $s'$ are coprime, choose integers $u, v$ with $un' + vs' = 1$. Multiplying by $k$ gives

$$
k = (ku)\,n' + v\,(ks').
$$

If $n' \mid ks'$, both terms on the right are divisible by $n'$, so $n' \mid k$. Hence every return time is a multiple of $n'$. Conversely, $k = n'$ gives $ks' = n's'$, which $n'$ divides, so $n'$ is a return time. Therefore the least positive return time is

$$
n' = \frac{n}{g}.
$$

**Visited slots.** Consider the $n'$ residues $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n'-1}$. They are distinct. Suppose $x_i = x_j$ with $0 \le i < j < n'$. Then $(j-i)s \equiv 0 \pmod n$, so $x_{j-i} = a$. But $0 < j - i < n'$, which contradicts the minimality just shown.

Each visited residue lies in the class of $a$ modulo $g$, because $g$ divides both $n$ and $s$:

$$
x_k = a + ks \equiv a \pmod g.
$$

The slots congruent to $a$ modulo $g$ are $a, a+g, \dots, a+(n'-1)g$ (taken within $0,\dots,n-1$), so there are exactly $n' = n/g$ of them. The $n'$ distinct visited residues lie in this set of size $n'$, so they exhaust it. The visited slots are therefore exactly the slots congruent to $a$ modulo $g$.

**Cycles.** The $g$ congruence classes modulo $g$ partition the $n$ slots. Starting from any slot, the recorder visits exactly its class, and returns to its start after $n/g$ steps. These classes are the $g$ disjoint cycles.

**Edge cases.** If $s = 0$, then $g = n$, $n' = 1$, and $x_1 = a$, so the return time is one. Each cycle is a single slot. If $n = 1$, the only slot is $0$, regardless of $s$. The argument never divides by $s$, does not assume $s < n$, and does not treat rotations of the labeled slots as a different schedule.

# Appendix: Return Period of a Fixed-Stride Slot Schedule

This appendix analyzes an idealized write schedule. The results follow from the model's arithmetic. They are not measured properties of any recorder hardware.

## Model

A recorder has n labeled memory slots, numbered 0 through n − 1, where n is a positive integer. It starts at slot a, with 0 ≤ a < n. After every write it advances by a fixed integer stride s ≥ 0. For k ≥ 0, let

  x_k = the residue of a + ks modulo n,

so x_k is the slot used at step k.

A *return* means x_k = a for some positive k. This is an exact equality of slots. It is not enough for two numerical representatives to look similar.

Let g = gcd(n, s), with the convention gcd(n, 0) = n. Because n ≥ 1, g ≥ 1, so dividing by g is always allowed.

## Claim

1. The least positive return time is n/g.
2. The slots visited from a are exactly those congruent to a modulo g.
3. Across all starting slots, the schedule has g disjoint cycles.

## Proof

**Step 1: Split off the common factor.** Write n = g·n′ and s = g·s′. Since g is the *greatest* common divisor, the remaining parts share no factor: gcd(n′, s′) = 1.

**Step 2: Restate a return as a divisibility condition.** By definition, x_k = a exactly when a + ks ≡ a (mod n), that is, when n divides ks. Substituting the factorizations, this says g·n′ divides g·k·s′. Cancelling the positive factor g, a return after k steps occurs exactly when n′ divides ks′.

**Step 3: A return forces n′ to divide k.** Suppose n′ divides ks′. Since n′ and s′ are coprime, there are integers u and v with

  u·n′ + v·s′ = 1.

Multiplying both sides by k gives

  u·k·n′ + v·k·s′ = k.

The first term on the left is a multiple of n′ because it contains the factor n′. The second term is a multiple of n′ because n′ divides ks′ by assumption. Their sum, k, is therefore a multiple of n′.

**Step 4: n′ is the least return time.** Conversely, k = n′ does give a return, because n′s = n′·g·s′ = n·s′ is divisible by n. By Step 3, every positive return time is a multiple of n′, so none is smaller than n′. The least positive return time is therefore n′ = n/g.

**Step 5: The schedule visits exactly n′ distinct slots.** Suppose x_i = x_j for some 0 ≤ i < j < n′. Then n divides (j − i)s, so x_{j−i} = a. That would make j − i a positive return time smaller than n′, which contradicts Step 4. So x_0, x_1, …, x_{n′−1} are n′ distinct slots. Because n′s is a multiple of n, x_{k+n′} = x_k for every k. Every later step therefore repeats one of these slots, and they are all the slots the schedule ever visits.

**Step 6: The visited slots form one residue class modulo g.** Every visited slot is congruent to a modulo g. The integer a + ks ≡ a (mod g) because g divides s, and reducing modulo n does not change the residue modulo g because g divides n. Among 0, …, n − 1, exactly n/g slots are congruent to a modulo g. By Step 5, the schedule visits n/g distinct slots, all of them in this class. It therefore visits every slot in the class and no others.

**Step 7: The cycles.** The g residue classes modulo g partition the n slots. By Step 6, a schedule started at any slot b runs through exactly the class of b and returns to b after n/g steps. The g classes are therefore the g disjoint cycles, each containing n/g slots.

## Edge Cases

- **s = 0.** Here g = gcd(n, 0) = n, so the return time is 1 and every cycle is a single slot: the recorder keeps writing to its starting slot. The proof still applies, with n′ = 1, s′ = 0, and u = 1, v = 0 in Step 3.
- **n = 1.** There is only slot 0, regardless of s. Then g = 1, the return time is 1, and there is a single one-slot cycle.

No step in the argument divides by s, assumes that s < n, or treats rotations of the labeled slots as a new schedule. The result therefore covers a zero stride and strides larger than n without modification.

# Appendix: Period and Reach of a Fixed-Stride Write Schedule

This is an idealized combinatorial model of the schedule. It is not a measured property of any hardware.

## Setup

A recorder has $n$ memory slots labeled $0,1,\dots,n-1$, where $n\ge 1$. It starts at slot $a$ with $0\le a<n$. After every write it advances by a fixed integer stride $s\ge 0$, wrapping around modulo $n$. Let $x_k$ be the slot after $k$ advances:

$$x_k \equiv a + ks \pmod n,\qquad 0\le x_k<n,\quad k\ge 0.$$

A **return** at step $k>0$ means $x_k = a$ as a residue modulo $n$. It does not mean that two numerical representatives merely look alike.

Let $g=\gcd(n,s)$, with the convention $\gcd(n,0)=n$.

**Claim.**
1. The least positive return time is $n/g$.
2. The slots visited from $a$ are exactly those congruent to $a$ modulo $g$. There are $n/g$ of them.
3. Over all starting slots, the schedule splits the slots into $g$ disjoint cycles, one for each residue class modulo $g$.

## Proof

Write $n = g\,n'$ and $s = g\,s'$. Then $\gcd(n',s')=1$. (If $s=0$, then $g=n$, $n'=1$ and $s'=0$, and this still holds.)

**Step 1: When does a return occur?** A return at step $k$ means $n \mid ks$. Dividing both sides by $g$, this is equivalent to $n' \mid ks'$.

**Step 2: A return forces $n' \mid k$.** Because $\gcd(n',s')=1$, there are integers $u,v$ with
$$u\,n' + v\,s' = 1.$$
Multiply by $k$:
$$k = u\,n'k + v\,(ks').$$
The first term is a multiple of $n'$. The second is a multiple of $n'$ whenever $n' \mid ks'$. So if there is a return at step $k$, then $n' \mid k$.

**Step 3: The return time is $n'$.** Step 2 shows that every positive return time is a multiple of $n'$, so none is smaller than $n'$. Conversely, $k=n'$ is a return, since $n'\,s = n'\,g\,s' = n\,s'$ is a multiple of $n$. Hence the least positive return time is $n' = n/g$.

**Step 4: The first $n'$ slots are distinct.** Suppose $x_i = x_j$ with $0\le i<j<n'$. Then $(j-i)s \equiv 0 \pmod n$, so $j-i$ is a positive return time. But $0<j-i<n'$, which contradicts Step 3. So $x_0,\dots,x_{n'-1}$ are pairwise distinct. Since $x_{k+n'}=x_k$ for all $k$, no further slots are ever visited, and the visited set has exactly $n'$ elements.

**Step 5: The visited set is a congruence class modulo $g$.** Since $g\mid n$, reduction modulo $g$ is well defined on residues modulo $n$. Since $g\mid s$, we have $x_k \equiv a + ks \equiv a \pmod g$. So every visited slot is congruent to $a$ modulo $g$. Exactly $n/g$ slots in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ lie in this class, and Step 4 gives $n/g$ distinct visited slots. The visited slots therefore fill the whole class.

**Step 6: The cycles.** The argument above applies to any starting slot. The $g$ congruence classes modulo $g$ partition $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, and each class is the cycle traversed from any of its members. So the schedule has $g$ disjoint cycles, each of length $n/g$.

## Edge cases

- **$s=0$.** Then $g=n$, the return time is $1$, and each of the $n$ cycles is a single slot.
- **$n=1$.** There is only slot $0$, so $g=1$ and the return time is $1$, whatever the value of $s$.
- **General.** The argument never divides by $s$, never assumes $s<n$, and never treats a rotation of the labeled slots as a different schedule. The slot labels are fixed, and only the residue of $a+ks$ modulo $n$ matters.

response:
Let \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\) and \(q=(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\) be probability vectors on the same \(m\geq1\) labeled outcomes, allowing zero entries. A coupling of two synthetic labels \(U,V\) is a nonnegative array \(J=(J_{ij})\) with row sums \(p_i\) and column sums \(q_j\). Its agreement probability is
\[
\Pr(U=V)=\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}.
\]
We show that
\[
\max_J\Pr(U=V)
=\sum_{i=1}^m\min(p_i,q_i)
=1-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m|p_i-q_i|.
\]
The maximization ranges over all couplings with these marginals, without any independence requirement.

For every coupling, nonnegativity and the marginal constraints imply \(J_{ii}\leq p_i\) and \(J_{ii}\leq q_i\). Hence
\[
\sum_i J_{ii}\leq\sum_i\min(p_i,q_i).
\]
To attain this bound, define
\[
c_i=\min(p_i,q_i),\qquad
\alpha_i=p_i-c_i,\qquad
\beta_i=q_i-c_i,\qquad
r=1-\sum_i c_i.
\]
The residual masses \(\alpha_i,\beta_i\) are nonnegative and satisfy
\[
\sum_i\alpha_i=\sum_i\beta_i=r,
\qquad
\alpha_i\beta_i=0\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
They represent unused probability mass after allocating \(c_i\) to agreement at label \(i\).

If \(r>0\), set
\[
J_{ij}=c_i\mathbf 1\{i=j\}+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_j}{r}.
\]
All entries are nonnegative, and the finite sums give
\[
\sum_jJ_{ij}
=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_j\beta_j
=c_i+\alpha_i=p_i,
\qquad
\sum_iJ_{ij}
=c_j+\frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_i\alpha_i
=c_j+\beta_j=q_j.
\]
Thus \(J\) is a coupling. Moreover, \(\alpha_i\beta_i=0\) gives \(J_{ii}=c_i\), so its agreement probability attains the upper bound. The residual product constructs one admissible joint distribution; it imposes no independence condition on the couplings being optimized and does not imply that the resulting labels \(U,V\) are independent.

If \(r=0\), the nonnegative residuals all vanish, so \(p_i=q_i=c_i\). Set \(J_{ii}=p_i\) and \(J_{ij}=0\) for \(i\ne j\). This attains agreement probability \(1\) without residual division. At the other boundary, \(r=1\), all \(c_i=0\), so the distributions have disjoint supports and the maximum agreement is \(0\); the construction above remains valid.

Finally,
\[
|p_i-q_i|=p_i+q_i-2c_i,
\]
and summing over labels yields
\[
\sum_i c_i=1-\frac12\sum_i|p_i-q_i|.
\]
Zero-probability labels remain included throughout, and the argument also covers \(m=1\). The optimization changes only how the two labels are paired, keeping both marginal probability vectors fixed.

response:
Let \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\) and \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\) be probability vectors on the same \(m\geq 1\) labeled outcomes. Entries may be zero. We want to pair labels \(U\) and \(V\) to maximize their probability of agreement while keeping their marginal distributions fixed.

A coupling is an array \(J_{ij}\geq 0\) with
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=p_i,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij}=q_j.
\]
Here \(J_{ij}=\Pr(U=i,V=j)\), so
\[
\Pr(U=V)=\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}.
\]
We will show that
\[
\max_J \Pr(U=V)
=\sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i)
=1-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m |p_i-q_i|.
\]

For any coupling, nonnegativity and the marginal constraints give
\[
J_{ii}\leq \sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=p_i,
\qquad
J_{ii}\leq \sum_{j=1}^m J_{ji}=q_i.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\Pr(U=V)\leq \sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i).
\]

To attain this bound, first assign as much mass as possible to each diagonal entry. Write
\[
c_i=\min(p_i,q_i),\qquad
\alpha_i=p_i-c_i,\qquad
\beta_i=q_i-c_i,\qquad
r=1-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i.
\]
The residuals \(\alpha_i\) and \(\beta_i\) are unused probability mass, not negative observations. They satisfy
\[
\alpha_i,\beta_i\geq 0,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=\sum_{i=1}^m\beta_i=r,
\qquad
\alpha_i\beta_i=0.
\]
The last identity holds because \(c_i\) equals at least one of \(p_i\) and \(q_i\).

If \(r>0\), define
\[
J_{ij}=c_i\mathbf 1\{i=j\}+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_j}{r}.
\]
Every entry is nonnegative, and the row and column sums are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}
&=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j
=c_i+\alpha_i
=p_i,\\
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij}
&=c_j+\frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i
=c_j+\beta_j
=q_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover,
\[
J_{ii}=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_i}{r}=c_i.
\]
Thus this coupling attains the upper bound. The product term is a device for constructing one coupling. It imposes no independence requirement on the couplings being optimized and does not imply that the resulting \(U\) and \(V\) are independent in general.

If \(r=0\), the nonnegative residuals all vanish, so \(p_i=q_i=c_i\). Set
\[
J_{ij}=p_i\mathbf 1\{i=j\}.
\]
This coupling has the required marginals and agreement probability \(1\), with no division by \(r\).

Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^m |p_i-q_i|
&=\sum_{i=1}^m (p_i+q_i-2c_i)\\
&=2-2\sum_{i=1}^m c_i,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves the alternative formula. At the other boundary, when the supports are disjoint, every \(c_i=0\) and \(r=1\), so the maximum agreement is \(0\). Zero-probability labels require no special treatment. When \(m=1\), both probability vectors equal \((1)\), and the \(r=0\) construction applies. Throughout, only the pairing changes, while both probability vectors remain fixed.

response:
Let \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\) and \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\) be probability vectors on the same \(m\geq 1\) labeled outcomes. Entries may be zero. A coupling is a nonnegative array \(J=(J_{ij})\) with
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=p_i,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij}=q_j.
\]
It specifies a joint distribution for labels \(U,V\), whose agreement probability is
\[
\Pr(U=V)=\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}.
\]
We will show that
\[
\max_J \Pr(U=V)
=\sum_{i=1}^m\min(p_i,q_i)
=1-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m|p_i-q_i|.
\]
The maximum is over all couplings with these fixed marginals, with no independence requirement.

For any coupling, nonnegativity and the marginal constraints give
\[
J_{ii}\leq \sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=p_i,
\qquad
J_{ii}\leq \sum_{j=1}^m J_{ji}=q_i.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\Pr(U=V)\leq \sum_{i=1}^m\min(p_i,q_i).
\]

To attain this bound, assign as much mass as possible to each diagonal entry. Write
\[
c_i=\min(p_i,q_i),\qquad
\alpha_i=p_i-c_i,\qquad
\beta_i=q_i-c_i,\qquad
r=1-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i.
\]
Here \(\alpha_i\) and \(\beta_i\) are the unused probability masses after assigning \(c_i\) to \(J_{ii}\). They are nonnegative, and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i
=\sum_{i=1}^m\beta_i=r.
\]
For each \(i\), at least one of \(p_i-c_i\) and \(q_i-c_i\) is zero, so
\[
\alpha_i\beta_i=0.
\]

If \(r>0\), distribute the remaining mass by setting
\[
J_{ij}=c_i\mathbf 1\{i=j\}+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_j}{r}.
\]
All entries are nonnegative. The row and column sums are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}
&=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j
=c_i+\alpha_i
=p_i,\\
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij}
&=c_j+\frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i
=c_j+\beta_j
=q_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(J\) is a coupling. Its diagonal entries satisfy
\[
J_{ii}=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_i}{r}=c_i,
\]
and hence it attains the upper bound. The product term constructs the residual part of this particular coupling. It neither requires independence in other couplings nor implies that \(U\) and \(V\) are independent under the full joint distribution \(J\).

If \(r=0\), the nonnegative residuals have sum zero, so \(\alpha_i=\beta_i=0\) for every \(i\). Thus \(p_i=q_i=c_i\), and we set
\[
J_{ij}=p_i\mathbf 1\{i=j\}.
\]
This coupling has agreement probability one and requires no division by \(r\).

Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^m|p_i-q_i|
&=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(p_i+q_i-2\min(p_i,q_i)\bigr)\\
&=2-2\sum_{i=1}^m c_i,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves the alternative formula. At the other boundary, when the distributions have disjoint supports, every \(c_i=0\), so \(r=1\) and the maximum agreement is zero. Zero-probability labels need not be removed, and the one-label case is included in the \(r=0\) construction. The optimization changes only how the two labels are paired, keeping both marginal probability vectors fixed.

response:
**Maximal agreement of paired labels with fixed marginals**

*Setting.* Let $p_1,\dots,p_m$ and $q_1,\dots,q_m$ be probability vectors on the same $m$ labeled outcomes, with $m \ge 1$. Entries may be zero. A *coupling* of $p$ and $q$ is an $m \times m$ array $J_{ij} \ge 0$ with row sums $\sum_j J_{ij} = p_i$ and column sums $\sum_i J_{ij} = q_j$. Any such array defines a pair of labels $U, V$ on a common probability space with $\Pr(U = i, V = j) = J_{ij}$, so that $U$ has distribution $p$ and $V$ has distribution $q$. The agreement probability of the pair is $\Pr(U = V) = \sum_i J_{ii}$.

*Claim.* Over all couplings of $p$ and $q$, the largest attainable agreement is
$$
\sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i, q_i) \;=\; 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^m |p_i - q_i| .
$$

*Upper bound.* Fix any coupling $J$. Since every entry is nonnegative, the diagonal entry $J_{ii}$ is at most its row sum and at most its column sum, so $J_{ii} \le \min(p_i, q_i)$ for each $i$. Summing over $i$ gives $\sum_i J_{ii} \le \sum_i \min(p_i, q_i)$. This holds for every coupling, with no assumption about how $U$ and $V$ are related beyond their marginals.

*Construction attaining the bound.* Write
$$
c_i = \min(p_i, q_i), \qquad \alpha_i = p_i - c_i, \qquad \beta_i = q_i - c_i, \qquad r = 1 - \sum_i c_i .
$$
Each $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ is nonnegative, and $\sum_i \alpha_i = \sum_i p_i - \sum_i c_i = r = \sum_i \beta_i$. For every label $i$, at least one of $\alpha_i, \beta_i$ is zero, because $c_i$ equals whichever of $p_i, q_i$ is smaller; hence $\alpha_i \beta_i = 0$. The residual vectors $\alpha$ and $\beta$ record probability mass left over after the shared mass $c$ is set aside. They are not negative observations and are not themselves probability vectors unless $r = 1$.

*Case $r > 0$.* Define
$$
J_{ij} = c_i\,\mathbf{1}\{i = j\} + \frac{\alpha_i \beta_j}{r}.
$$
Every entry is nonnegative. The row sums are
$$
\sum_j J_{ij} = c_i + \frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_j \beta_j = c_i + \alpha_i = p_i,
$$
and the column sums are
$$
\sum_i J_{ij} = c_j + \frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_i \alpha_i = c_j + \beta_j = q_j,
$$
so $J$ is a coupling of $p$ and $q$. On the diagonal, $J_{ii} = c_i + \alpha_i \beta_i / r = c_i$, because $\alpha_i \beta_i = 0$. Therefore $\sum_i J_{ii} = \sum_i c_i$, which matches the upper bound.

The product term $\alpha_i \beta_j / r$ is a device for filling in the off-diagonal mass so that the row and column constraints close. It does not assert that $U$ and $V$ are independent, nor that the coupling being optimized has any product structure. In this coupling the two labels are, in fact, as dependent as the marginals allow: whenever $U$ lands on shared mass it equals $V$ with certainty. Labels with $p_i = 0$ or $q_i = 0$ require no special treatment; they simply contribute $c_i = 0$ and at most one nonzero residual.

*Case $r = 0$.* Then $\sum_i c_i = 1$, so $c_i = p_i = q_i$ for every $i$ and both residual vectors vanish. Set $J_{ii} = p_i$ and $J_{ij} = 0$ for $i \ne j$. Row and column sums are $p_i = q_i$, every entry is nonnegative, and the diagonal sum is $\sum_i p_i = 1 = \sum_i c_i$. No division by $r$ occurs, and the bound is attained with $U = V$ almost surely.

*Alternative form.* For each $i$, $\max(p_i, q_i) + \min(p_i, q_i) = p_i + q_i$ and $\max(p_i, q_i) - \min(p_i, q_i) = |p_i - q_i|$, so $|p_i - q_i| = p_i + q_i - 2c_i$. Summing over $i$,
$$
\sum_i |p_i - q_i| = 1 + 1 - 2\sum_i c_i = 2\Bigl(1 - \sum_i c_i\Bigr),
$$
which gives $\sum_i c_i = 1 - \tfrac12 \sum_i |p_i - q_i|$, and also identifies $r$ as $\tfrac12 \sum_i |p_i - q_i|$.

*Boundary remarks.* If $p$ and $q$ have disjoint supports, then $c_i = 0$ for every $i$, so $r = 1$ and the largest achievable agreement is zero; the construction in the case $r > 0$ then reduces to $J_{ij} = p_i q_j$. If $m = 1$, then $p_1 = q_1 = 1$, $r = 0$, and the agreement is $1$. Zero entries in either vector and the one-label space are covered by the statement as written and need no separate argument.

*Interpretation.* The optimization is over the pairing of the two labels, that is, over the joint array $J$, with both marginal distributions held fixed throughout. Neither $p$ nor $q$ is altered. The quantity $\sum_i \min(p_i, q_i)$ is thus the best agreement rate one could report for synthetic labels drawn from $p$ against reference labels drawn from $q$ under any admissible pairing, and $\tfrac12 \sum_i |p_i - q_i|$ is the unavoidable disagreement.

Let $p_1,\dots,p_m$ and $q_1,\dots,q_m$ be probability vectors on the same $m$ labeled outcomes, where $m \ge 1$ and entries may be zero. A coupling is an array $J_{ij} \ge 0$ with
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij} = p_i \quad \text{for every } i,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij} = q_j \quad \text{for every } j .
\]
It describes two labels $U, V$ on a common probability space with $\Pr(U=i,\,V=j) = J_{ij}$, and their agreement probability is $\sum_i J_{ii}$. We claim that the largest agreement attainable over all couplings is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i) \;=\; 1 - \tfrac12 \sum_{i=1}^m |p_i - q_i| .
\]

**Upper bound.** Fix any coupling $J$ and any label $i$. Because every entry is nonnegative, the diagonal entry is at most its row sum and at most its column sum:
\[
J_{ii} \;\le\; \sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij} = p_i,
\qquad
J_{ii} \;\le\; \sum_{k=1}^m J_{ki} = q_i ,
\]
so $J_{ii} \le \min(p_i,q_i)$. Summing over $i$,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii} \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i).
\]

**Construction.** Write
\[
c_i = \min(p_i,q_i), \qquad \alpha_i = p_i - c_i, \qquad \beta_i = q_i - c_i, \qquad r = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^m c_i .
\]
The residuals $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are nonnegative and record unused probability mass at label $i$, not negative observations. They have the same total,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i = \sum_{i=1}^m p_i - \sum_{i=1}^m c_i = r,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m \beta_i = \sum_{i=1}^m q_i - \sum_{i=1}^m c_i = r ,
\]
and $\alpha_i \beta_i = 0$ for every $i$, because $c_i$ equals whichever of $p_i, q_i$ is smaller and that residual is zero.

*Case $r > 0$.* Define
\[
J_{ij} = c_i\,\mathbf 1\{i=j\} + \frac{\alpha_i \beta_j}{r} .
\]
Every entry is nonnegative. The row and column sums are the required marginals:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij} &= c_i + \frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_{j=1}^m \beta_j = c_i + \alpha_i = p_i, \\
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij} &= c_j + \frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i = c_j + \beta_j = q_j .
\end{aligned}
\]
On the diagonal, $\alpha_i\beta_i = 0$ gives
\[
J_{ii} = c_i + \frac{\alpha_i \beta_i}{r} = c_i,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii} = \sum_{i=1}^m c_i ,
\]
which attains the upper bound. The product $\alpha_i\beta_j/r$ is a device for writing down one joint distribution with the right marginals. It does not assert that every coupling, or even this coupling as a whole, has independent coordinates.

*Case $r = 0$.* Then $\sum_i c_i = 1 = \sum_i p_i$ with $c_i \le p_i$ for every $i$, so $c_i = p_i$ for every $i$, and likewise $c_i = q_i$. Set $J_{ii} = p_i = q_i$ and all off-diagonal entries to zero. The row and column sums are $p_i$ and $q_i$, and the agreement is $\sum_i p_i = 1 = \sum_i c_i$. No division by $r$ is needed.

**Alternative formula.** For each $i$, since $c_i$ is the smaller of $p_i, q_i$,
\[
|p_i - q_i| = \max(p_i,q_i) - \min(p_i,q_i) = p_i + q_i - 2c_i .
\]
Summing over $i$ and using $\sum_i p_i = \sum_i q_i = 1$,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m |p_i - q_i| = 2 - 2\sum_{i=1}^m c_i,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m c_i = 1 - \tfrac12 \sum_{i=1}^m |p_i - q_i| .
\]

**Remarks on special cases.** If the two distributions have disjoint supports, every $c_i$ is zero and the largest agreement is zero. Labels with zero probability, and the case $m = 1$, require no change to the statement or the proof. Throughout, the optimization is over how the two labels are paired, with each marginal distribution held fixed; it does not change either probability vector.

**Setting.** Let $p=(p_1,\dots,p_m)$ and $q=(q_1,\dots,q_m)$ be probability vectors on the same $m\ge 1$ labeled outcomes, so that $p_i\ge 0$, $q_i\ge 0$, and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=\sum_{i=1}^m q_i=1 .
\]
Entries may be zero. A coupling of $p$ and $q$ is an $m\times m$ array $J=(J_{ij})$ with
\[
J_{ij}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=p_i\ \text{ for every } i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij}=q_j\ \text{ for every } j .
\]
Such an array is the joint distribution of two labels $U,V$ on a common probability space with $\mathbb P(U=i)=p_i$ and $\mathbb P(V=j)=q_j$, and the two labels agree with probability
\[
\mathbb P(U=V)=\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}.
\]
We want the largest agreement probability over all couplings with these fixed marginals.

**Claim.** For every coupling $J$ of $p$ and $q$,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}\;\le\;\sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i)\;=\;1-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m |p_i-q_i| ,
\]
and there is a coupling for which equality holds.

**Upper bound.** Fix a coupling $J$ and a label $i$. Every entry of $J$ is nonnegative, so dropping the off-diagonal terms from the $i$th row sum and from the $i$th column sum gives
\[
J_{ii}\le \sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=p_i,
\qquad
J_{ii}\le \sum_{k=1}^m J_{ki}=q_i .
\]
Hence $J_{ii}\le \min(p_i,q_i)$ for each $i$, and summing over $i$ gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}\le \sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i).
\]

**The residual decomposition.** To build a coupling that attains this bound, write
\[
c_i=\min(p_i,q_i),\qquad \alpha_i=p_i-c_i,\qquad \beta_i=q_i-c_i,\qquad r=1-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i .
\]
Since $c_i\le p_i$ and $c_i\le q_i$, all of $\alpha_i$, $\beta_i$, and $r$ are nonnegative. The residuals $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are the parts of $p_i$ and $q_i$ not yet placed on the diagonal; they are leftover probability mass, not negative observations. Both residual vectors have the same total,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i=1-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i=r,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m \beta_i=\sum_{i=1}^m q_i-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i=r .
\]
Moreover, for every label $i$,
\[
\alpha_i\beta_i=0 ,
\]
because either $p_i\le q_i$, in which case $c_i=p_i$ and $\alpha_i=0$, or $p_i>q_i$, in which case $c_i=q_i$ and $\beta_i=0$.

**Case $r>0$.** Define
\[
J_{ij}=c_i\,\mathbf 1\{i=j\}+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_j}{r},\qquad 1\le i,j\le m .
\]
Each entry is a sum of nonnegative terms, so $J_{ij}\ge 0$. The row sums are
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_{j=1}^m \beta_j=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{r}\cdot r=c_i+\alpha_i=p_i ,
\]
and the column sums are
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij}=c_j+\frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i=c_j+\beta_j=q_j .
\]
So $J$ is a coupling of $p$ and $q$. On the diagonal, the residual product at the same label vanishes, so
\[
J_{ii}=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_i}{r}=c_i ,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i=\sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i).
\]
This coupling attains the upper bound. The product form $\alpha_i\beta_j/r$ is only a device for placing the off-diagonal mass so that the marginals come out right. It does not say that $U$ and $V$ are independent under $J$, and it says nothing about the coordinates of any other coupling.

**Case $r=0$.** Then $\sum_i c_i=1$. Since $c_i\le p_i$ for every $i$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$, this forces $c_i=p_i$ for every $i$, and by the same argument with $q$, $c_i=q_i$. Thus $p=q$. Set
\[
J_{ii}=p_i=q_i,\qquad J_{ij}=0 \text{ for } i\ne j .
\]
The $i$th row sum and column sum are both $p_i=q_i$, every entry is nonnegative, and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m J_{ii}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i .
\]
No division by $r$ is needed, and the bound is again attained.

**The alternative formula.** For any two numbers, $\max(p_i,q_i)+\min(p_i,q_i)=p_i+q_i$ and $|p_i-q_i|=\max(p_i,q_i)-\min(p_i,q_i)$, so
\[
|p_i-q_i|=p_i+q_i-2c_i .
\]
Summing over $i$,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m |p_i-q_i|=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i+\sum_{i=1}^m q_i-2\sum_{i=1}^m c_i=2-2\sum_{i=1}^m c_i ,
\]

## Proposition

Let $p=(p_1,\dots,p_m)$ and $q=(q_1,\dots,q_m)$ be probability vectors on the same $m$ labeled outcomes, with $m\ge 1$. Entries may be zero. A coupling is an array $J=(J_{ij})$ with $J_{ij}\ge 0$, $\sum_j J_{ij}=p_i$ for each $i$, and $\sum_i J_{ij}=q_j$ for each $j$. It describes labels $U,V$ on a common probability space, with $\Pr(U=i,V=j)=J_{ij}$. The agreement probability of $J$ is $\sum_i J_{ii}$.

**Claim.** The largest agreement over all couplings is attained and equals

$$
\max_J \sum_i J_{ii}=\sum_i \min(p_i,q_i)=1-\tfrac12\sum_i |p_i-q_i|.
$$

## Setup

Define

$$
c_i=\min(p_i,q_i),\qquad \alpha_i=p_i-c_i,\qquad \beta_i=q_i-c_i,\qquad r=1-\sum_i c_i.
$$

These quantities have the following properties.

- Since $c_i\le p_i$ and $c_i\le q_i$, we have $\alpha_i\ge 0$ and $\beta_i\ge 0$.
- For each $i$, either $p_i\le q_i$, in which case $c_i=p_i$ and $\alpha_i=0$, or $q_i<p_i$, in which case $c_i=q_i$ and $\beta_i=0$. Hence $\alpha_i\beta_i=0$ for every $i$.
- $\sum_i\alpha_i=\sum_i p_i-\sum_i c_i=1-\sum_i c_i=r$, and likewise $\sum_i\beta_i=r$. Since $\alpha\ge 0$, this gives $r\ge 0$.

The vectors $\alpha$ and $\beta$ record probability mass in each marginal that is not matched at the same label. They are nonnegative masses, not signed deviations.

## Step 1: Upper bound for every coupling

Let $J$ be any coupling and fix $i$. Because all entries are nonnegative,

$$
J_{ii}\le \sum_j J_{ij}=p_i,\qquad J_{ii}\le \sum_k J_{ki}=q_i.
$$

Therefore $J_{ii}\le \min(p_i,q_i)=c_i$. Summing over $i$ gives $\sum_i J_{ii}\le \sum_i c_i$. This step uses only nonnegativity and the marginal sums.

## Step 2: Attaining the bound when $r>0$

Define

$$
J_{ij}=c_i\,\mathbf 1\{i=j\}+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_j}{r}.
$$

This is well defined because $r>0$. We check the required properties.

- **Nonnegativity.** Each term is a nonnegative number divided by a positive number.
- **Row sums.** $\sum_j J_{ij}=c_i+\alpha_i\cdot\frac{\sum_j\beta_j}{r}=c_i+\alpha_i=p_i$.
- **Column sums.** $\sum_i J_{ij}=c_j+\frac{\big(\sum_i\alpha_i\big)\beta_j}{r}=c_j+\beta_j=q_j$.
- **Diagonal.** $J_{ii}=c_i+\alpha_i\beta_i/r=c_i$, because $\alpha_i\beta_i=0$.

So $J$ is a coupling, and its agreement is $\sum_i c_i$. Combined with Step 1, this is the maximum.

Labels with zero probability need no separate treatment. If $p_i=0$, then $c_i=\alpha_i=0$, so row $i$ of $J$ is identically zero. If $q_j=0$, column $j$ is identically zero by the same argument.

The term $\alpha_i\beta_j/r$ is one additive piece of the array. It is a device for placing the unmatched off-diagonal mass so that the marginals are correct. The optimality argument uses only nonnegativity and the row and column sums. Nothing in it requires $J$ to factor, and $J$ is not asserted to have independent coordinates.

## Step 3: The case $r=0$

If $r=0$, then $\sum_i\alpha_i=0$ with each $\alpha_i\ge 0$, so $\alpha_i=0$ for all $i$. Similarly $\beta_i=0$ for all $i$. Hence $p_i=c_i=q_i$ for every $i$, so $p=q$.

Set $J_{ii}=p_i$ and $J_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$. The row sums are $p_i$, the column sums are $q_i=p_i$, and the agreement is $\sum_i p_i=\sum_i c_i$. No division by $r$ occurs in this case.

## Step 4: The alternative formula

For real numbers $a,b$, we have $\max(a,b)=a+b-\min(a,b)$, so $|a-b|=\max(a,b)-\min(a,b)=a+b-2\min(a,b)$. Setting $a=p_i$ and $b=q_i$ and summing over $i$ gives

$$
\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_i p_i+\sum_i q_i-2\sum_i c_i=2-2\sum_i c_i,
$$

using $\sum_i p_i=\sum_i q_i=1$. Rearranging gives $\sum_i c_i=1-\tfrac12\sum_i|p_i-q_i|$.

## Boundary cases

- **Disjoint supports.** For every $i$, $p_i=0$ or $q_i=0$, so $c_i=0$ and the maximal agreement is $0$. This agrees with the alternative formula, since $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_i p_i+\sum_i q_i=2$.
- **One label ($m=1$).** Here $p_1=q_1=1$, so $c_1=1$ and $r=0$. Step 3 gives $J_{11}=1$, and the maximal agreement is $1=1-\tfrac12\cdot 0$.
- **Zero entries.** The minimum handles zero entries directly. The only division in the construction is by $r$, and it occurs only when $r>0$.

## Conclusion

Step 1 shows that no coupling has agreement above $\sum_i\min(p_i,q_i)$. Steps 2 and 3 exhibit a coupling that attains this value in every case, and Step 4 gives the equivalent form $1-\tfrac12\sum_i|p_i-q_i|$. The comparison optimizes only how the two labels are paired. It keeps each marginal $p$ and $q$ fixed and does not change either probability vector.

response:
# Maximal agreement probability for paired labels

**Setup.** Let p = (p_1,…,p_m) and q = (q_1,…,q_m) be probability vectors on the same m labeled outcomes, with m ≥ 1. Entries may be zero. A coupling is an array J = (J_ij) with J_ij ≥ 0, Σ_j J_ij = p_i for every i, and Σ_i J_ij = q_j for every j. It is the joint distribution of two labels (U, V) on a common probability space with U ~ p and V ~ q. Their agreement probability is P(U = V) = Σ_i J_ii.

**Claim.** The maximum of Σ_i J_ii over all couplings J is

Σ_i min(p_i, q_i) = 1 − ½ Σ_i |p_i − q_i|.

Only the pairing of the two labels is optimized. Both marginals stay fixed, and no independence condition is imposed on the couplings being compared.

## Upper bound

Fix any coupling J. Since all entries are nonnegative, J_ii is at most its row sum and at most its column sum:

J_ii ≤ Σ_j J_ij = p_i,  J_ii ≤ Σ_k J_ki = q_i.

Hence J_ii ≤ min(p_i, q_i). Summing over i gives Σ_i J_ii ≤ Σ_i min(p_i, q_i).

## Construction attaining the bound

Define

- c_i = min(p_i, q_i),
- α_i = p_i − c_i ≥ 0,
- β_i = q_i − c_i ≥ 0,
- r = 1 − Σ_i c_i.

Here α_i and β_i are the probability mass of p and q at label i not used for agreement. They are not negative observations. Two facts follow.

1. **Equal residual totals.** Σ_i α_i = Σ_i p_i − Σ_i c_i = r, and likewise Σ_i β_i = r. Because r is a sum of nonnegative terms, r ≥ 0.
2. **Disjoint residual supports.** c_i equals p_i or q_i, so α_i = 0 or β_i = 0. Therefore α_i β_i = 0 for every i.

**Case r > 0.** Define

J_ij = c_i 1{i = j} + α_i β_j / r.

- *Nonnegativity:* every term is nonnegative.
- *Row sums:* Σ_j J_ij = c_i + (α_i / r) Σ_j β_j = c_i + α_i = p_i.
- *Column sums:* Σ_i J_ij = c_j + (β_j / r) Σ_i α_i = c_j + β_j = q_j.
- *Diagonal:* J_ii = c_i + α_i β_i / r = c_i, by fact 2.

So J is a coupling with Σ_i J_ii = Σ_i c_i, which equals the upper bound.

The product α_i β_j / r is only a device for spreading the unused mass of p over the unused mass of q. It does not make U and V independent. J is a mixture of a diagonal part, which forces agreement, and a residual product part. Neither J nor any other optimal coupling is claimed to have independent coordinates.

**Case r = 0.** Then Σ_i c_i = 1 = Σ_i p_i, and c_i ≤ p_i for every i, so c_i = p_i for all i. The same argument with q gives c_i = q_i, hence p = q. Set J_ii = p_i = q_i and J_ij = 0 for i ≠ j. This is a coupling with row and column sums p_i = q_i, and its agreement is 1 = Σ_i c_i. No division by r occurs. The case m = 1 always falls here, since p = q = (1).

In both cases the maximum equals Σ_i min(p_i, q_i).

## The alternative formula

For each i, |p_i − q_i| = p_i + q_i − 2c_i, because max(p_i, q_i) = p_i + q_i − c_i and |p_i − q_i| = max(p_i, q_i) − c_i. Summing over i gives

Σ_i |p_i − q_i| = 1 + 1 − 2 Σ_i c_i,

so Σ_i c_i = 1 − ½ Σ_i |p_i − q_i|. ∎

## Boundary cases and zero entries

- **Zero-probability labels** need no special treatment. If p_i = 0 or q_i = 0, then c_i = 0 and the formulas above apply unchanged. The construction gives J_ij = 0 for every j when p_i = 0, and J_ij = 0 for every i when q_j = 0.
- **Identical distributions (r = 0)** give maximal agreement 1, using the diagonal coupling above.
- **Disjoint supports** give c_i = 0 for all i, so r = 1 and α = p, β = q. The construction is then J_ij = p_i q_j, and the maximal agreement is 0. Here the optimal coupling happens to be the independent one, but only because the supports are disjoint.
- **A one-label space** has p = q = (1), which is the r = 0 case with agreement 1.

response:
Let $p=(p_1,\dots,p_m)$ and $q=(q_1,\dots,q_m)$ be probability vectors on the same $m\ge 1$ labeled outcomes. Some entries may be zero. A coupling is an array $J=(J_{ij})$ with $J_{ij}\ge 0$ and

$$
\sum_{j=1}^m J_{ij}=p_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m J_{ij}=q_j .
$$

It describes two labels $U,V$ on a common probability space with $\Pr(U=i,V=j)=J_{ij}$, so $U$ has distribution $p$, $V$ has distribution $q$, and the agreement probability is $\Pr(U=V)=\sum_i J_{ii}$. We claim that the largest agreement probability over all couplings is

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m \min(p_i,q_i)\;=\;1-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m |p_i-q_i| .
$$

The comparison varies how the two labels are paired. Both marginals stay fixed, and neither probability vector changes.

**Upper bound.** Let $J$ be any coupling. Since all entries are nonnegative, $J_{ii}$ is at most its row sum and at most its column sum:

$$
J_{ii}\le \sum_{j}J_{ij}=p_i,\qquad J_{ii}\le \sum_{j}J_{ji}=q_i .
$$

Hence $J_{ii}\le \min(p_i,q_i)$, and summing over $i$ gives

$$
\Pr(U=V)=\sum_i J_{ii}\le \sum_i\min(p_i,q_i).
$$

**Construction attaining the bound.** Define

$$
c_i=\min(p_i,q_i),\qquad \alpha_i=p_i-c_i,\qquad \beta_i=q_i-c_i,\qquad r=1-\sum_i c_i .
$$

Then $c_i,\alpha_i,\beta_i\ge 0$. The quantities $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are the parts of $p_i$ and $q_i$ not matched by $c_i$, that is, unused probability mass, not negative observations. Two facts about them are used below. First, both residual vectors have total mass $r$:

$$
\sum_i\alpha_i=\sum_i p_i-\sum_i c_i=r,\qquad \sum_i\beta_i=\sum_i q_i-\sum_i c_i=r .
$$

Second, $\alpha_i\beta_i=0$ for every $i$, because $c_i$ equals $p_i$ or $q_i$, so $\alpha_i=0$ or $\beta_i=0$.

*Case $r>0$.* Define

$$
J_{ij}=c_i\,\mathbf 1\{i=j\}+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_j}{r}.
$$

All entries are nonnegative. Summing over $j$ gives

$$
\sum_j J_{ij}=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_j\beta_j=c_i+\alpha_i=p_i,
$$

and summing over $i$ gives

$$
\sum_i J_{ij}=c_j+\frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_i\alpha_i=c_j+\beta_j=q_j .
$$

So $J$ is a coupling. Its diagonal entries are

$$
J_{ii}=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_i}{r}=c_i,
$$

because $\alpha_i\beta_i=0$. Therefore $\sum_i J_{ii}=\sum_i c_i$, which equals the upper bound. The product $\alpha_i\beta_j/r$ is only a device for building one joint distribution with the required marginals. It does not make the coordinates of every coupling independent, and it does not make the coordinates of $J$ itself independent, since $J$ also contains the diagonal term.

*Case $r=0$.* Then $\sum_i\alpha_i=0$ with each $\alpha_i\ge 0$, so every $\alpha_i=0$. The same holds for $\beta_i$. Hence $p_i=c_i=q_i$ for all $i$, so $p=q$. Set $J_{ii}=p_i=q_i$ and all other entries to zero. The row and column sums are $p_i$ and $q_i$, and $\sum_i J_{ii}=1=\sum_i c_i$. No division by $r$ occurs.

In both cases the upper bound is attained, so the maximum agreement is $\sum_i\min(p_i,q_i)$.

**The alternative formula.** For any real numbers $a,b$ we have $|a-b|=a+b-2\min(a,b)$. Thus $|p_i-q_i|=p_i+q_i-2c_i$, and summing over $i$ gives

$$
\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_i p_i+\sum_i q_i-2\sum_i c_i=2-2\sum_i c_i .
$$

Rearranging,

$$
\sum_i\min(p_i,q_i)=1-\frac12\sum_i|p_i-q_i| .
$$

**Boundary cases.** If $p$ and $q$ have disjoint supports, then for each $i$ one of $p_i,q_i$ is zero, so every $c_i=0$, $r=1$, and the largest agreement is $0$. Zero entries need no special treatment, since the construction divides only by $r$, never by an entry of $p$ or $q$. A one-label space ($m=1$) forces $p_1=q_1=1$, so $r=0$ and the case above applies unchanged.

$$
\sum_{j} J_{ij}=p_i \quad\text{for every } i,
\qquad
\sum_{i} J_{ij}=q_j \quad\text{for every } j.
$$

It is the joint law of two labels $U,V$ on a common probability space with $U\sim p$ and $V\sim q$. Their agreement probability is $\Pr(U=V)=\sum_i J_{ii}$. The largest agreement over all couplings is

$$
\max_J \sum_i J_{ii}
=\sum_i \min(p_i,q_i)
=1-\frac12\sum_i |p_i-q_i| .
$$

**Upper bound.** Let $J$ be any coupling. A diagonal entry is at most its row sum and at most its column sum, since all entries are nonnegative:

$$
J_{ii}\le \sum_j J_{ij}=p_i,
\qquad
J_{ii}\le \sum_k J_{ki}=q_i .
$$

Hence $J_{ii}\le c_i$, where $c_i=\min(p_i,q_i)$, and summing over $i$ gives

$$
\sum_i J_{ii}\le \sum_i c_i .
$$

**Residuals.** Define

$$
\alpha_i=p_i-c_i\ge 0,
\qquad
\beta_i=q_i-c_i\ge 0,
\qquad
r=1-\sum_i c_i .
$$

Since $\sum_i p_i=\sum_i q_i=1$,

$$
\sum_i\alpha_i=1-\sum_i c_i=r,
\qquad
\sum_i\beta_i=1-\sum_i c_i=r .
$$

In particular $r\ge 0$. For each $i$, $c_i$ equals $p_i$ or $q_i$, so $\alpha_i=0$ or $\beta_i=0$, and therefore

$$
\alpha_i\beta_i=0 \quad\text{for every } i .
$$

The residuals describe probability mass not yet matched on the diagonal. They are not negative observations.

**Attaining the bound when $r>0$.** Define

$$
J_{ij}=c_i\,\mathbf 1\{i=j\}+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_j}{r}.
$$

All entries are nonnegative. The row sums are

$$
\sum_j J_{ij}
=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{r}\sum_j\beta_j
=c_i+\alpha_i
=p_i ,
$$

and the column sums are

$$
\sum_i J_{ij}
=c_j+\frac{\beta_j}{r}\sum_i\alpha_i
=c_j+\beta_j
=q_j .
$$

So $J$ is a coupling. Its diagonal is

$$
J_{ii}=c_i+\frac{\alpha_i\beta_i}{r}=c_i ,
$$

because $\alpha_i\beta_i=0$. Thus $\sum_i J_{ii}=\sum_i c_i$, which equals the upper bound.

The product $\alpha_i\beta_j/r$ is only a device for placing the leftover mass in one valid joint distribution. It does not make the coordinates of $J$ independent, and it says nothing about the other couplings.

**Attaining the bound when $r=0$.** Here $\sum_i\alpha_i=\sum_i\beta_i=0$ with every term nonnegative, so $\alpha_i=\beta_i=0$ and $p_i=q_i=c_i$ for all $i$. Set $J_{ii}=p_i=q_i$ and all other entries to zero. The row sums are $p_i$, the column sums are $q_j$, and

$$
\sum_i J_{ii}=\sum_i p_i=1=\sum_i c_i .
$$

No division by $r$ occurs.

$$
\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_i p_i+\sum_i q_i-2\sum_i c_i=2-2\sum_i c_i .
$$

$$
\sum_i c_i=1-\frac12\sum_i|p_i-q_i| .
$$

\end{cases}
\]

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_i

\equiv \sum_{j=1}^{c}b_j
\pmod 2.
\]

\[

x_{ic}&\equiv a_i-\sum_{j<c}x_{ij}\pmod 2
&& (i<r),\\

\end{aligned}

&=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{c}x_{ij}
  -\sum_{j<c}\sum_{i=1}^{r}x_{ij}\\
&\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{r}a_i-\sum_{j<c}b_j\\
&\equiv \sum_{j=1}^{c}b_j-\sum_{j<c}b_j\\
&=b_c.
\end{aligned}
\]
The completion is therefore valid.

For a fixed free block, the first \(r-1\) row requirements force the entries \(x_{ic}\), the first \(c-1\) column requirements force the entries \(x_{rj}\), and the last row requirement forces \(x_{rc}\). Hence the valid completion is unique. Conversely, any valid array restricts to one free block, and these same requirements reconstruct its border. Restriction and completion are inverse maps, so every valid array is counted exactly once.

If \(r=1\) or \(c=1\), the free block is empty and has one choice. The same formulas and verification apply with empty sums equal to zero, including when \(r=c=1\). Thus the stated count holds for all positive dimensions. \(\square\)
